"Mr. Waddell.writes in a pleasant and earnest style, sifting the ey.periences he has had in various parts of the country with a Niew to presenting something to the reader which is well wortlscsnsidering.' —Warsington Examiner, June 27th, 1 1891. "The papers are,wrkten from a remarkable knowledge of Scriptune, and recommknd themselves by their quiet earnest- ness of ttyle:"—Scotsmor, March B,3rd, 1891. "With Chia ikey to the character of the work, the pages Which foLlow prove interesting reading, and reveal the author as a close and aprreciative observer of nature, and one who sees sermons in -atones,,books in tii3 running brooks, and good in everything."—Press9n Heregd, April 4th, 1891. div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

MORAL by a Tailor—Things are not what they seam. ALL snobs are todies, and toady to some other snobs. THE man who can't find anything to do is generally afraid he will. A MAN has a right to his opinions as long as he keeps them to himself. PENNSYLVANIA allows a man to marry his mother- in-law, but he doesn't. MASTER of the house—" if any one calls tell them lam not in." Servant of the period—" And what will I tell them if they don't call 7" A CONTRIBUTOR writes :—"A send you a posthu- mans poem. If published, send me two copies." All right—addressed to which place? ONE of the cheerful things about the prevalence of hydrophobia is the statement that Ouida's pets are dogs and that her villa at Florence is filled with them.
SISTERLY! Elder sister—" Oh, you fancy your- self very wise, I daresay, but I could give you a wrinkle or two ! " Younger sister—" No doubt— and never miss them."
EMPLOYER—" Don't you see what's on the door r Pat—" A bit ov paper, sur." Employer—" It says, Please shut the door.' " Pat—" Faith, I didn't bear it, sur." _ .
, JONES, you said you were connected with the fine arts; do you mean that you are a sculptor 2" "No, sir, I don't sculp myself, but I furnish the stone to the man what does."
To say that a procession was three hours in pas- sing a given point dosen't necessarily show that it was a very long procession, since the given point might have been a public-house.

Mns. ELBERON—"It seems to me Mrs. Exeter wears loud colours." Mr. Elberon—" Be charitable, my dear. Perhaps you don't know that poor Mrs. Exeter is almost totally deaf." These modern inventions are well enough in their way, but it is quite useless to talk of them seriously to the autograph collector who has sent a cleverly couched query to some public man, and receives a prompt answer written with a "type-writer." "Now," said the irate mother to her family of one boy and four girls, who had been misbehaving themselves, "I am going to whip you all," and she seized on Jimmie to receive the first instalment of the chastisement. "Mother," said Jimmie, "ladies first, always." A LAWYER addressing a jury on a case proved by strong circumstantial evidence, repeated often that "ninety-nine guilty men should escape rather than that one innocent man suffer." The Judge, in charging the jury, told them the "ninety-nine guilty had long since escaped." AT a recent meeting in Paris a speaker pathetic- ally inquired, "Why don't the great men of France bestir themselves? Why do they remain cold and unmoved at the calamities of our country 7 " "Be- cause they are cast in bronze," shouted a sarcastic voice in the gallery. AN Irish soldier was stationed in a petty French town which had a very pretentious gate. A grocer, dilating on its grandeur, asked him what the Irish would say if they possessed it. "Faith, they'd say," was his reply, "we'll kape the big gate shut or the dirty little town will be after runnin' out of it."

A, LADY who had been teaching her four-year- old the elements of arithmetic was astounded by his running in and propounding the following problem :—" Mamma, if you had three butterflies and each butterfly had a fly in his ear, how many butterflies would you have 7" The mother is still on the problem. " WHEN I reckon up what it costs me for my Scotch shooting-box, and what I lose by neglecting my business," said a nouveau riche to a friend, "I find that every grouse I shoot costs me five pounds." "Then you can thank your stars that you only hit ciao in every ten that you shoot at," was the reply. Mits. S., who had just lost her husband, was receiving a visit from a friend who tried to con- sole her. "Come, my dear, be reasonable. You must try to bear up under the grief." " Dont be alarmed," groans the afflicted one, wiping her eyes. "I am resigned at heart; only you know what my nerves are. It takes very little to upset them." GOLLY—" You look tired, old fel', watcher been doing 7" Dolly (briefly)—" Literary work." Cholly (surprised)—" Don't say What branch, old man 7" Dolly—" Well, you see, I know a man who writes for papers, and this morning he asked me to help him count the words in an article he was going to send down-town. Mighty hard work, I assure you. Almost as hard as writing, don'teher-know." BEAUTIFUL GIRL (at dog fancier's)—" Why, papa, there are no nice English pugs here. Father—" I see; guess we have have got into the wrong place. But what magnificent watch dogs they have here What breed is that handsome animal, Mr. De Brute?" Experienced Dealer—" He is a cross between a bull- dog and a tiger. That dog, sir, if given the word, would swallow a dude at one gulp." Father (quickly) —'l'll take him."

GUEST.—" I want a room." Clerk—" You can't get one, sir. All full." Guest—" Can't I get a bed, then ?" Clerk—" Haven't got one in the house, sir." Guest—" Got one out of the house 2" Clerk --".oh, yes." Guest—" Well, I'll take that. Where is it?" Clerk —"Out in the back yard, sir. It's the strawberry bed. Don't roll over on the berries. Good-night, sir." "JONES," said one friend to another in my bear- ing not so long ago, "Jones, Mr. Robinson is dead, and I want you to sit up with the body to-night." "My dear Smith, I can't," the other said. "Oh, but you must. I counted on you certainly, as a personal friend, Smith. Come, consent." "I am youi friend, Smith; but can't. This is for Robinson. If it was your father, Smith, or if it was you, I would sit up with the body with the greatest plea- sure in the world—the greatest pleasure; but not for Robinson. No, sir 1" COUNTRY editor (to new assistant)—" Mr. Smith, you write, An explosion in a Belgian coal mine last week caused the death of one hundred and thirty- seven men.' That is not an editorial paragraph, it is simply a statement of news." New assistant= "Yee, sir." Country editor—' Such slipshod jour- nalism won't do. You should have added, "The sympathy of the whole world will be extended to the families of these unfortunate men,' or some- thing of that sort. Matters to be of an editorial nature must voice an opinion." A YOUNG lady belonging to one of our first families returned from a walk. Her mother, who is very strict with her, asked—" Where have you been ?" "I have just been taking a little fresh air." '" Alone ?" "Alone 1" Are you sure of it 2" "Of course I am; why do you ask 2" "Oh, nothing at ail, except when you went out you took with you a parasol, and you came home with a gentleman's cane in your hand." The young lady has taken the matter to avizandum, and will bring in a verdict at an early date.

A MEMBER of a Boston family was preparing to leave for Europe, and his wife, while packing his trunk, said, "Here is my picture; shall I put it in with the other things ? " "Yes, certainly; for I should feel lost without it. You know I take it with me wherever I go." "Yes," replied the wife; but I don't believe you ever look at it I " "Indeed I do, every night of my life ! " rejoined the loving spouse. The little velvet case was put into the trunk as usual. When the husband returned and the trUnk was being unpacked by the happy couple, the wife found the case, and taking it out, said, "Well, tell me now—did you look at my picture while you were away?" "Look at it? Why it was the greatest comfort to me! " The wife opened the empty case and showed him that she had taken the picture out and packed only the case; the likeness had remained at home in her own drawer.

SAID Dogberry—" What ought Ito do? I told that Polish Jew to take one-and-sixpence for these drinks, and he got confused, and given me one-and- sixpence change out of a florin. Ought Ito tell him of his mistake, or devoutly spend the eighteen- pence elsewhere " ? Then spake Outsider, who has qualified for the Mastership of the Roll—" If you look upon Vintners as a corporation, you can keep it; if as an individual you can't." Then said Dogberry —" if I say anything about it now, the poor man will get the boot for making a mistake. In the Interests of his wife and children, we'll have the other drinks somewhere else." So they adjourned. "My Son," said a stern father to a seven year old hopeful, "I must discipline you. Your teacher said you were the worst boy in the school." "Well, papa,': was the reply, "only yesterday she said I was 3ust like my father."

div.head: " CAPITAL " CHAT.
div.p: " CAPITAL " CHAT.

It is now an open secret tint Mr. Balfour will lead the Tories in the next House of Commons. There were members who clung to Lord Randolph Churchill to the last. But this faithful remnant has now turned from his display of " manners " on the Grantully Castle in sheer disgust. The opinion is that Lord Randolph's colleagues in the Cabinet took an accurate measure of his capacity for making himself disagreeable.

The reappearance of Mr. Justin M`Carthy, on Tuesday night, was hailed with satisfaction by his colleagues, who have not seen him in the House for several weeks past. He has been seriously indis- posed. but considered himself well enough to come into the House and vote. He has not, however, taken an active part in the discussions on the Irish votes. He looks fairly well, but is somewhat ex- hausted, and needs rest.

Owing to other business before the court, it is now definitely settled that the Russell matrimonial case will not be heard until after the Long Vacation. The petition is that of the Countess Russell for a judicial separation by reason of the alleged cruelty of her husband, Earl Russell, grandson of Lord John Russell, to whom she was only married a little over six months ago. The petitioner is the daughter of Lady Scott, widow of Sir Charles Edward Scott, banker.

Lady Aberdeen's beautiful little shop in Mot- comb-street (between Belgrave-square and Lowndes- square) has not taken long, writes a correspondent, to make a character for itself. Every post brings both applications from Irish workers for permission to forward the fruits of their industry, and pack- ages of various dimensions from those to whom per- mission has already been granted. The demand for Irish needlework, plain and fancy, is certainly on the increase.

Mr. W. 11. Smith having announced in the House of Commons a few nights ago that it is not in ac- cordance with usage for her Majesty's Ministers to invite foreign guests to thiB country, a movement has been set on foot among the members of the In- stitution of Civil Engineers with the object of in- viting the President of the French Republic to pay a visit to England in the autumn. Several of the members of the Council are enthusiastic about the project. President Carnot is a distinguished engi- neer himself, and has been engaged in some of the greatest modern engineering achievements in France.

Bull-fights, at which the animals are baited to death, continue to take place in France, in spite of official prohibitions. Our Paris correspondent writes: The bull-fight at Bordeaux went off on Sunday without any incident. A bull having been deliberately killed at the previous performance, the authorities had given notice that on a recurrence of such a thing, the performances would be stopped. In the neighbouring department of Landes, how- ever, the Government circulars continue to be set at defiance. At Mont de Marsan, where the annual fete is taking place, three bulls were killed on Sun- day.

Just thirty years ago General Nicolai, the son of a well-known ambassador, and whose name was once on everybody's lips in connection with the Russian war, mysteriously disappeared. Last week, as Father John Louis, he died at the Grand Chartreuse, in consequence of an accident, and it turns out that his cell has been given to his nephew, one of the De Broglies, who is known as Father Dom Charles, and has long been believed by his former friends of the Jockey Club to be travelling in the interior of Africa. A few years since M. de Broglie was both known in Paris and 14ndon as one of the smartest examples of the French jeunesse do74e.

A passage in a recent controversy between Sir William Harcourt and Mr. Chamberlain derives fresh interest from the above reported rumour of Ministerial intentions next session. Sir William Harcourt wrote on the 4th of this month the follow- ing words: "Mr. Chamberlain has had many plans of Home Rule. What particular scheme he may at the present moment favour I have not the advant- age of knowing. Perhaps the mystery may be re- vealed to us when it is produced next session under the auspices of a Tory Government. It may be destined to have as fortunate a career as that of free education."

A Dublin paper, which is not likely to be in the confidence of Mr. John Morley, publishes a state-, ment the to effect that the right hon. gentleman, failing in health and despondent in spirits, is about to retire from public life. The source from which this information comes does not commend it to serious consideration, but as some of the Tory papers here are giving it circulation it may be useful to state that Mr. Morley has so greatly benefited by his stay at Cromer that the last, traces of his recent illness have disappeared. He has taken a house at Cromer for three months, of which a little over two months remain. At the expiration of that time he will re- turn to town and to his active participation in political life.

Mr. Balfour's announcement on Monday night of intention on the part of the Government to intro- duce next session an Irish Local Government Bill has created a feeling of some uneasiness in Tory circles. It is true the Chief Secretary was careful to style the measure one dealing with local govern- ment, but it is remembered that the Bill which last night passed through Committee in the House of Lords establishing free education was modestly in- troduced as an "Assisted Education Bill." There is a disposition in Ministerial circles to believe that the Government measure will turn out to be a Home Rule Bill,going as far towards the realisation of the Liberal programme, as did the Bill in charge of Sir Wm. Dyke.

The tunnels of the wonderful railway now in course of construction through the Andes for the purposes of establishing communication between the Argentines and Chili are being bored,it appears, by the aid of the electric current. The highest of the tunnels is about 10,000 feet above sea level, while the pierced mountain is about 12,000 feet. From Juncal, in Chili. to Quebeda Navarro, in the Argentines—a distance of about 14 miles--there are. it is stated, no fewer than eight tunnels, of a total length of nearly nine and a half miles. It having been found impracticable to employ steam engines from the great expense of raising machines and fuel to so great an altitude, it was decided to utilise the water-power available in the valley for supplying the necessary powers ; and the great turbines are reported to be doing their work well.

We have not, as it seems, heard the last of the sensational stories that were circulated some little time ago by Mr. Stanley concerning Mr. Jameson and Major Barttelot. Mrs. Jameson has for some weeks past been in the heart of Africa carefully making inquiries as to the accuracy of the horri- ble details given of the cannibal story. She has visited her lyisband's grave in the African jungle, and she has personally interviewed some of the chiefs and several of the warriors and carriers with whom Mr. Jameson was brought into contact. She will shortly return to this country, when she will make public her reply to Mr. Stanley. I learn on very good authority that it will cause a decided sensation,and will clear away much of the mist that now Buz rounds the story of the doings of the ill- fated rear guard while waiting on the banks of the Aruwimi.

Superstition dies hard. Two young women, while bathing the other day at Bundoran, on the coast of Donegal—a beautiful seaside place much frequented by visitors and excursionists—were car- ried out to sea by the tide. A boat was soon got out from the harbour, and the bodies were so quickly found that had prompt measures been taken life would probably have been restored. Instead of taking them out of the water, however, the boat- men attached a rope to them, and towed them i ashore, n deference to a popular supersitition that it is unlucky to take a corpse into a boat. When the bodies were got to land, everything possible was done by the doctors and others—but in vain, which is not surprising, for the mere towing of the bodies half a mile through the sea would Le suffi- cient to cause death.

Many stories about. Mr. Spurgeon are now coming to light for the first time, and in most of them there is a humorous point. He has a wonderful memory for faces and names, and he seldom makes a mis- take. Speaking at an annual college supper to a gentleman who had been present at a similar gather- ing in the previous year he said "Glad to see you, -Ir. Partridge." The guest was surprised to find himself recognised, but replied "Idy name is Pat- ridge, sir," " Ah, yes," wAs the instant rejoinder; "won't make game of you any more." The more practical side of Mr. Spurgeon's character, is incli-
ACROSS THE ATLANTIC.
BY " TOWNSMAN.° V.-AMONG THE AMERICANS.
AMERICAN HOUSE S .-TITE AMERICAN STOVE.- HOME LIFE.-HOTEL LIFE.

Almost the first thing that arrests the attention of a visitor to an American city is the peculiarity of the houses. To one accustomed to the compact stable, brick-built dwellings that line the narrow streets of an English town, the first glimpse of the small, mean-looking,wooden shanties of an aspiring American city gives rise to sensations of a novel and somewhat contemptuous character. Everything about the houses is so utterly different to the state of things prevailing in England, that you are apt to make comparisons, and in those comparisons, of course, the unaccustomed structures get the worst of it. But it needs only a 'short acquaintance with the strange dwellings and their surroundings to modify your impressions, and before long you begin to entertain a preference for what had at first sight provoked your contempt. The vast majority of trans-Atlantic houses are built entirely of wood, and are described as "frame houses." Those of the early settlers are of the "Noah's Ark" style of architecture—if there be any " style " in it—but 'those of more recent construction embrace every variety of style, and every modern convenience. Some of the latter are really imposing erections, and now and again their grandeur is enhanced by skilful attempts to imitate stone. As a rule the dwellings are detached, or semi-detached, and the plots on which they stand are converted into lawns in front and gardens behind. Nearly all of their dwellings have piazzas and balconies, and every window has a sun shade. The exteriors are painted with bright colours, and as the colours are as varied as the owners' tastes, some startling contrasts are to be seen. Internally the houses are beautifully fitted, and possess an air of comfort to a marked degree. But, except in the case of those of the well-to-do, the houses present a peculiar feature by way of possessing two doors. Enquiring the reason for this peculiarity, you learn that rents are so high that it is necessary to sub-let the houses, and thus nearly every house of moder- ate size is occupied by two famalies. One door, therefore, leads to the rooms on the ground floor, and the other to the upper rooms. The doors are usually placed side by side of the house, and in some cases a flight of staits erected outside leads direct from the street to the upper portion of the dwelling. Other families, again, live in regular flats in large and commodious buildings ; whilst many Americans take up their permanent abode in one of the many hotels which aboun 1 in the cities.

On one occasion he, in the midst of his sermon, turned to the deacons who occupied seats immediately behind him, and with- out appreciably interrupting the course of his ser- mon said in a low voice" pick-pocket Mrs. So-and- so's pew," and resumed the thread of his discourse. Two deacons left their seats, and passing out by the stairs behind re-entered the Tabernacle on the area floor from opposite, one of them bringing with him the policeman stationed at the door. .The pickpocket was duly taken out, most people supposing it was merely a case of fainting.

div.head: AMERICAN STOVE.
div.p: THE AMERICAN STOVE.

On entering an American house, English people, are not long before they miss the fire grates. No grates, such as are used in England, are to be seen anywhere. The houses are artificially heated in winter by means of a great hot air stove, which is placed in the cellar, and which communicates with every room in the house by means of zinc pipes. These stoves must be very injurious to the people as there is no ventilation to the rooms. There is no open chimney to carry off the bad air, and an Am- erican would as soon think of flying as of opening a window. Some of the householders fire-up in the winter in fine style, and of course suffer for their folly. With the thermometer at 75 degrees, I was more than warm, but I learnt that it was no un- common thing for the Americans to keep their rooms at • about 100 degrees day and night in the cold weather. The result was, that when they went into the air, they were so sensitive to the cold that they were obliged to load themselves with clothing, and they were always thankful to get home again. These people were remarkable for their sallow complexions, and their suspectibility to draughts. The hot air is;very enervating. At first it is almost stilfiing, and after a brief exper- ience it is a positive treat to a new corner to get into the open air. For my own part I would rather be starved out than suffocated, so I always opened my bedroom window on going to rest, and left it open during the night. I arrived just at the tail end of winter, and for some days we had a "succession of samples" in ti:e way of weather. Rain, snow, and frost followed each other daily, but, nevertheless, my window was left open, and I felt all the better for it. To my great relief, how- ever, with the advent of the 'merry month "the stoves were "shut down" as the Yankees say, and the only heat I experienced afterwards was from the sun, and the cooking stove. The latter is en- tirely different to anything at home. It is an un- couth-looking object at first, which occupies a con- siderable space in the kitchen, as it has to be kept well away from the wooden walls of the house. It comprises a fire, an oven, and a hot water vessel, and accomodates half-a-dozen pans at a time. It saves a lot of labour ; and after seeing a cooking stove in active operation for a few weeks, you ap- preciate its merits. As ,the hot weather approaches, the range. again gives place to a smaller cooking stove which is worked by gasoline, and can be ope- rated just as necessity arises.

div.head: NO HOME LIFE.
div.p: NO HOME LIFE.

But, as a matter of fact, there is very little of the home life as it exists in the old country. American women have no relish for household duties, and as you pass along the streets your attention is fre- quently arrested by notices of "Furnished apart- ments for light housekeeping." The very frequency of the notice affords abundant testimony to the indolence of the ladies, and if further proof were wanted it could be found in the dining rooms which are so freely distributed throughout all American cities. If you decide to patronise a cer- tain restaurant for meals, and are at all of an obser- vant turn, you will notice amongst the customers heads of families who will take their seats at the appointed hours with the regularity of clockwork. A few minutes later they will be joined by their wives, and then the children will make their ap- pearance and take their places at what is to them the family table. It seems a queer way of living to an Englishman, but you soon become familiar with these unconventionalities, and look for the ap- pearance of other customers as if they were old friends.

div.head: LIFE IN HOTELS.
div.p: LIFE IN HOTELS.

Hotels in America are " run " upon two plans, known as the American and the European. The American plan means that visitors sleep and take their meals in the same hotel at a fixed charge per day for bedroom and food; whilst on the European plan you simply occupy the bedroom, and take your meals where you please. This plan is the one most frequently adopted. To this, doubtless, the numerous restaurants owe their success. It is un- doubtedly the cheaper way of living, though the cost of a room on the European plan (4dols. week- ly) can be reduced to half or one third the amount by taking a room in a private house. The latter, too, will invariably be a larger and better apart- ment, and possess a greater degree of comfort. Restaurants are also conducted on similar lines to the hotels. You can have a regular meal at a fixed price, or you can order certain dishes and pay for just what you order. To regular customers at the prix five a concession is made on the week's tickets equivalent to the pnce of a dinner. In passing along a street you will notice through what ap- pears to be an open shop window, a number of gentlemen seated in chairs ranged along each side of the" shop' engaged in. reading the newspapers, and, as you think, waiting their turns with the barber. Further examination, however, reveals the fact that the middle of the place is occupied, not with the barber's chairs, but with square tables, littered with the daily newspapers and other printed matter. This is really the entrance to an (hotel; and every day you will see the chairs filled by gentlemen eagerly engaged in the same absorbing occupation of reading .the current news. At the top end of the room is the hotel office, where all guests register and where all enquiries are answered. But a fuller description of American hotels I hope to give later on when I shall touch upon the mag- nificent hotels in the city of Chicago.

div.head: WARRINGTON TANS IN AMERICA. LETTERS FROM MR. WINSTANLEY.
div.p: WARRINGTON TANS IN AMERICA. LETTERS FROM MR. WINSTANLEY.
(Concluded from last week.)
MOSES VERSUS DARWIN.

May 3rd: I read carefully the lecture you sent me by Professor Davidson before the Wesleyan ministers. There certainly are some grave admis- sions for a Wesleyan parson to make, but, if I re- member aright, Professor Beet admitted quite as much in his addresses on the early witnesses of Christianity. I spoke with him once on Darwinism; he is a thorough believer in Darwin's theory of evolution of species, but how he can reconcile that with Genesis I cannot understand. I have read the whole of Darwin's works, and I humbly but firmly beg to disagree from him. The more I see of nature, the more I am certain there is no such thing as evolution of species. It is too great a subject to discuss by letter, but I tell you this—farmers are better judges than all the bookworms in creation, and they all assert that it is impossible. I still am a "special creationist." Whether the Mosaic account is or is not true I am not concerned, but one thing I know, and that is, that there is more wisdom and more philosophy in one chapter of the book of Moses than in all the life of a bubble- burster If the writings of the far off day, when men were searching for God, are crude and sometimes almost disgusting, still there are lessons and laws which are even now guiding nations in their advance to civilisation and justice. Will Mr. writings,ever guide nations hundreds of years hence? 1 trow not ! DEATH OF A HORSE: A TERRIBLE STRUGGLE.

I have lost my old mare, the first stock I e'er bought. She was a true old horse, and just as great a pet as you ever saw. My nephew turned her out tv pasture last Saturday with her halter on, and she must have been scratching her head with her hind foot and got her shoe fast in the strap under her throat. She had struggled until she pounded her head all to pieces, and her eyes were almost out. She lived until Tuesday evening in great agony. She was in foal by a first-class ani- mal, and would have foaled in a short time. We were up with her all night, on Saturday night, put- ting on poultices and bathing her. On Monday morning about half-past four, we were going to dress when she raised her head and tried to whinny; she knew all we said to her, and my nephew says a lot more. She would put her nose into John's poc- ket for an apple or a carrot, and let Harry play about her any way he wished. She is a great loss to me, as she was worth 150 dollars. lam happy to say we are all well, though la grippe has had hold of us all more or less.

div.head: DIVORCE MADE EASY.
div.p: DIVORCE MADE EASY.

May 17th: Out of every four or five men you come in contact with out here, you are sure to find one who is either divorced or living away from his wife; the true home life is rudely broken up to gratify some selfish lust. This sort of thing is very prevalent out here.

div.head: READING.
div.p: READING.

I used to be a devoted reader, but now I hardly ever take up a book to read; there is so much in nature to see, and so much work to do that my lei- sure time is more limited than it ever was before. Do not think lam grumbling. This is just the life I have looked forward to for a number of years: My son John is a great reader; he sits up every night after we retire to enjoy his books. He gaiDed access to the Oddfellows' library, and has got books from there all this winter.

div.head: HORSE-BUYING A SPECULATION.
div.p: HORSE-BUYING A SPECULATION.

I have bought a brood mare, but I am afraid I have been sold, .as I fear she is a little bit lame. She is a fine-looking bay mare with black mane, and if sound enough to work, she will be a cheap one. I have been running round all this week seeing horses for sale. There are lots of them, and some very good ones, but for these &good price is wanted, 220 dollars being refused for working horses. This horse-buying is quite a speculatiou, and I do not like it.

div.head: SICKNESS IN THE FAMILY.
div.p: SICKNESS IN THE FAMILY.

We have been having quite a spell of sickness. First my wife was sick (but I am happy to say she is quite restored to her usual health), then little Harry started and Edith. I was afraid for some three or four days that we should lose Edith, but the doctor managed to kill the fever, and, thank God, they are both up now and walking around again, though Edith is about the colour of the paper lam writing on, so white and thin is she. Just a little way from here there were six buried in one day out of one house, leaving two little children to the wide world, and every day there are some taken to the burying ground on the hillside, carried away by that dreadful la grippe. We are having quite a time with it. VISIT OF THE PRESIDENT.

May 31st: I did not tell you in my last that we had the president, Mr. Harrison, in Salem. He is a fine-looking man, but to my taste Mr. Wanamaker, the post-master general, is the best speaker. He has a ready address, and is quite at home, however great the crowd. In Sunday school he is at his best, and will hold the attention of the scholars for an hour at once very easily. In my opinion there are more fairly good speakers in proportion to the population amongst Americans than amongst Eng- lish people. Of course the grammar may be a little different, but all the same the speakers are intelli- gent and some of them very fluent; in tact, they can " gas " by the hour.

div.head: CROPS.
div.p: THE CROPS.

Our crops are looking fine; in. fact everybody says the place never looked better than now, and if I live and can work I will make it look better still in a few years. Our strawberries are the finest around here, and, indeed, they are two weeks earlier than those of most of our neighbours,some of whom are a little piqued over it. Yesterday we gathered thirty boxes and sold them to the dealers for 20 cents per box. They are selling them at 25 cents, or a shilling per box, but next week they will be down to ten cents, as the people will rush th em into the market; so you see the benefit of having eally fruit. California strawberries have been here about three weeks,but they are not a patch on ours, which are almost too big to put in the mouth at once, so you may judge the size of them.

div.head: LIVE STOCK.
div.p: THE LIVE STOCK.

Our new mare folded last week, and a very nice fold it is. It is of a half-bred trotting stock, and I hope we shall be able to raise it. The colt I raised from the old mare is now two years old,and she is a beauty, and very intelligent. IV e are just now teaching her to run in a light wagon; you cannot call it breaking her in,as she is sogentle and will do anything you tell her. But don't imagine she can- not jump, for she can jump the highest fence we have, and come round to the house just like a great dog. I may tell you that lam now "super" at the Sunday school. Some of the scholars are thirty years old. I hope I may be able to do some good, for it is my only motive.

div.head: CONTENTMENT.
div.p: CONTENTMENT.

June 14th : I certainly think this is the best part of my life. My work is light, my home simple and comfortable, and it just suits me to ramble round the orchard and watch things growing. I would not change places with the Czar of Russia. If we only have health we do not need wealth, and cer- tainly there is not much danger of getting wealthy out here, but still we are making a comfortable liv- ing. "You appear to have had some winter in lay, and according to the papers it has been very cold at Whitsuntide. Why don't you live in a civilised climate like ours. When it rains here, why it does rain, and when the sun shines it is gloriou s. Just now we are having some fine showers, and they are refreshing all nature. E 7en the cows give more milk, and some apple and pear trees are flowering again, although laden with fruit, and the straw- berries are starting afresh with flowers and fruit. By the way we sold ten dollars' worth of straw- berries, besides having all we need for home use— not so bad for the first year after planting, though another year we hope to do a lot better.
BACCARAT AND THE MONARCHY. A PROMISING CROP.

What about the baccarat scandal and the Prince of Wales? The heir to the throne of England an associate of dishonest gamblers ! I think it will be time for a change of Government when the old lady dies; what do you think? 1 havejust had a stroll round the wheat fields with my wife, and I couldn't help contrasting what it was this time last year with what it is now. If nothing happens to stop the growth I shall expect twice as much or more to the acre. We have had salmon and green peas for weeks now.

It is reported that on Sunday evening a boat was cap- sized in a squall off Donegal town, and that five of its six occupants were drowned. On the same evening a boat was upset on Ruswarp dam, Whitby, and two lives were lost.

div.head: LETITIA THORNTON.
div.p: LETITIA THORNTON.
BY LOIJISA BIGG. AUTHOR. Off " CLARE WELSMAN," ETO.
CHAPTER vir.

During that week's visit, Dillon and Detitia walked and drove and talked together daily, and very much enjoyed each other's society; Miss Priscy was beginning to fear that they enjoyed it too much, but, what was to be done by the most discreet of dames de compagnie 7 Lmtitia was the mistress of the Firs and Dillon was her cousin. Affairs must take their course, but she trembled for her darling scheme for Ltetitia's future and was irritated with Mr. Dclafield for his inaction. He certainly seemed in no hurry to push his suit, but whether from over-confidence, or fear of a refusal, Miss Priscy could not divine. Dillon was fast becoming convinced that La3titia was the woman of women for him, but was equally convinced that it would be presumptuous and dishonourable to tell her so, and that she was reserved for some more fortunate suitor.

The Tuesday morning fixed for Dillon's depar- ture was ushered in by a wind that whistled through the bare trees and struck the corners of houses and barns with wild uncertain movement. The dawn was veiled and held back by murky clouds, and it was long before day at last broke, accompanied by a thin driving sleet. The wind was icy- cold, and no birds Were to be seen. The most cheerful sight in the dining-room at the Firs was the great fire of blazing crackling logs on the hearth, for Letitia came down looking chilled and out of spirits, and Dillon was pale and silent. Miss Priscilla, who was in bed with a cold, was perhaps the most to be envied of the household, for she was shaken by no youthful passions, and was success- fully: endeavouring to keep herself warm by the aid of an enormous duvet, a gas fire, and hot tea and toast.
"You cannot go to-day," said Ltntitia, as she and Dillon stood after breakfast, looking out at the desolate prospect.

"I think f shall have to." "But Aunt will be so disappointed if you leave while she is upstairs." "Do you really wish me to stay, Letitia?" " Yes ' she said in a low voice,'' "I should be very glad if you would." "Then I will put off going till to-morrow,' he said, "how the snow is gathering on the lawn and under tho hedges." . .

"And yet i is so light that you hardly see it fall. I never saw such a strange snowstorm, and the wind shifts every minute," answered L2etitia. The snow thickened as the clay wore on, and the country lay under a sheet of white. People fastened up doors and windows, but the fine, hard granules forced their way in through unsuspected cracks and stood in heaps within the houses. Living creatures were driven indoors wherever it was possible, and children kept at home from school. A few adventurous skaters ventured on the pond upon the village green, but even there the weather conquered, and with blue faces and wet coats they dragged home before mid-day. And the snow never ceased; not for a moment was the air clear of it, and the drifts grew deeper and deeper as the wind whirled it hither and thither. How soft and pure and delicate it looked! At first some of the boys rolled it into snowballs and made sport with it, but not for long; they too were chilled and dulled by its persistence. By the afternoon the lanes were filled half-way up the hedges, and there were deep drifts in the wide roads. There was a ghostly silence only broken by the fitful wind, and the sky kept its dull leaden hue. Most of the villagers were at home, for what work could go on in such weather? and sat grouped round their fires.

Tom Preston and Bob were at home, for the sheep were driven into shelter near the farm, and were peaceably munching turnips, unhurt by the tempest. It was about 4 o'clock when Tom said tc Mary, "I think I'll just step over to the farm and see as it's all right. The master may have some. thing to say to me." "1 wouldn't turn out for the chance," said Mary, "you've got all the sheep in, and what else can there be?

"1 won't be gone more than half-an-hour." "Oh, Tom, 1 wish you'd stay at home, it is such an unked evening, and your work's done.'' "Why, what is the matter, lass ?" said Tom, "you didn't use to be so timorous." Ho stooped down and kissed her, as he did whet they were courting, and whistling Bob from his warm couch, lie went out into the storm. The little garden was heaped with snow, and it had drifted so high against the door that Tom had tc push it out of his way before he could get out, and Bob, plunging from side to side, sank nearly to the top of his legs. Mary watched them slowly making their way down the lave, and then sat down by herself, unreasonably depressed. What was likely to befall them between the cottage and the farm I It was only half-a-mile and she was foolish to be so fearful; she told herself so a dozen times, but she could not drive her fears away. The half hour passed, and he did not return; 5 o'clock came, and then with cruel slowness the minutes crept on to 6. She strained eyes and ears, looking and listening till all kinds of dreadful fancies seized her, and she grew half crazy with the loneliness and anguish ol watching. A sound at last a hand on the latch of the little gate, and then footsteps crushing the snow. She ran to the door, her heart throbbing wildly, but it stood still as death when she saw, not her Tom, but Fraser, one of the farm labourers. "Is Tom here r' he asked, before she oould speak. "No," she said, "not since the afternoon—not since it went four ,• haven't you seen him? hasn't he been at the farm?' She was trembling so that she could hardly stand, and leant against the oak press for support. "Well no, not exactly," said Fraser slowly, young Billy Simpson, he told us as how he met him a-coming up, but it could not have been him, I fancy, for we have seen nowt of him. After what Billy said, We kep' expecting an, and so I thowt I'd come and see if un had started for t' farm."

"Oh, what shall I do r cried Mary, wringing her hands and running out to the door. It was terribly dark, and the snow and sleet were sweep- ing across the fields, driven by a fitful wind. "You just stay here," said Fraser kindly, for he had a wife at home and was a tender-hearted man in his rou At fashion. "I'll stop over to the farm and talk to master, and let you know about Tom in no 'time; don't be downhearted, my gal." And he tramped off resolutely through the ever-deepen- ing drifts. I cannot describe the horror of Mary's watching through the time that followed ; that endless hour that seemed sucking the life out of her bosom. Then there were footsteps again; but not Tom's, oh, not Tom's! She could not rise to open the door, though someone was knocking loudly. A hand lifted the latch, there was the gleam of a lantern, and Mr. Grange, the farmer for whom Tom worked, came in, scattering the snow from his coat end heavy boots, and looking anxiously round. "Then Preston has not come back ?" he said.

"No, sir," said Mary. The voices, both his and hers, sounded strange and far off to her ears, and she hardly know what was passing. "1 am afraid he has missed his way," said the farmer, "but I cannot think how, because the road tO the farm is fairly clear; Frazer and I 11;.ve just made our way well enough, and the snow is much deeper than when Preston started from here. I have been seeing after the cows at Brown's End. We were so taken up with the home farm, that they got forgotten, and it's well I went, for the poor beasts would have been smothered by morning, the snow is so desperately deep out there." "Perhaps Tom thought of the cows and went after them too—l will go and see !" cried Mary. "No, you stay here, Mrs. Preston," said Grange; "we will have out the dogs and all our men at once and we are sure to find him and bring him home to you; he cannot have gone far." Ile tried to speak cheerfully, but he was far from confident and secretly very uneasy. "Tom 'll have taken shelter somewhere, master; he warn't no fool to go a wandering such a night as this," said Fraser; but the speech was simply caused by a sight of Mary's white face, and had no foundation in any real belief.
"I will come with you," cried Mary again; "I must; I can find him better than anyone; I know I can!"

"But, my poor girl, you cannot walk in such a eight; we .will do all that men can." "I must come !" cried Mary, with a new strength, the strength of despair; and she began wrapping a shawl tightly round her and putting a thick handkerchief over her head.

"If thee must come, lass, I'll carry thee through the worst of it," said the compassionate Fraser, and tke party set out through the darkness. The turn to Brown's End was about midway on th? road between the cottage and the farm, and there they paused, shouting at the top of their voices against the whistling of the_ wind.

" " Go back to the fiouse, FrasiF, and send out all men there, and call at Jerry's cottage, and at Thomson's on the way; tell them all to come here and help us look for Preston." Fraser was not generally very quick in his move- ments, but that night he made marvellous speed in spite of the snow, and before long there were at least a dozen strong men plunging through the drifts towards Brown's End.

"Keep well together," shouted Mr. Grange, "and make for the outhouses; he may have gone into one of them and fallen asleep." They worked on through the blinding snowfall, sometimes sinking waist-deep; sometimes fallin, down; on they went, and Mary with them, lifted and dragged between two of the strongest, and numbed with cold. It was such a night as no one living could recollect in England ; a night that brought woe to many a home. There was at first no trace of the barns visible, so thickly the snow lay oTer the brown roofs, but at last, after losing their way a score of times and growing drowsy and, weary with labour and exposure, they stumbled against the fencing that enclosed the cow- house,

div.head: CHAPTER VIII.
div.p: CHAPTER VIII.

Just before the lamps were lit at the Firs, Lmtitia, who had spent the afternoon in Miss Prisey's room, came down into the library, where Dillon sat writing. The light of his solitary wax candle fell upon his paper and defined his figure, but the room lay in deep shadow except for that oasis of light.

"What' a day !" said Letitia, shuddering, "I can fancy all kinds of dreadful things happening; I feel as if someone was dying out in the snow." "It might well be," answered Dillon, looking out across the dreary fields. They were both silent for a while, and then Leetitia rang the bell, and tea was brought in and lights, and the shutters were closed. The conver- sation was not a very animated one, for he was thinking as he looked at the soft outlines of her head and neck, and the slender jewelled hands clasped in her lap : "I must not stay here; I shall certainly betray myself; and what has a penniless fellow like me to do with her?' While she on her side said to herself, "If only he had been different to the rest! What a fool I am to look for that ! I shall never find it— never."
She went upstairs slowly to dress for dinner, and it was nearly seven o'clock when she heard a hurried step on the landing, and someone knocked at her door.

" La3titia, Letitia, come here 1" cried Dillon's voice. She threw a shawl over her shoulders and went out to him. He was looking strangely excited, and drew her to the staircase window. "Look there," he said, pointing to some red sparks of light in the distance. "Listen—don't you hear them calling? I must go to them ; there is something the matter, and they want help." "But the snow ! " she cried, "you will be lost— you shall not go alone." "I am not afraid," he said smiling brightly, for his spirits rose at the thought of action, and he ran downstairs into the hall and began putting on his rough great coat. Forgetful of everything but his safety, La3titia followed him. He was just open- ing the door, when she glided up to him and caught his arm.

"I will not let you go alone," she cried, clinging to him, "the groom shall go with you." The heavy folds of the erimson shawl fell away from her bare neck as she held him back. He drew it tenderly round her, and stooping kissed her upturned face,

-" Let him follow me, if you will; I shall go straight along the road ; hark they are calling again—God bless you, Lmtitia !" He was gone, and when she had sent off the groom and seen him follow Dillon along the road, she went back to her room in a strange confusion of thought and feeling. She wished he had not gone, yet she would not have had him stay, and she was frightened at her- self. Surely she must have seemed over bold or he would never have dared to kiss her. And he had kissed her as if he loved her, and she had uttered no rebuke. Then she sat wondering what the lights and voices meant; she went to the land- ing windows, and could trace a faint glimmer for awhile, and then all was dark again, and she only heard the ceaseless moan of the wind and the beat- ing of the sleet against the glass. Dillon mean- while, accompanied by the groom, followed the exploring party at a distance, and reached the cow- house a few minutes after they had climbed the fence as related in the last chapter. They were examining every corner of the wide enclosure, and poor Mary, with the snow lying white on her shawl Ind hair was leading the search with feverish haste, but all to no purpose, for no trace of her husband was visible.

In a few words Dillon heard the story of Tom's loss from Alr. Grange and joined energetically with the rest in trying to discover some sign of him. The cows were warmly housed as Mr. Grange had left them an hour or two ago, and the gate of the yard was locked. Several of the men were grow- ing so drowsy with exposure to the cold that a homeward move became absolutely necessary, and they all left the enclosure, stumbling back over the fence, and keeping as nearly as possible to the now almost obliterated path they had made in coming. They had not gone many paces when a voice aried suddenly— " Halt ! " and e,veryone stood still and listened. It was Dillon wtio spoke, for his ears sharpenect by travels through many wild countries had caugut distant sound.

"What is it, sir?" asked Mary, who had recog- nised Dillon, and was keeping' near him with an instinctive confidence in his power to help her. "It is a dog's bark," he answered ; "it comes from that field to, the right," and without another word he started off in the direction of the far-off sound, the rest following irregulariy like a line of unwieldy spectres.

A heap of snow-, and poor faithful Bob digging at it. For an hour he has kept on gently scratching that narrow space as the snow drifted over it, and now he whines a thankful recognition to the coming helpers. Lower the lantern, and look closer—there is a face dimly visible, white and lifeless as the snow. Not the face of Jack Mayles, the village drunkard—he is cursing ,the night over a pot of beer and gin in the alehouse—it is not Jack, whom. nobody wants. Not young Mr. Melville, who, at twenty-four has spent half his fortune, and ruined two Hampton girls—he is safe enough at home, passing vile jests wall boon companions and plot- ting fresh mischief—not Mr. Meville. without whom the world would be better. Not Old Par- sons, the helpless paralytic, who longs to be out of the troublesome business of living. It is Tom Preston, whose wife loves him and who loved his. wife; Tom Preston, the honest and blameless, who has done his duty every day, and now, ever zealous in his master's interests, has done more than bin duty, and is dead. Carry him home and leave him with his old mother and his widowed bride and his faithful dog, for here is a hurt that no man can heal, ani.l silence is better than speech.

div.head: CHAPTER IX.
div.p: CHAPTER IX.

The bell of Hampton in the Hills wirryinging rer afternoon service on the second Sunday in February, and one after another the villagers straggled across the snowy fields and through slippery lanes to the Church. There were not many worshippers that day, for there was a good deal of sickness about the virlaQe, and many a household was anxious and busy at home. Among the few who came was poor Mary Preston, for the first time since her trouble. She had not meant to come and had sat at home staring at the fire, in the morning, but when the bells began ringing in the afternoon, old Mrs. Preston came in and said to her, "When art thee rtoinz to Church. lass? I wish. thee would'st try and begin. My Tom wasn't the one to ha' liked thee to sit moping at home. I'd go with thee but for the old man. ' _ _

- And Mary, partly to escape from the old lady's talk, and partly because she had little spirit left to resist, obeyed her and had slowly dressed and come. The way was very bitter to her, a very via dolorosa, across those fields where the horrible white snow yet lingered, and she would gladly have lain down and died as the man she loved had done. The sky was laden above her, and the leafless trees bore no sign of hope on their black branches. She was a poor toiling woman who had to look a rough future in the face and had no silken cushions or sympataetie friends at home to soften her widow- hood. The neighbours had been very kind to her awl had done all they could to help her, but each had her own burden to take up, and when Mary's sharpest trial was over they were forced to leave her and attend to their own old folks and little ones. There was a chilling wind to add to her misery, and she was shivering with cold and weak- ness when she reached the porch, and paused a moment before she entered to gain breath and courage to go in alone. Hampton Church was a small, old-fashioned place, with a gallery, over the west end and llizh

pews. Down the middle aisle was a row of free seats, and it was to one of these that Mary made her way. They were not very comfortable seats, for the wood was hard and slippery, and they were not cushioned like the cosy family pews on either side of' them, with their great red hassocks, and ledges for the prayerilooks. A few of her neighbours dropped in and took their places on the benches in front and behind, but no one came to share Mary's seat. Several mentally resolved to walk home with her after the service, but it was felt to be a sort of intrusion to sit with a mourner on her first Sunday; that was a thing for her kin to do, and so they left her by herself. She kept her thick veil down, and did not notice who was in the pews near, though she heard the doors of one or two close with a sharp click near at hand. She did not know that a warm heart was aching for her sorrow, and wondering how to help her. Miss Lxtitia had come into the church a short time after Mary had taken her place, and when she rose from her knees, her eyes fell upon the forlorn figure below her, in its homely, black garments. The most elegant widow's mourning had never especially impressed Letitia, but there was some- thing in Mary's heavy crape bonnet and coarse weeds, that struck to her very heart, and filled her soft eyes with tears. She could not think of any- thing but Mary, and as the church grew dusky in the lowering afternoon she kept looking at her and longing to comfort her. Presently the widow raised her veil, for the churoh was warm, and she felt sick and faint, and then her rich neighbour saw how pale and worn her face was, with its blank look of despairing woe. The Litany was being read and the congregation was kneeling. With an irresistible impulse Lmtitia glided down from her pew, and kneeling beside Mary, slid her ungloved hand in hers. Mary was as much amazed as if an angel from heaven had come down to her. The little jewelled hand seemed to confuse her brain. Miss Lxtitia in her beautiful velvet dress, and the diamonds on her fingers to take her hand in its cotton glove, and kneel down on the stone floor! Gradually the astonished shyness wore off and a comfort she could not comprehend stole over her. Tnere was such warmth and softness and strength in that friendly clasp that little by little the world grew less blank and painful to Mary's sense. She could not reason about it, she could only feel it as the closing sentences of the Litany echoed through the darkening church. Letitia stole back as silently as she had come, and Mary wondered whether it was all a dream. She would have thought it must be, only that the sense of comfort and refresh- ment stayed with her, and made her homeward way through the cold and snow less dreary. Two days afterwards another messenger came to comfort her—she was so ill all night that they thought she would have died, but when the sun- shine of a sharp winter's morning shone through the cottage windows, a little girl was lying by her side, and a'ray of hope lightened* the darkness of her sorrow. And at mid-day when Letitia came tripping lightly over the crisp path with a basket of comfortable things for mother and child, the widow looked up at her with a wintry smile gleaming across her tears, and Bob, who was lying at the top of the stairs, wagged his tail as if he was aware of what had occurred and fully approved of it.
( To be continued).

div.head: ARRIVAL OF THE PRINCE OF NAPLES.
div.p: ARRIVAL OF THE PRINCE OF NAPLES.

The Prince of Naples,iCrown Prince of Italy, arrived in London on Wednesday night. He was met at Dover- by Count Tornielli, Italian Ambassador, with Colonel the Hon W. Carrington and Celonel Slade, who has been appointed equerries during his stay in England. On his arrival at Charing Cross his Royal Highness was met by the Prince of. Wales, with Sir Dighton Probyn,General Ellis, and the staff of the Italian Embassy. On leaving the station the Royal party was enthusiastically cheered' by a large crowd, including many Italians, resident in London. The party drove to the residence of the Italian Ambassador. The Crown Prince dined with Lord and Lady Alington, the dinner being followed by a ball, at which the Prince of Wales was also present.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE AT CORTON.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE AT CORTON.

Mr: Gladstone has benefited considerably by his residence at Corton. He has taken long walks with— out fatigue, and has been showing great interest in a Volunteer encampment, which has been formed at Corton. A short time before he was taken ill, Mr. Gladstone made an engagement to attend at Newcastle a meeting of the Liberal Federation, the dates for the gathering being arranged in accord- ance with his convenience. There is some reason to fear that he will not feel it prudent in existing cir- cumstrnces to undertake the journey and face the labour and excitement of addressing such meetings as are certain to gather at this centre of Liberalism
THE PRINCESS OF WALES AND MRS.

GRIAIWOOD. The appeal of the rrincess of Wales for subscrip- tions on behalf of the heroine of Manipur, Mrs. Grimwood, has met with a ready response from the ladies of the land. The sum of £1,500, it is said, will be available, the Queen being one of the largest contributors to the amount. At one time there was a desire on the part of the Indian Office to sliub Mrs. Grimwood on account of the free manner in which she criticised those responsible for the conduct of the expedition, but the Queen soon changed that. So impressed was Her Majesty by the heroism. displayed that she paid Mrs. Grimwood special honour, and when the Indian officials saw the way the wind was blowing they very adroitly shifted their sails.

div.head: MR. SPURGEON'S ILLNESS.
div.p: MR. SPURGEON'S ILLNESS.
LETTER FROM MR. GLADSTONE.

The following letter from Mr. Gladstone was sent on Saturday morning to Mrs. Spurgeon : " Corton,"Lowestoft, July 16, 1891. My dear Madam, —ln my own home, darkened at the present time, I have read with sad interest the daily accounts of Mr. Spurgeon's illness, and I cannot help conveying to you the warmest assurance of my sympathy with you and with him, and of my cordial admiration, not only of his splendid powers, but still more of his devoted and unfail- ing character. May I humbly commend you and him in all contingencies to the infinite stores of Divine love and mercy, and subscribe myself, my dear Madam, faith- fully yours, _
_ _ (Signed) "W. E. GLADSTONE." The followilag reply was forwarded by Mrs. Spurgeon : _

." Westwood, Upper Norwood, SE., July 18, le9l. Dear Mr. Gladstone,—Yoar words of sympathy have a special significance and tenderness, coming from ODO who has just passed through the deep waters which seem now to threaten me. I thank you warmly for this ex- pression of regard for my beloved husband, and with all my hesrt I pray that the consolations of God may abound towards you, even as they do to me. Although we cannot yet consider the dear patient out of danger, the doctors have to-day, issued a somewhat more hope- ful bulletin. I feel it an honour to be allowed to say that I shall ever be your grateful friend, (Signed) "S. SPURGEON." On a flyleaf of the above Mr. Spurgeon, with some effort, penned the following lines as postscript "Yours is word of love such as those only write who have been into' the King's Country,'and have seen much of His face. My heart's love to you.—(Signed) C. 11. SPURGEON."

Mr. Spurgeon was no better on Wednesday night. His condition, in fact, causes his friends great anxiety. The following bulletin was issued yesterday at 5.1.5 D.M. :—" I think the Rev. C. H. Spurgeon,on the wholel a very little better.
" (Signed)
R. M. MILLER, M.D."

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT:
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT:

HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter past four. THE RECENT VOLUNTEER REVIEW.—Lord BftowNLow told the Earl of Wemvss that the reason the Volunteer Artillery were not represented at the reoent review be- fore the German Emperor was the want of spaceien Wimbledon Common fcr the guns. Tux EDUCATION BILL.—In Committee on the Elemen- tary Education Bill, Lord EGERTON of TATTON's amend- ment on Clause 1 providing .for the payment of the fee grant quarterly was agreed to.—Lord SANDPORD moved to reduce the age of pupils in respect of which the fee grant of 10s. per annum should be paid from -15 to 14 years of age, but the amendment was negatived.—Earl SPENCER moved alhew clause providing for the appro- priation of any surplus where the fee grant exceeds the annual amount received in fees, but this was also re- jected .—The Bill, as amended, ultimately passed 'through Committee. BiLL3 ADVANCED.—The Chartered Accountants' Bill passed through Committee.—The Slander of Women Bill and the Relieving Offices (Scotland) Bill were read a third time. The House adjourned at 8.15. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 3 o'clock. A STRANGER'S" MISCONDUCT.—Momentary alarm was caused in the House by the action of a man in the strangers' gallery who, so soon as questions had begun, stood up and commenced to shower down packages of papers on to the floor of the chamber. The attendants at the bar immediately secured the papers, which proved to contain statements concerning a grievance at Wool- wich Arsenal, while the officials in the gallery remon- strated with the stranger, and eventually, despite his protestations, ejected him. The man was conducted from the precincts of the 'House by the inspector a police. BRINE PUMPING BELL.—The Lords amendments to the Brine Pumping Bill were agreed to, and the Leeds and Liverpool Canal Bill was ordered for third reading. • FEMALE FACTORY INSPECTORS.—Mr. MATTnEws in- formed Mr. 0. V. Morgan that the Government did not intend to appoint women factory inspEttors, as the pre- sent system was working well, Mn. DE ConAiN.—lrhe SPEAKER Communicated to the House a letter he haa received from Mr. DeCobain in re- lation to the chargesmade against him. The letter was accompanied by a medical certificate, and asked that the order calling upon him-to be in his place on Thursday should be suspended until his health permitted him to return to this country to meet his accusers. The hon. gentleman was saidto be sufferingfrom extreme nervous prostration, and thathis removal now might be attended with serious results.—Mr. GOSCHEN did not think a de- cision in the case could be come to that day, andsaid the Government woula make a proposal when they had read the documents. Strvem—The House then went into Committee of Supply, when severalvotes were agreed to.—On the vote for the expenses ofthe Chief Secretary's office and subor- dinate departments, Mr. WEBB, as a protest against Mr. Balfour's administration movell to reduce his salary by £1,000.--Severalffrish members condemned the policy adopted by the Chief Secretary.—The right hon. gentle- man defended the action of the Government, and in the course of his remarks stated that next 'session a measure of local government for Ireland would be introduced on the lines of the Bills passed for Scotland and tngland.— The amendment was, after some further discussion, nega- tived, and the vote agreed to. The House adjourned at 125 a.m. HOUSE 'OF LORDS—TuEsDAY. The House metat-ten o'clock, when the Royal assent Was given by commissionto fifty-six public and private bills. 13-• MISCELLANEOUS:— The Pilotage Provisional Orders No. 1) Bill was read a third time and passed. The Local Registration of Title (Ireland) Bill passed through committee, its object being to provide a simple and in- expensive registry for tenant purchasers. The Crofters' Common Grazings (Scotland Bill) and the 'Ranges Bill were read a third time and passed. The Highways and Bridges Bill went through committee. Their lordships adjourned at ten minutes to eight o'clock.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TIIESDAT.

A formal meeting of the House of 'Commons—the second this session—was held in the morning for the purpose of hearing the Royal assent given to fifty-six public and privatebills.—The sitting was then suspended until three o'clock. The House resumed at three o'clock, at which hour the Speaker took the chair. ChrESTIONS.—Mr. MAi-nt?s informed Mr:Talbot that there was no appeal against a refusal by the justices of the peace to grant new licenses for the sale of intoxicat- ing liquors. The Local Government -A-ct provided for the repayment from the county funds and the costs of justices in defending legal proceedings in certain cases. Mr. Matthews, in reply to 'Mr. David Thotnas,refused to give a return as to the working hours and meal times of every colliery in the United Kingdom. Mr. Rmass, replying to Mr. Howell, said it was not-intended in any alteration of book post rules to confer any peculiar and exceptional privilege on friendly societies. Sir J. Fsa- ' oussos informed Mr. Atkinson in connection with the Duke of Norfolk's mission to theTatican, that there was no intention to appoint a permanent representative there. Sir W. HART-DYKE explained to Mr. T. Ellis the reasons why a grant had been refused to a school at 'Gellioeddd , in the parish of Llangwm. Ma. DE COBAIN.—Mr GOSCIIEN in the course of a dis- cussion on Mr. de Cobain's position, suggested that in- dependent medical testimony as to his health should be Obtained, but ultimatelysit was decided to let the matter drop for the Session. • SITPPLY.—The House went inte Committee of Supply on the Civil Service Estimates. HOUSE OF LORDS.—WEDNESDAY.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at eleven o'clock. The only oth* peers present were Lord 'Denman, Lord Herschell,and Lord Watson. The reports of amendments to the Land Registry (Middlesex Deeds) Bill and the Lunacy Bill were received and agreed to. The House adjourned at ten minutes past eleven o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WxprEsuex. The Speaker took the chair at twenty minutes past twelve o'clock, and ten minutes later a :quorum was lormed. CIVIL SERVICE ESTIMATES.—The House went intoACom- mittee of Supply on the Civil Service Estimates, and on the vote of £50,000 for salaries and expenses in connec- tion with the relief of distressed • districts in Ireland Mr. Balfour explained the general method on whidli the Government had proceeded. Mr. Healey acknowledged that the Government had done very useful work, tut thought that enough of attention had not been paidto Donegal. After some further comments by Irish mem- bers the vote was agreed to. On the vote of £42,38'2 for law charges (Ireland) Mr. S. Buxton moved a reduction of £lOO in order to raise the question whether the Attor- ney General should be allowed to take private practise. Mr. Osborne Morgan and Mr. S. Gedge supported the reduction on the like grounds, but the reduction was negatived, as was also a proposed reduction of the vote hich included the salary of the Public Prosecutor. The House adjourned at twenty minutes to seven -o'clock.
'HE VOTE ON THE ATTORNEY-GENERAL'S SALARY.

There was some cross-voting in the division on,Wednes- day afternoon, upon ,the motion of Mr. Sydney Buxton to reduce the vete for the Attorney-General's salary, by way of protest against law officials of the Crown taking private practice. At least one Conservative (Mr. Gedge) and several Liberal Unionists voted with the Opposition front bench in the minority; while the majority, although mainly composed of members of the Government and Conservatives, also included Mr: W. B. Beaumont, Mr. Lewis Fry, Mr. Jasper More, Mr. Wiggin, and other Liberal Unionists.

div.head: HOUSE OF LORDS.-THIIRSDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF LORDS.-THIIRSDAY.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat at a quarter past four. The Post Office Act Amendment Bill was read a first time and the Public Health (London) Bill, was agreed tO. THE FACTORIES AND WORKSHOPS BILL.—On the con- sideration of the report of amendments to this Bill. Lord DE RAMSEY proposed to reinstate clause 3 of the Bill. The clause related to the transfer of factory inspection from the sanitary inspectors to the local authorities.— Lord De Ramsey's motion was then agreed to.—Lord TIMING moved the insertion of a new clause, placing dairies in the rural districts under the supervision of the sanitary inspectors. After further discussion the amendment was pro form d agreed to, the subject to be brought up again on the, third reading.—The Bill then Passed through its report stage. BILLS ADVANCED.—The report of amendments to the Education Bill was considered and agreed to.—The County Council (Elections) Bill, the Penal Servitude Bill, and the Markets and Fairs (Weighing of Cattle) Bill also Passed their report stage. The House adjourned at 25 minutes to eight. HOUSE OF COMMONS. —THURSDAY.
The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.—The Lords' amendment to the Manchester Ship Canal Bill were brought and agreed to.

R. STOREY'S CASE.-Mr. MATTHEWS informed Mr. R. Reid that he did not see any ground for an inquiry into the conduct of the magistrates in regard to the Silkworth Colliery disturbances. Mr. Storey complained that the

police of the county of Durham had used the law as an engine of oppression against him in order to get civil actions against themselves withdrawns and he thought their conduct called for the interference of the Home Secretary. , • THE CHINESE RIOT, &C.—Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT in- quired 'what steps had been taken by the Government for the protection of the British residents on the Chinese coast. Sir James FERGUSSON described the measures adopted by the British Admiral on the Chinese station, and said the Chinese Government had given assurance that a rigorous investigation would be made into the anti-foreign riots, and that none of the guilty persons .should go unpunished. Two men had been executed at Wuhu, two condemned to death at Wusuch, and several mandarins degraded. Replying to a question by Dr. Rentoul as to the perilous position of certain mission- aries in Morocco, Sir James said it was due to their in- judicious zeal, which had drawn forth complaints from the Moorish Government. Mn. Da COBAIN AGAIN.—Mr. T. W. RUSSELL asked whether, in view of the practical disfranchisement of. East Belfast, the Chancellor of the Exchequer would take the fact into account in considering the course the Government would pursue in Mr. De Cobain's case. Mr. GOSCHEN said he had come to the conclusion that they should not take into account the political convenience ofthe electors of Belfast, and he moved the discharge of the order for Mr. De Cobain's attendance. After a short discussion the motion was agreed to. Irma LAND BlLL.—Theillouse afterwards proceeded to consider the Lords' amendments to the Irish Land Bill. It was resolved to disagree with a new cliuse relating to the liability of the tenant after agreement for the sale of the holding with an amendment having a retrospective effect. Several other amendments made by the House of Lords were also struck out. A Committee was appointed to draw up reasons for disagreeing with certain of the Lords' amendments. The Coinage Bill was read a second time THE ABDUCTION BY KURDS.

SO-17J-BOLAIS. TUBSDRY NIGHT.—The Sheikh Mustafa and his suite arrived yesterday from Suleimanie, in Turkey, for the purpose of delivering Miss Greenfield. -The rioters are dispirited and. wavering. It is probable they will surrender their prisoner to the local authority
----0-.... KNIGHTING- THE LORD MAYOR.

The Queen has been pleased to confer the dignity of a Baronetcy of the United Kingdom upon the Right Hon. Joseph Savory, Lord Mayor of the City of London, and her Majesty h also been pleased to confer the honour of knighthood upon Mr. Sheriff Farmer and Mr. Sheriff Harris in connection with the recent Visit of their Imperial Majesties the German Emperor and the Empress to the GuildhalL
THE ALDE RSHOT POLICE SCANDAL.

At Aldershot, on Monday, two police officers were charged with perjury and conspiracy in the case of Alice Millard. The officers arrested the girl and treated her with great roughnesss,as she stated; and shewas actually kept in a cell for three days before being taken into court. When she was brought up the charge preferred against her was disproved by irrefutable evidence, and she was at ,oTrce set at liberty. The • hearing of the charge against the policemen was again adjourned. On Wednesday the evidence for the defence being closed, the magistrates dismissed the count in regard to conspiracy, there being no evidence in support of it, and committed the two prisoners for trial on the charge of perjury,bail 'being allowed in one surety of £25 each and one of £5O. tin the same case Superintendent Brenson was summoned for refusing to grant bail to Miss Millard when she applied for it. After evidence had beentaken, the Bench ,found the charge proved, and fined the superintendent 55., with 15s. costs.

div.head: VISITS OF THE PRINCE AND PRINCESS
div.p: VISITS OF THE PRINCE AND PRINCESS
OF WALES.
BATTIIRSBA.

Battersoa.was en fete on Monday,, the occasion being a visit of the'Prince and Princess of Wales for the ceremony of laying theloundation stone of the Battersea Poly- technic. The institution, which will be one of the most importantin South London, is to be erected at a total cost of £685000 and will cover a site of two and a half acres. The Prince and Princess of Wales were accomi panied by. the Princess Louise. The address was read by Mr. Evan Spicer, chairman of the Committee, and the Prance expressed gratification at the success which had attended the scheme. The stone was thendaidtafter the presentation of a silver trowel by Mr. Edward Mount- ford, architect.

div.head: BIR.IfINGHAM.
div.p: BIR.IfINGHAM.

The Prince and Princess of Wales visited Birmingham, on Tuesday, to open the new Law Courts. Their Royal Highnesses arrived at New-st. Station at a.quarter to one, and were escorted by a troop of Lancers. They proceeded by a circuitous route to the courts, where several addresses werepresented, after which the Prince performed the opening ceremony. Their Royal High- nesses having inspected part of the Ibuilding, proceeded to the Council House to luncheon. They left "again for London at four o'clock.

div.head: SOUTH LONDOX.
div.p: SOUTH LONDOX.

A" People's Palace" for the New Cross district of South London, provided by the Goldsmith's Coinpany at a total cost,including an endowment of Lli,ooo a, year, estimated at about a quarter of a million, was opened on Wednesday afternoon by the Prince of Wales, who was accompanied by the Princess and their two unmarried daughters.
ST. ELPHIN'S CLERGY DAUGHTERS'
SCHOOL, WARRINGTON.

The brealcring-up concert and prize distribution to. the pupils attending this school took place on Tues- day afternoon. The audience included the Ven:the Archdeacon of Manchester (who distributed the prizes) ; the kßector of Warrington (the Rev. F'. W. Willis), the Rev. Canon Penrhyn (rector of Win- wick), The Rev. E. J. Willcocks (headmaster of the Grammar School), the Rev. Isaac Phillips (Orford), the Rev. H. V. Pigot (St. Paul's), the Revs. U. S. Hodgson and 17.1 C. Timins (Parish Church), the Rev. • Louis Savatard, Blackburn; the .Rev. C. de Blois, Winslow, Blundellsands ; the Rev. E. T. Wigg, Roy- ton; the Rev. L. Gardiner Preston; and the Rev.; J. Morris, Manchester; dim; Beal, head mistress:;' Miss Webb, second mistress; Miss Jones, mathe- matics; Miss Law. English; Miss Briggs, English; Miss Bluth French and German; Miss Ridgway and Miss MacCarthy, music. The pupils, each of whom wore a white dress, with a coloured sash, oc- cupied seats on a temporary platform at the end of the room. The ,cone.ert was an excellent one. Miss Ridgway conducted, and the accompani- ments were skilfully played by Miss MacCarthy. The Ven. Archdeacon afterwards proceeded to distri- bute the prizes, in which he was assisted by the Rector. The certificates which had been received from the Univer- sity of Cambridge were also distributed.—The ARCH- DEACON in the course of his address advised the pupils not to discontinue their physical exercises. He could as- sure them that he had been delighted to see their tennis courts; he wished they had been barer than they were at the present moment. He had been told they played "rounders," and he hoped they played other games, in which he thoroughly believed because they afforded not only health but enjoyment—the. enjoyment which should come from recreation. After speaking of intel- lectual requirements, he remarked that there was a great change coming over England with zegard to woman's position. It had very much altered since the time of their mother/3 ; very much since the time of their grand- mothers. There had been a revolution in England—a great change in Society, and there was a more marked separation in many respects between the rich and the poor. There was, therefore, all the greater need for the influence of educated women. Things were now possible for educated women, and all kinds of work wore open to them, which it would have been utterly impossible for them to have undertaken 50 years ago. Society had changed its views, and there was greater freedom for .them to work, and it had come just at the time when the demand for it was greatest. •
