div.head: EXAMINER, SAT URDA Y, JULY 25, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SAT URDA Y, JULY 25, 1891.
FRIGHTFUL DISASTER ON THE t SRIP CANAL. FALL OF A TRAIN INTO A CUTTING.
LOSS OF TEN LIVES.

A frightful accident, by which ten men have lost their lives, and four have been injured, occurred on the lace section of the Ship Canal, at half-past one o'clock, on Saturday morning. The accident was due to the blunder of a youth, now in custody on a charge of man- slaughter, who turned the train from the rails on the canal bank into a short siding. Travelling at a great pace, it went headlong against the rock by which the siding was closed in, and fell 35 feet below, in the middle of a body of workmen. . The section extends from Ellesmere Port to the mouth of the river Weaver. lace, from which it takes its name,ian lovely Cheshire village, about half a mile away from the line of the canal. The accident happened at a part of the cutting which is known as the Ince Rocks, which extend for a mile,or about a third of the distance between the wooden colony at lace and Ellesmere Port. The work here is of an exceptionally difficult sort, for in some places the surface of the earth is not less than 70ft. above the level of the canal bed. The lace section is to be opened for traffic in the course of another month, the only incomplete works of any importance being within the straight furrow which has been sawn through this seam of rock. To conclude the operations well within the riven time, they are carried on both by day and night. About 800 men were engaged on the night shift of Friday, and they were spread' in gangs through this portion of the cutting, blasting, digging away with pick and spade, and filling wagons with the hard-won spoil. Sixty-two men formed the gang working within near neighbourhood of the place of the accident.

and taken before the Chester magistrates on the charge Of manslaughter: Only. a week before he had been befOre the same Bench charged with a petty theft. A remark which he made probably indicates the nature of his de- fence. When the train made its first effort to climb the hill he kept the points perfectly right. The train had to come back; and the explanation of Pratt is that he thought this was another train consisting of " empties." Had they been empties it would probably have been the proper thing to put them on the branch line' that they might thence thread their way down in the bed of the canal. Pratt has been engaged for nine months on the works' but this was only his third shift as pointsman. The following is a list of killed and injured P.^. KILLED.
J. Crawford, Stapleford, near ;rarvin. C. Merc;er.Frodsham Bridge. J. Price (59 hut, Ince), friends supposed to be in Ame- rica
Y. Hinton, nothing known. W. Willis, supposed to be from Leaton. • T. Jones, nothing known. .1* Heaton, known only as coming from Liverpool. W. Doyle, Sweetman's Avenue, Blackrock near Dub- lin. _ _
.... J. Welsh, known only as coming from Liverpool. C. Cork, supposed to be from Crosby, near Liverpool.
INJURED.

P. Doyle, brother of the above W. Doyle. J. Smith, or Israel Lee, Lymm, lodging at 49 hut, Ince. J. Smith, 1. Ryder-st., Wavertree-road, Liverpool. J. Firth, 43, Church-st., Runcorn. AFTER THE ACCIDENT.

During the day the scene of the accident was visited by a large number of people. Navvies and their wives hurried up from different sections of the canal to see if any of their kin were among the killed. Excellent work in directing the relieving party and :in making other ar- rangements was done by the Ship Canal officials, among whom were Mr.Jones(agent of the Ince section),Mr.John Price (chief agent), and Mr. H. W. Clarke (chief engineer of the section) ; while Dr. Bennett. (of the Ship Canal Hospital, Ellesmere Port), Dr. Jones (Liverpool), Dr. Newbolt, and Dr. Bredin (of Ellesmere Port) did their utmost to relieve the sufferings of the injured. Happily the widespread report of Sunday that three of the men injured by the terrible accident at ince on the Manchester Ship Canal works early on Saturday morning had died from the injuries they received has turned out to be incorrect. Instead, the injured men—John Firth, Patrick Doyle, Tom Smith, and Israel Lee—now lying in the Ellesmere Port Hospital, are making fair progress towards recovery. Early on Monday morning the fol- lowing telegram was received by Mr. Jones, the agent of the section, from Lord Egerton of Tatton, the Chair- man of the Company :—" Jones, Ship Canal. Ice,— Deplore sad accident. Please express my sympathy with sufferers. Do all possible for them and bereaved families. Report cause of accident and all particulars.—Tmox, London."

bodies of the pen there, he made inquiries about Pratt and found he. had'absconded, having run away to Elles- mere Port, on seeing what.be had done.. The sergeant apprehended him at Ellesmere Port. In answer to the charge, prisoner replied, "I thought they were empty waggons."—The Clerk: Was he in charge of the points ? —The officer: Yes sir.—The Chairman: What, a little boy like that in charge of points ?—The Bench decided not to take further evidence, and remanded prisoner until Tuesday morning next, he being detained at the Hoole Police Station, Chester. THE CHARGE AGAINST THE POINTSMAN.

At the Chester offices of Mr. W. H. Churton, clerk to the Cheshire magistrates, on Tuesday morning, before Sir Thomas Frost and Mr. B. C. Roberts, the lad, George Pratt, was again brought up charged with the man- slaughter of ten men in the dreadful accident at the Ship Canal, at lace early on Saturday morning. Mr. Churton said that he understood the police would not be prepared with the case for Cheshire Assizes which opened on Mon- day next, and it would be necessary to have one or two remands.

Superintendent Walker said the police were not ready witk the evidence, so that he should have to ask for a remand until such time as they would be enabled to go fully into the case. Mr. Churton said the magistrates suggested that the prisoner should ly3 formally remanded to Hoole until Friday, so as to enable him to be brought before the coroner. _ _ _

The prisoner, interrogated by Mr. Churton, said he was born at Hollin's Green, near Warrington, and he would be 17 years of age next May. His father's name was William Pratt. Mr. Churton said he was told it had been the practice for lads employed at the Ship Canal to overstate their ages so that they might receive bigger wages. He did not say that that applied to the prisoner. Superintendent Walker said the lad was not 17, but had just turned 16. The prisoner, in reply to Superintendent Walker,admitted that he ran away from home a fortnight after last Christmas. He had been home at Hollins Green once since, on which occasion he saw his father. His father was then a labourer on the Ship Canal, and residing at Hollins Green, wbich was six miles from Warrington. Acting Sergeant Brewster said the police had written to the address,but the lad's parents could not be found.
—Prisoner was then remanded until Friday, and Super- intendent Walker promised the magistratcl to communi- cate with the police with a view to finding the prisoner's parents.

div.head: HOW IT HAPPENED.
div.p: HOW IT HAPPENED.

During the night shift a large quantity of spoil was obtained in the cutting, a great deal of it stones and rock and the rest earth. Before midnight 23 waggons had been filled. Two or three at a time they were taken lup the steep line which threads the bank to the shelf, and from the shelf they were backed further up to the .overland junction and some hundred yards beyond it. 'These operations were conducted by the aid of Wells lights. The points at the overland junction were in charge of a youth named George Pratt, aged 16, who is now in custody. Ellesmere Port was the destination of the 23 waggons of spoil, and the two engines " Altrin- cham " and " Northwich " were told off either to drag or to push them to that place. This would have been an easy enough matter had the overland mute been any- thing like an ordinary level railway line. But this was far from being the case. The pointsman Pratt, sitting on his lever, was in the middle of a sort of saucer. On his left the 23 trucks, with the two engines behind, were mounted on a small hill; on his right the overland linel climbed a fuller height; the23o yards of line leading tol the dead end from which he had to keep the train I branched downwards also to the right hand. Pulling on full steam, the two engines sent their loads down. the hill with a fine speed, passed the pointssafely on the level ground, and then sought to mount the hill in front of them. Failing in this they went back to the small hill from which they started. Now occurred the fatal blunder of the youth Pratt. The points were all right as they stood. Had he left them and gone away all would have been well. But for some purpose he deliberately, with some effort, pulledthe switch across, so that any train going towards Ellesmere would be turned into the 230 yards length ending in the wall of rock. Meanwhile the engine drivers were preparing for a more successful effort to mount the hill with their burden. They put on, fuller speed than before, rattled downhill into the level of the bowl, and then the next thing they knew was that instead of climbing they were going down on the branch line to the dead end. Seeing the waggons cantering down the driver of the •" Altrincham " shut off steam, but, aware that disaster was certain, he gave the warn- ing to the stoker and roperunner, and they all jumped out. On the "Northwich " steam was not shut off, but the three men got clear. Immediately afterwards there came a great crash as the waggons hurled themselves against the rocky wall, smashed the great part of it away, and then one after another toppled over with all their spoil on the unfortunate men working in the cut- ting below. So fearful was the impact against the rock, one of the drivers states, that the second engine abso- lutely leapt upon the first before they both, as one mass of metal, rolled over the almost perpendicular cliff. Had the waggons not been laden the disaster would have been less serious. There appear not to have been any men immediately below the cliff, but unfortunately the heavy rocky stuff was swept some distance out, afrd the list of ten victims, who were struek and almost buried by the mass, was the restlt.

Work was hurriedly suspended by themen,in the gang and the alarm given to the authorities at Ice. Mr. E. D. Jones, agent forthe section, was quickly en' the spot, and under his direction the bodies of the deadmen were recovered and removed.to the stables a short distance away. Four wounded men were conveyed by an engine to the Canal Hospital at:Ellesmere Port, 'where their wounds—which acre serious but not likely to be fatal— were attended to. Two other men who were hurt less badly were carried to the wooden huts in 'which they lodged. When the last body was cleared-away, soon after three o'clock, the work of removing the dhbris was begun,and this occupied the greater part of the morning. Most of the waggons were smashed to pieces and the engines were very greatly mangled. When the accident occurred the youth Pratt ran away to Ellesmere Port. Here,laterin the day,he was arrested

div.head: IDENTIFYING THE BODIES.
div.p: IDENTIFYING THE BODIES.

The work of identifying the bodies was done during the coroner's inquest, at Ince, in the morning. The scene was a heart-breaking one. The coffins containing the bodies were arranged in the harness room. Over reach was placed the lid, on which was :the dead man's name. One woman was taken to coffin after coffin to identify her husband. Face cloth after face cloth was removei, but it was not until she came to the end of the gruesome rows that she recognised the mangled re- mains of her husband. She broke down, wept, and fainted. The body of William Doyle was identified by the dead man's mother. She was an old 'feeble body,but she knew her son, although his face was disfigured. She stroked his face, she placed his feet carefully and loving- ly together. Then she nearly gave way, looked round 'for the last time at the body of her deceased son, and was led out of the stable. Many of the jury had tears in their eyes, before the dismal business was over. All the bodies, except one, were identified by relatives or friends during the inquest proceedings. The only body unrecognised wrs that of James Welsh, who was only known to have come from Liverpool. Towards after- noon, two of the dead man's sisters arrived at the Inca :settlement, and he was identified. Welsh was an Irish- ' man, and his sisters intend taking his remains to Liver- pool in order that a " wake " may be held. The man John Walsh, who was killed in the disaster, has been identified by his uncle, John Hough, who stated that the deceased came from Vauxhall-rd,Liverpool. The uncle and two sisters of the deceased removed the body on Monday night to Liverpool for interment.

div.head: PRATT BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: PRATT BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

On Saturday morning, at the Chester County Petty Sessions' before; Mr. li. D. Trelawny and other magis- trates, the boy, George Pratt was brought up and charged with the manslaughter of the ten men who , were killed at Ellesmere Port that morning.—The Clerk (Mr. W. H. Ckurton) said that was a very seriaus charge , against thebof who was brought there last Saturday on another charge, when he was ordered to pay certain I costs by instalments. He was brought up that day I charged with the manslaughter of several men. A very serious accident happened at Thee, last night, whereby ten men were killed and four were seriouslyinjured, and he believed the accident was caused by the prisoner , turning the points.—in offices: Yes: he was turning the wrong points.--The Clerk (continuing) : By which a train was precipitated down an embankment 60ft. deep, resulting in in ten men being killed and four were seri- ously injured. The boy was brought there, having been apprehended by the police. They wished to apply for a remand to bole in the first instance. They did not propose to go into the case that day, but only to have sufficient evidence for a remand.—Acting-Sergeant Brewster said from information be received about an accident on the Ship Canal at Ince, and after seeing the

div.head: Sole Proprietors— RAZE R & CO., 11, Ludgate Sq.,
div.p: Sole Proprietors— RAZE R & CO., 11, Ludgate Sq.,
LONDON, E.C.
THE INQUEST OPENED.

The inquest on the bodies of the men killed in the dis- aster on Saturday was opened at the Mission Hall, Ince Huts, on Monday, by the Cheshire Conorer. A message from Lord Egerton of Tatton, chairman of the Ship Canal Company, was read, which said, "I deplore the sad accident. Please express my sympathy with the sufferers, and do all that is possible for them and their bereaved families." Several officials of the Canal Com- pany were present,and the proceedings were also watched by Mr. Leonard Hall, agent to the Navvies and General Labourers' Union, on behalf the relatives of the killed and injured men who are members of the Union. Mrs. Doyle, mother of the two lads, one of whom was killed, was also present.

Mr. Jokph Foyer, chairman of the Chester Board of Guardians, was elected foreman of the jury:, which con- sisted principally of large farmers in the neighbourhood. Mr. Arthur Newman, solicitor (of Messrs. Grundy, Ker- shaw, and Co., Manchester),represented the Canal Com- pany. Mr: Topham, chief contractor, with Mr. Whit- worth, secretary, and Mr. Jones, agent for the lace Sec- tion, were also present. The Coroner, in opening the proceedings, said: Gentle- men, you have been called together to investigate one of the most painful disasters on record in the County of Chester. I may say the circumstances under which the unfortunate accident happened were of an extremely painful character, and I have no doubt you will join as in expressing deep sympathy w,ith the friends of the unfortunate deceased who, whilst engaged at their work at midnight, unfortunately were doomed to sudden death. The Coroner said it would be convenient to visit the locus in quo, then view the bodies, and not take more than evidence of identity that day for various obvious reasons. He suggested an adjournment to Thursday, and this was agreed to.

_ Mr. Newman expressed the Canal company's deep sympathy with the bereaved relatives, and promised to give every facility to the Coroner and jury, saying the company courted the fullest inquiry. The jury then viewed the scene of the accident and the bodies. On returning to the Mission Hall, fully half-an- hour afterwards, evidence of identification was given. John Willis of Leaton Station, near Shrewsbury,iden- tified the body of his son, William Willis, who had been a clerk, but had latterly been working at the Ship Canal at Ince, as a labourer. He was 20 years of age, and unmarried.

James Cork, of Childer Thornton, recognised the body of his brother, Charles Cork, 34 years of age, a labourer, and single. Thomas Mercer, of Frodsham Bridge, identified the body of his son, Edward Mercer, 19 years old, a single man.

Emnca Wood, a hut-keeper, gave evidence regarding another corpse, that of a man she knew only as "Jim." He was 45 and single. He had lived at her hut as a lodger for three months, but she never thought of asking his name.

George James Hardy. clerk at the Canal works, iden- tified this body as that of James Hinton by his name on the books. He was a labourer, and had been at the Canal about ten weeks. Witness also identified the body' of a man known as Eaton, but he could not tell his Christian name. He was about 30 years of age. There was another body identified which witness thought be

knew, but, as the man had worked there only tafwo days, he could not speak positively. The Coroner.-r-Did yon know whether any .of these men were in a benefit society? Witness.—No. - The Coroner.—We had better find that out. The Foreman.—How many men were there working in the gang at the time of the accident? Witness.—Sixty-two at the time. lam positive of that, because I counted them on my book after the accident. I called them together,took their number,and found who were missing. They were all working very hear to each other. The Foreman.—Were there any others slightly injured besides those who were taken to hospital? Witness.—Not that lam aware of. James Crawford, wheelwright, Tarvin, identified the body of his brother, Thomas Crawford, 42, labourer, single John Price, of Chester, identified the body of his step- brother, entered in the books as "J. Price," but whose proper name was Robert. He was a labourer, 41 years old, and married. Mr. Newman :- Wheere is his wife? Witness: In gaol at present, at linntsford. Mr. Newman: Where does she live when not in goal? Witness: At Handbridge, Chester. Catherine Doyle, from Black Rock, Dublin, identified the body of her son, :Patrick Doyle, labourer, 20 years old. Witness had also another son injured in the .acci- dent, and now at the Ellesmere Port Hospital. She went to see him first on Sunday, before viewing the body of her other son. The Coroner now informed her the in- jured son was progressing favourably, according to the doctor's statement. _

Superintendent Walker said he had carried the case as far as he could on actual knowledge of the deceased, and only-two remained unidentified, whose names were sup- posed to be Welsh and Jones. A woman named Jones had come from Runcorn with the intention of identifying one of the unknown as Jones, but although she saw him a fortnight ago, she could not recognise him now, and he was not disfigured. A missionary undertook to try and ascertain deceased's identity.

The Coroner, in adjourning:the inquiry, paid a high compliment to the Ship Canal Company for their careful treatment of the dead. He had seen all the bodies de- cently laid out and coffined. The inquest was then adjourned to Thursday. THE ENGINE DRIVER'S STATEMENT.

John Swann, the driver of the wrecked engine North- wich, in an interview at Chester. on Saturday, said he took charge of a pilot engine attached to 23 waggons at six o'clock on Friday evening his business being to bring full waggons of mineral rubble away at Ince Rocks. About 12.45 on a pitch dark night he noticed they were on the wrong road, going downhill instead of up. See- ing the danger and the impossibility of preventing it, he , shouted to the fireman, George Hodge, and the guard, ' Alfred Bullock, "Jump off, and :let them go. We are going to have a smash-up." They all leaped and fell on the batter. He was much cut and shaken, and when he had recovered himself the train and both engines had rolled over the embankment into the channel of the canal. The ten men killed by the train were fearfully mutilated, and he could not sleep for thinking of them. The lad must have been half asleep to have turned the points wrong on that road. When they got over what was called" the lead "it was too late to do anything. The lad in charge of the points was 16 years old, and was on duty from six o'clock to five the following morn- ing. The lad ought to know his duty if he was 16 years old., He (the driver) always kept his lamps trimmed, and if he had waited two minutes more before jumping they would all have been killed. It was as near death's door as ever he had been in his life. FUNERAL OF THE VICTIMS.

Six of the victims of the disaster were buried at Ince Parish Churchyard on Tuesday. On the entire Ince sec- tion of the canal work was suspended from eleven to two, in order to give the comrades of the deceased an opportunity of attending. The mournful ceremony opened at the Mission Hall, Ince, near which the six coffins had lain since the opening of the inquest. Mr. Robert Morris, canal missionary officiated. This brief ser- vice over, the procession was formed. First came the six coffins borne on the shoulders of navvies and other workmen, then the bereaved relatives, next the Ship Canal officials of that section, and an immense throng of navvies bringing up the rear. The procession was over a quarter of a mile long, three or four deep, and the company was roughley estimated at 600 or 700 persons. Throughout the route to the church, nearly a mile, on every hand were visible manifestations of sympathy and mourning. The officiating clergy were the Rev. the Hon. R. Grimston, superintendent of titae Ship Canal Mission, and the Rev. E. 0. Rawson, vicar of Ince. The brief but impressive service in the Church included the hymm "Jesus, lover of my soul," and at the graveside "Rock of ages" was sympathically rendered. The peoffins were covered with beautiful white wreaths sent , by the Ship Canal Company, the schoolmistress from the 'Ship Canal Schools, and from the Ship Canal huts of the llnce section. Representing the Manchester Ship Canal Company there were present Mr. W. H. Topham, chief agent of the Canal; Mr. J. Price, head agent of the first six sections; Mr. E. D. Jones, agent for the Ince sec- tion; Mr. C. H. Cox cashier; Mr. J. Bushell, sub- cashier; Messrs. Woodhouse, W. H. Towers, and W. B. M'Kenzie, clerks; Mr. E. Deakin, engineer; and Mr. H. W. Clarke, engineer for the Ince section. During the latter portion of the service the Rev. R. Grimston delivered an appropriate address touching on the sad event. On Tuesday night special services were held at the Mission Hall by the Rev. Mr. Grimston Mr. B. Morris, and Mrs. Garnett (a lady who takes greSt interest ) in the navvies). A funeral service will be held at the same place.

div.head: ADJOURNED INQUEST.
div.p: THE ADJOURNED INQUEST.

The inquest on the bodies of the ten navvies who were killed on the Manchester Ship Canal, at :Ince, on Satur- day, was resumed by Mr. Coroner Churton, at the Mis- sion Hall, Ice, on Thursday morning. A number of persons were present,_and much interest was manifested
, - in the proceedings. The Ship Canal Company was repre- sented as on the previous occasion.

The youthful(POintsman, George Pratt, who is charged with the manslaughter of the men, was present in cus- tody of Superintendent Walker. Hannah Harrison, of Higher Broughton, Manchester, identified the remaining unknown body as that of her brother, James Jones, whom she had not seen for a year,

' John Swann, the engine driver of the train, described the incident of the train getting on to the wrong line and ' the accident which followed. He stated that he had to return three times over the points in order to get a good start up the incline. The third time the points were against him, and he found he was on the wrong line. He and others on the engine had to jump off to save their lives. They ran down the incline at about twenty miles an hour. He did not think the load was too great for the power of the engines. He saw that they were in danger just before the catastrophe occurred,and shouted to his mates and jumped off with them, but he had no time to sound the whistle, and was not sure whether he properly shut off steam. Mr. Newman, on behalf of the Ship Canal Company, said the company would not dispute liabilities for any valid claims that might be made. In reply to Superin- tendent Walker witness said if the lad Pratt had not touched the points when they ran down the hill the third time they would have gone upthe incline all right. The lad would have been right in sending the waggons , down the dead end if they had been empty and there had been no more than six of them. George Powell corroborated the evidence of Swann. Henry Bevan, a walking ganger in the employ of„the company,spoke to the duties required of points-boys and others in the company's employ. Pratt he described as an intellectual lad, who had been engaged as a points- boy at Ince since the Tuesday right prior to the acci- dent, but it was not his duty to alter the points unless signalled to do so froki the engine. Witness added that the engines were overweighted with the twenty-three waggons, and the only explanation he had to give for the train being unable to run up the hill was that there had been dirt on the axles. No men were employed on the points at the canal, all that kind of work being done by lads. They had never had a simirar accident before. Other evidence having been given, the pointsboy Pratt was examined. He admitted that he was the cause of the accident, and explained that he turned the poi. te because he thought the waggons were empty. The lau stated, in reply to questions that he was born in Essex, and had worked for two and a half years on the Ship Canal, and for the last 18 months had been employed at the points.

The Coroner thought the accident was 'attributable to inadvertence on the part of the boy. The engines, he said, were overloaded, and he thought it would be more satisfactory if lads of more mature age were employed at such responsible work.

VERDICT. The verdict of the jury was that the deceased acci- dentally met their deaths by the falling of the waggons and engines over a precipice caused by the inadvertence of the boy Pratt, and recommended that no one under 21 years of age should be employed in so responsible a post during the night.

NORTHWICH MAN AND HIS TWO SONS DROWNED IN VANCOI7VER. A painful sensation has been created in North- wich by the announcement in the press that Mr. J. H. Edwards, with his two boys and two friends, were drowned on Monday whilst boating at Victoria, Vancouver, Mr. Edwards has been in business as a jeweller in Northwich for a number of years, and left five weeks ago with two of his four boys for Vancouver, intending to settle there. The sad news ! was confirmed by an official telegram received at Northwich from Victoria on Ph ursday morning.

div.head: WA R RINGTON FRI ENDLY SOCIETIES.
div.p: WA R RINGTON FRI ENDLY SOCIETIES.

On Sunday the second annual church parade of the members of Warrington friendly societies took place. The members assembled at 2.15 p.m. in front of the Town Hall, where they were marshalled in Troces,zion by P. D.G.M. -George Roughley, P.P.G.M. Charles Horrabin, P.P.C.S. James Parr, P.D.M. Andrew Joynson, Lodge Secretary Robert Sewell, and Court Secretary J. Hiinkinson. Amongst the officials present -were :--National 1.0. Oddfellows : G.M. H. R. Onions. D.G.M. George Smith, Pro. G.M. James Myers. ProV. C.S. W. Wood, P.G.A. Charles Falshaw, D.G.M. James Bramhall, D.G.M. Jatnes T. Wilson, D.T. Joseph J. Hands, D.S. Issac Newton. Grand United Order of Oddfellows: D G.M. Matthew Massey, D.D.G.M. William Oxley, D.T. John Pownall, D.S. Thomas Taylor. . Independent Order of Odd-- fellows : P.G.M. Gilbert Riley, D.P.G.M. Frank Webster, D.T. Thomas Wadsworth, C.S. John Emson.. Warrington District Society of Druids: Thomas Eden, D.C.S. Thomas Roberts. D.T. William Barlow, D.D.G.M. James Simcock. Ancient Order „ of Shepherds, A.U.: P.C.S. Peter Kirkham. D.P.C.S. John Dun, D.P.C.S. James Lowe, D.T. John Allen, P.C.S. Abel H. Mather. Ancient Order of Forresters: D.C.R. William Crutt, D.D.C.R. Henry James,. P.D.C.R. David Clayton, and D.C.S. Llewellyn Davies. Headed by the brass band from Messrs. Fletcher and Co's. works, the procession passed along Sankey.st., Buttermarket-st., Irlam-st., and Church-st. to the parish Church for divine service.. Prayers were read by the Rector (Rev. F. W. . Willis), and the lessons —Deut. xxviii. and Romans xiii.—by the Rev. C. C. Elcnm, vicar of St. Agnes's, Liverpool.. The pulpit was occupied by the Rev. C. C. Elcum, who based his discourse on the word "I stretch forth my hands unto thee." (Psalm cxliii. 6.) The offertory was divided between the Infirmary and the potrochial day nursery, in the proportion of two-thirds and one-third respectively. After service. the members marched back to the open space by the Town Hall, and, thanks having been accorded the Rector, the preacher, and the Mayor, the com- pany dispersed.'
DEATH OF MR. SAMUEL HOLDEN OF THELWALL.

Mr. Samuel Holden, of the Ascog, Thelwall, an old tradesman of Warrington. died on Sunday. To the younger generation the deceased, who had attained the venerable age of79,was comparatively unknown for it was as early as the year 1849 when he came to Warrington to act as manager for Messrs. J. and J. Stanton, distillers, Bridge-st. He remained with the firm until the year 1872, when he left Warrington, much to the regret of his employers, by whom he was deser- vedly respected, and by the inhabitants generally. He now joined Major Pickmere in the acquisition of the old- established business in Nantwich, established by the late Mr. John Hall, wine merchant, and became a member of the firm,which was thenceforward known by the name of " Pickmere and Holden." In 1878 he retired from business, and for several years travelled on the Continent, generally wintering in the Riviera, and both he and his wife derived considerable benefit from their periodical change of quarters. At length, no doubt anxious to rest, and to spend the - remainder of his days in comparative retirement, he built a house at Thelwall, which he called " Ascog." which means the retreat (of the cuckoo, in which hiS taste and skill are well exemplified. Three weeks ago he was compelled, owing to pain and weakness, to take to his bed, from which he never rose, and on Sunday morning last, at six o'clock, he passed away. Deceased was married in the year 1844 at Greenwich to Miss Eliza Blundell, whose father was at one time manager for Messrs. Dakin and Co. These gentlemen preceded Messrs. Stanton and Co.. in the ownership of the distillery, which was, we believe, established as far back as 1760, probably even earlier, as there is a letter in the possession of the present firm addressed to Messrs. Dakin and Company, and dated" January, 1782." The deceased was a Conservative in politics, and he was. also strongly attached to the Church of England. He was at one time one of wardens at the Warrington Parish Church, and manifested much interest in the restora- tion of that ancient building. He was a member of the old Amateur Dramatic Societyrand of the Warrington Field Naturalist' Society. Mr. Holden's death will be re- gretted not only by his widow, but by a large circle of friends in Warrington and many other places. The re- mains of the deceased were interred in the graveyard of Thelwall Parish Church, on Tuesday. Owing to the ex- tensive alterations which are being made in connection with the church, the first part of the burial service was read by the Vicar,the Rev. T.- P. Williamson, at " Ascog," the late residence of the deceased gentleman. At 4.15 promptly, the funeral cortege left for the church. The hearse came first, followed by Mr. Anthony Holden, nephew of the deceased, and Mr. W. E. Stephen- son, godson, Mr. Stephenson, Major Pickmere, Mr. Travers Pickmere, Mr. William Tinsley, Mr. W. H. Bleckly, Admiral Jones Parry, Dr. White, Dr. Sherratt (the deceased's bedical attendants), Mr. J. T. Picton, Mr. Seddon, Mr. Barlow, Mr. Ed. Greenall, Mr. Anthony Holden Manchester), and Mr. Stevenson, Clifton Thorpe,. Ashby de la Zouche. The procession was met at the church gate by the Rev. T. P. Williamson, vicar of the parish, who impressively read the remaining portion of the burial service. The coffin was of fumed oak, with massive brass mountings, and bore upon it a plate with the simple inscription, "Samuel Holden, died 19th of July, aged 79 years." Messrs. J. and W. Dutton acted as undertakers. The following is a list of the ladies and gentlemen who had forwarded wreath or crosses :—Miss Ascroft, Mr. and Mrs. M. B. Stewart, jun., Glasgow; Major and Mrs. Pickmere, Thelwall; Mrs. Holden, widow; Mr. and Mrs. J. C. Stephenson, Thorpe; the Rev. W. J. Stanton, Greenfield; Mr. William Barlow, Warrington ; Mr. and Mrs. William Tinsley, Thelwall; Mr. and Mrs. J. Seddon, Bolton ; Master Sidney and Miss Muriel Seddon.

This may seem hard upon employers ; but how much harder would it be upon workmen, if this were not the law! It is no use saying of a navvy, for instance, that he engages on a danger- ous job with his eyes open, and he must take his chance. If the job has to be done—and be would not be employed otherwise—the least that can be done is to minimise the risk in every possible way. The cost has to be counted in the destruction of an embankment ; and it should be counted, too, in the destruction of human life, if it can be shown that reasonable care for its protection has not been exercised. With regard to the making of the Ship Canal, our own feeling is that the number of fatalities since the commencement is disproportion- ate to the time which has elapsed, to the nature of the work, and to the number of men employed. If we are wrong in our impression, and if it should be shown that the average has not been exceeded, we should still urge that the time has come for taking steps to reduce that average, either by stricter supervision, or a more stringent application of the Employers Liability Act. Property is cared for in this country, but life should be cared for even more than property. [ Since the above was placed in type, the adjourned inquest has been held, and the jury have returned a verdict to the effect that the acci- dent was caused by the boy Pratt through inad- vertence ; and they recommend that no one under 21 years of age should be. employed during the night in the responsible position of pointsman.]

THE new Churchmanship of the Rev. G. S. Reaney Rev. G. S. REANEY, formerly Again. pastor at Wycliffe Church, War- rington, does not seem to sit very comfortably upon him. Re has not got used as yet to the divinity which hedges Apostolic succession ; and his mind still runs upon Dissenters. In the current issue of the" Newbery House Magazine," there is an article from his pen upon "Dissent at the May Meetings." While professing to give a dispassionate review of the situation, there is evidence all through of a bias which warps the judgment. There is not a little of such covert sneers as that contained in the refer- ence to "the small congregation in a dingy chapel down a lane in some decaying country town." Has Mr. REANEY by becoming a Church parson already forgotten Christianity and its Founder? What of the famous birth in a stable? Is that too dingy a place for him to hold in remembrance? And would it be utterly despised by men of the reformed REANEY type, if it were established that the stable was actually "down a lane in some decaying country town ?" The newly-enrobed church curate forgets himself. He forgets, too, the " village Zion" people who have treated him kindly; and is in great danger of making himself ridiculous. What, for instance, are we to think of his specially associating Congregationalism with the doctrine of" two or three met together :in Christ's name constituting a congregation ? " If he still believes in the doctrine, why couple it with "variety of error ? " And if he does not now believe in it, he ought to set about explaining away the Scripture upon which it is founded. Mr. REANEY may change; but the truth does not change; it is not a weathercock.' • One of the points which this new critic 'of Dis- sent raises is that the May; Meetings demonstrate the variety of Nonconformist sects, and their mutual antagonisms. But there needs no ghost come from the grave to tell us this, or that there would be no lessening of variety, or of antagonism, if, as Roman Catholics would suggest, the Church of England were thrown in as another Dissenting sect. Indeed, so far as antagonism goes, there is nothing to rival the church of Mr. REANEY'S latest adoption— judging from the way in which Ritualists and anti- Ritualists fly at each others' throats. It is urged, too, that there is evidence of egotism and depres- sion at the May Meetings, as if it amounted to anything even if it were so? Is Mr. REANEY free from egotism, and is he never depressed? As to the allegeti "rapid development of Secularism amongst Dissenters," that is certainly a bad sign, if it means that everything is based upon the obtainment of a "living," as is too often the case in the Church of England. But if it means that Dissenters are awaking to the necessity of prepar- ing for the world to come by making the best of this world, it is a very good sign. But what Mr. REANEY is really thinking of is that there is grow- ing evidence of a tendency amongst all classes to combine in the movement for liberating the Eng- lish church from State patronage and control ; and in freeing education from denominational fetters. There was a time when he could be counted upon to take a share in this righteous struggle; but he has joined the party of loaves and fishes, and he will fight, we suppose, for what he regards as his share. Still be "needn't be nasty" about it; and he would do well to show a little more regard for VA) church—or rather churches—he has left behind him. Under the head of " Newberiana," in the magazine in which his article appears, some account is given of the doings of an ex-clergyman -of the Episcopal Church in Ohio, who, like Mr. REANEY, has been saying hard things of the body from which he has seceded. After one of these attacks, RABBI GorrHELL thus spoke :

"If I had been in the presence of my brother <turning to him), and if I had entertained doubts and suspicions similar to his. I would have quietly slipped out of the Church with which those doubts collided, keeping my lips tightly sealed. Ido not think that, I could do such a great injury to the church that gave me my ordination vows as to do- cry it publicly. Such a course does a great injury to the cause of religion, without helping us to solve itS problems." The editor of the magazine adds " Vehement applause followed, and the gentleman rebuked was wisely silent. The rebuke was keen, while it was courteous—and also deserved."
There is a moral in this for Mr. REANEY ; and it is to be hoped he will read, mark, learn and in- wardly digest it.

div.head: DROWNED AT SUTTON WEAVER.
div.p: DROWNED AT SUTTON WEAVER.

A boy named Alfred Joynson, nine years of age (son of Mr. George Joynson, a farm labouter in the service of Mr. John Bate), was drowned in a pond at Sutton Weaver on Tuesday evening. It ap- pears that the lad, who was unablelto swim, jumped into the pond, which is 15 feet deep. He was una- ware of the depth of the water. He called for assist- ance, and as it was not forthcoming, the nearest house being half a mile away, he was drowned. The lad left his parents' house about eleven o'clock on Tuesday morning. He went with Thomas Bate, aged seven years, and another boy named Daniel Hartwell, who was going to fish, to a pond on Mr. Bates's farm, Northwich-road, Sutton Weaver, and Was drowned in the pond. An inquest was held by Mr. uoroner Worsley, at Mr. Bates's farm, on Wed- nesday. George Joynson, jun.,farm labourer, father of the deceased, said he never knew him to go into the water. Ile could not swim. The little boy, 'Thomas Bate, said when they reached the place the deceased said, "It is a good place to swim," and took all his clothes off, and went in. He sank twice, and did not come up a second time. Witness Went and told a man on the railway, and he got an 4PPluatus and tried to get the body out of the Water. Police-Sergeant Costello, who assisted to recover the body, w hich was found about a quarter- Past four o'clock, said the water was about ten feet deep where the deceased was drowned.—The jury returned a verdict that the boy was accidentally drowned.

159TH APPEARANCE. At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Saturday, Elizabeth Tither,of unsettled residence,was charged with disorderly conduct. It was her 159th appear- ance, and she was committed to prison for 14 days. LAWN 3lowEßs.—Graland, 51. Bridge-st., Warrington. and at Earlestown.—Advt. _ •

- THE POLICE TELEPHONE, Considerable progress has during the past few days been made in the erection of the police tele- phone from Leigh to Newton, Earlestown, Padgate, Widnes, and Warrington. The poles have been erected as far as Lane-head, and the wires attached as far as Shepherd's Inn, Lowton. BASSINETTES.—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger. 51, Bridge-et., Warrington.—Advt. ACCIDENT TO A CRICKETER. On Saturday, Mr. Henry Twist, the assistant overseer for Windle, who is also a leading member of the St. Helens Cricket Club, went to Tranmere to assist the London and North-Western Junction team against the homesters. The -wicket was very fast, and on Mr. Twist going in to bat,a fast ball "kicked up " and struck him between the eyes. Medical assistance was obtained, and it was found that Mr. Twist had sustained severe injury. No permanent injury was caused. J. &W. DUTTON'S SUMMER SALE now on. Sankey Street, Warrington.—Advt. RIVAL NEWSPAPER EDITORS AT ST. lIELENS. ' Mr. Henry Lindon Riley, solicitor, and editor of the "St. Helens Lantern," applied to Dr. Gaskell and Mr. Walmsley-Cotham, at the St. Helens Police Court, on Wednesday, for a summons for threats against Mr. William Swarbrick. proprietor and editor of the " St. Helens Chronicle.' The circum- stances did not transpire, but the summons was set down for hearing on Friday. On Thursday, by the intervention of a mutual friend, the "little differ- ence" between Mr. Swarbrick and Mr. Riley was amicably settled, and the magistrates will not be troubled with the summons. J. Sc. W. DUTTON'S SUMMER SALE now on. Sankey Street, Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
"FAIR PLAY,"—Unsuitable, because libellous. "A Li.ver of Music" replied last week ; but we did not then, nor do we now, see that any good and is to be served by extending the controversy.
Very touching has beer_ the exchange of sym- pathy between Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Spurgeon. Each can say of the other— How sweetly do you minister to love, That know love's grief by his complexion!

It is announced that the illness which has laid up Mr. W. H. Smith, the leader of the House of Com- mons, is :" asthenic gout." This sounds formid- able; but it simply means gout accompanied by debility. Astheny is a medical term for "loss of strength—diminution of the vital forces."

The Cunard Company have reprinted one of the letters of " Townsman " which are appearing in the" Examiner." It is the one which gives a vivid description of the "Scenes in the Steerage" in the voyage out ; and, as it pays a well-deserved compliment to the management of the Cunard, Company, they are making good use of the article for advertising purposes.

Tuesday, August 25th, has been fixed upon as Licensing Day for Warrington. What to the magistrates mean to do? Drift aimlessly as they did last year; or will they appoint a sub-committee to report upon the matter as they did the year previous ? Anything is better than the disposi- tion to— Linger shivering on the brink, And fear to launch away.

Mr. H. R. Lacey, of St. Helens, was hurt and badly shaken in the trap accident, at Warrington, on Thursday night week. A shock of this kind cannot be other than harmful, especially to a man over seventy years of age. Mr. Lacey is however progressing satisfactorily. As chairman of the St. Helens Library Committee, he has done good work; and we hope he may long continue to do good work.

The Archdeacon of Manchester showed himself liberal-minded in the address which he delivered, on Tuesday, on distributing the prizes at the War- rington Clergy Daughters' School. In the course of his speech, he quoted, Erasmus, Emerson, and the Koran. The extlract from the latter is a saying to be taken to heart. Think of it ye brewers and manufacturers who add pile to pile : —" When men die, people will ask what property have they left behind them ? But the angels will ask what good deeds have they sent before them ?"

Emerson, who was aptly quoted, can be studied with advantage upon education as upon everything else. He has reached the high water-mark of thought upon almost every topic of moment to the human race. He was a believer in technical edu- cation long before the phrase became current coin. But Milton's definition of education yet stands good, for ho says it "fits a man to perform justly, skil- fully and magnanimously all the offices, both pri- vate and public, of peace and of war."

The Cheshire Standing Joint Committee is do- ing its work in a thorough manner. Compared with the old jog-trot style of pre-County Council days, the proceedings on Saturday were revolu- tionary. Fancy attention being called to the fact that, although there had been eighteen convictions of publicans during the quarter, only one license had been endorsed:" But it is pretty much the same in boroughs ; the magistrates seem to be afraid in this respect to do their duty.

Mr. Lister raised a question which has been dealt with in this column, and that is as to the number of persons sent to prison for the first time for the non-payment of fines and costs. He" wants to know, you know " with a view to fines and costs being reduced, if it be found that the heavi- ness of their imposition does more harm than good. He stated that in Manchester as many as 7,000 persons had been sent to prison in one year for non-payment of fines and costs. How suggestive!

But the principal matter for consideration was a proposal to give the police "a right of appeal in person to the Joint Standing Committee in cases where they consider themselves unjustly treated by the decision of the Chief Constable. Will it be believed that there were five members present who objected to sanction this principle of elementary justice? The Chief Constable said he was being shorn of his powers; but the Corn- mittee looked upon the matter as sharing respon- sibility with him; and decided in favour of the appeal and other regulations. - - What next? At the quarterly meeting of the Unreformed Presbyterian Presbytery of Glasgow (North), held in Cowcaddens Church, the Rev. 0. L. D. Horne, moderator, it was . decided, after due deliberation, to accept an offer of " £l.OO per year for a period of at least five years" for permis- tion to put round the gallery "a beautifully got- up card' advertising somebody's soap. Oh, the power of the bawbee over the heart of a Scotch- man! When it is a struggle between Piety and the Penny, Piety goes to the wall.

It is gravely stated that while the matter was under consideration, Mr. Mackenzie, elder, and wine and spirit merchant, said that he would like to remind them that the pulpit had five large panels, and that each panel could be let, say, one for prize medal oatmeal, another for blacking, and so on:' "And so on " would mean a panel for Mr. Mackenzie's "best Scotch"—while the fotirth could be set apart for "Dublin Stout," the fifth panel being reserved for the words:—" My house should be a house of prayer; but ye have made of it an advertising den."

The Maybrick insurance case is a puzzler. It is odd, in the first place, to go outside the terms of the policy as to what should void the insurance; but, in the second place, it does seem like sound public policy to say no insurance money shall come to a person who commits a murder, or to the representatives of the murderer. And yet Mr. Maybiick's children cannot profit by the pre- miums which Mr. Maybrick paid in his lifetime! It is the Insurance Company that profits; and there is a fitness in things in its being styled the "Mutual Reserve"

div.head: SUCCESSFUL WIDNES MUSICAL STUDENTS.
div.p: SUCCESSFUL WIDNES MUSICAL STUDENTS.

Miss Plicebe Swindells, of Lacy-st., Widnes, Miss F. Stead, Farnworth, and Miss Minnie Merrin,of Albert-road, Widnes, have succeeded in passing the Trinity College (London) local examination in musical knowledge re- cently held in Liverpool. SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY AT HALE.

The annual flower service, in connection with the anniversary of the Unitarian Sunday schools, Hale, was held in the chapel on Sunday. The quaint little building itself was made to look picturesque and pretty by a pro- fusion of various kinds of floral decorations. The preacher, both morning and evening, was the Rev. G. A. Payne, of Knutsford. Special hymns were sung, and the choir at each service rendered an anthem. The collections were in aid of the Sunday school fund. EMIGRATION.—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canada, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Zealand, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the" Examiner" ()flied, by Cunard, Guion, American. Aus- tralian, Oriental, and other lines.—John Walker, agent. Examiner ' Oitice. Bewsey-et.. Warrington.—Adrot. FLOWIIR SERVICE AT HALTON PARISH CHURCH. On Sunday, special flower services were held in the above church, the preacher being the Rev. S. Wilkinson. Very beautiful flowers were brought to the church by the congregation at each service, and early on the following day, were sent to the Chester and Warrington Infir- maries. The offertories will be divided between the before-mentioned institutions.

THEFT BY A RUNCORN DOMEST2C SERVANT. Charlotte Horne, 17 years of age, was brought before Runcorn magistrates on Saturday to answer a charge of stealing £3 belonging to Michael McGrath. The pri- soner was a domestic servant to George Duckett, fish monger, Church-st., and McGrath is a fish, salesman lodging with his employer. On Saturday McGrath went to Liverpool and returned on Monday when he found the sum of £3 had been taken from his box. The police ascertained that the prisoner had been spending money very freely and arrested her on suspicion. She con- fessed her guilt, and was fined £1 or a fortnight's impri- sonment.

div.head: _INQUEST AT RUNCORN.
div.p: _INQUEST AT RUNCORN.

Mr. J. IL IVorsley, coroner, on Saturday, held an in- quest at Runcorn Burial Board, on the body of a boy whose body was found in the Mersey on Friday morning. The body was identified as that of John Wilson Hunter, aged nine years, son of a man of that name, who lives at 7, Hood-st., Liverpool. The evidence showed that on the 9th iust, the boy was on Waterloo Pier, steps catch- ing crabs, and in making a grab at one he lost his foot- ing and fell into the water and was quickly swept away by the tide. His body was found floating in Garston Deep and taken in tow by Edward Hignett,a flatman, of 46, Mason-st. The mother of the deceased said the Ser- geant at Dale-st., Detective Office, told her there was no life buoy nearer than Princess Dock and there was no chance of sending one to the boy.—A verdict of Acciden- tal Death was returned,

div.head: FATAL ACCIDENT TO A FARMER.
div.p: FATAL ACCIDENT TO A FARMER.

George Woodruff, farmer, Halewood, 29 years of age, has been found dead in a ditch in Old Hutt-lane, Hale- wood. Deceased had been dealing In horses, &c., for the past six months, and on Friday attended Warrington Fair, returning home about six p.m., in company with William Leekas, gamekeeper. He then drove to the Wild West Show," Liverpool. Deceased drove the horse there and back, calling at several public-houses on the way. They returned safely to Old Hutte-lane about 11.15 p.m., when Leekas got nut of the trap and proceeded to his lodgings, which are about 300 yards away. Deceased was not afterwards seen alive. As stated above, he was found on Saturday morning at six o'clock, by James Allen, farm labourer, lying in a ditch dead and cold. There were no signs of a struggle hav- ing taken place. The mark of the near wheel of the trap was close to the hedge, the wheel must have been two feet lower than the level of the road where the off wheel would be. The horse had taken the trap home, and was found in the farmyard about the same time tnat deceased was discovered. RUNCORN SONS OF TEMPERANCE.

At the fortnightly meeting of the above order on Satur- day, a cleverly written paper on "Local Option or Pro- hibition," was read by Mr. Edward Key, who sketched the past history of the drink traffic. He showed that in the past, Parliament had not only greatly restricted the trade, but had closed all the distilleries for 9 months in the years 1796-7 on account of a famine from which the country suffered at the time. The result of this action was so beneficial to the morals and genezal good order of the people, that places such as Bath, Salisbury, Bristol and Liverpool, petitioned Parliament for a con- tinuance of the act. Mr. Key declared himself strongly against compensation,and spoke of the enormous advan- tages of prohibition. As to the attitude of temperance reformers at Parliamentary elections, he urged all, irres- pective of party bias, to vote straight on this all import- ant question, and to consecrate their votes to the noble cause of temperance. There was a capital discussion, in which the following officers and members took part, Messrs. L. Inglesfield,Thomas Heesom, Daniel Bisbrown, S. H. Temperley, and S. Ashley. Mr. Thomas Clarke occupied the chair. FRERXASONRY AT RUNCORN.

The members of the Ellesmere Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons (758) celebrated the festival of St. John, the other evening, at the Masonic Hall, Devon- shire-square. The lodge was opened in due and solemn form by Brother J. Cooper, W.M. The W.M.-elect was then presented for installation by Bro. W. Mellor, P.M., P.P.G.J.D., supported by Bro. Annett, P.M., and the retiring W.M. Bro. Cooper proceeded in an impressive manner to instal Bro. J. Littler, S.W., as W.M. for the ensuing year. The newly-elected W.M. then invested the following brethren as officers :—J. Cooper, I.P.M. ; C. W. Phillips, S.W. ; T. S. Burgess, J.W. ; T. Sharrocks, S.D. ;W. Hankinson, J.D. ; A. Linaker, I.G. ; W. R. Wass, P.M., treasurer (re-elected) ; T. H. Annett, P.M., secretary; J. Coxhill, P.M., D. of C., P.P.G., A. D. of C.; W. E. Lancaster, organist, J. Le Ceuteur, almoner; T. Lydiate, tyler. At the conclusion of the formal business, the members sat down to a banquet, at which the customary loyal and masonic toasts were proposed and honoured. An interesting event was the presenta- tion of a P.M. jewel and life governorship in the Cheshire Masonic Educational Institute to Bro. Cooper, I.P.M. The jewel was a beautiful one, of chaste designs, supplied by Bro. Rooker, of Birmingham. The visitors present were Brothers Woolrich, Liverpool; Taylor, Lymtn ; Shilcoek, 1.P.M., 1250, Warrington; and F. Wilkinson, Widnes.

div.head: CHARGE AGAINST A RUNCORN PUBLICAN,
div.p: CHARGE AGAINST A RUNCORN PUBLICAN,

Before Mr. Brundrit and Mr. H. Reynold, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Eliiabeth Pegg, keeper of the Sloop Inn, Loch-st., was summoned to answer a charge of having sold intoxicating liquor to a drunken man named George Smith.—Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys pro- secuted on behalf of the police, and Mr. C. H. Lewin de- fended.—The evidence adduced showed that on Saturday evening, the 11th inst, at half-vast six, Constables Jones (who was in plain clothes) and Hughes were on duty in Church-st., and saw Smith come staggering along in a very drunken condition. He turned up Loch-st., and as the officers thought he was going home they allowed him to proceed. He however, went into the Sloop, and the constables immediately followed. In the taproom they found eight men, including Smith. A pint of freshly drawn beer was on the corner of the mantlepiece, and while the Constables were inquiring whose it was, Smith sad "That's my sup it," and he commenced drinking it. Mrs. Peg.' said she had not served him with any beer. but she did net know whether her daughter had served him or not. Smith refused to give his name and address, and was taken into custody, when he said he would not move a foot until he got change for a two-shilling piece he had given Mrs. Pegg.—lnspector Bowyer gave evidence as te Smith's drunken condition.—The defence was a total denial that the man had been served in the house. The man had been working thee tides on the Ship Canal without sleep, and Mrs. Pegg had earlier in the day told him to go out as he could not sleep there. Mrs. Nether, the defendant's daughter, said she served a man named Williams with the pint of beer claimed by Smith, and from hiin she received a two-shilling piece and gave it to her mother to change.—The Bench were of opinion that there was considerable doubt as to whether Smith was served or not, and dismissed the case.
THE EXAMINER, SAT'U,RDAY, JULY 25, 1891.
A SCHOLARSHIP FOR A HALEWOOD STUDENT.
Mr. R. N. Bennett, of Halewood,a student at the Royal Institution School, has been awirded the 7 ate scholar- ship, which is of the value of, £7O per annum for three years, tenable at any University.
WANTON MISCHIEF AT WIDNES.

Before Mr. Deacon at Widnes Police Court, on Wed- nesday, Catherine Hynes, a bad character, was charged with having broken a plate glass window valued at £1 10s. at the Waterloo Vaults on Monday night. The evidence showed that the prisoner out of mere wanton- ness threw a brick through the window after the publican had retired to rest. As she had been previously convicted about 40 times, she was sent to the Assizes for trial.

div.head: MAP OF WIDNES.
div.p: MAP OF WIDNES.

Mr. J. S. Sinclair, the surveyor to Widnes Local Board has prepared a map of the township divided into wards and half-mile squares and circles, besides indicating the public buildings, works, railways, streets, &c. Interest- ing statistics are also given. The price is one shilling. BRUNSWICK RAMBLING CLUB RUNCORN. The" ramble" of this club took the form of a drive to Aston, on Saturday last, and about 40 members took advantage of the opportunity to visit the grounds and hothouses of Aston Hall. Tea was provided in Aston schoolroom. The conveyances were supplied by Messrs Yarwood.

CAMDEN MOTEERS' MEETING, RUNCORN. About 40 members of this meeting had an excuision to Chester, on Monday last. They performed the journey in three brakes supplied by Messrs. Yarvrood Bros., and, although showery at the start, the weather became beautifully fine, mid the drive outward and homeward was highly enjoyable. The many attractions of the an- cient city were enjoyed to the full, and a most pleasant day was spent. SUCCESS OF MR. S. B. CHADWICK, OF RUNCORN._

In recent years Mr. S. B. Chadwick, J.P.' of Crofton Lodge, Runcorn, has gone in extensively for horse breed- ing, and we are pleased to record his success as an exhi- bitor at the Royal Manchester, Liverpool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Show at Bury this week. In the draught horse class Mr. Chadwick carried off the first prize for the stallion foaled in 1889 ; the third prize for a brood mare four years old, under 16 hands with foal at root; and the second prize for a pair of draught horses in harness any breed.

div.head: CRUELTY TO A HORSE AT WIDNES.
div.p: CRUELTY TO A HORSE AT WIDNES.

Henry Edgerley, contractor, was summoned before the Widnes magistrates on Thursday, to answer a charge of working a horse whilst in an unfit state. Inspector Dowty said on the 7th inst. he saw one of the defend- ant's horses drawing a cart which was heavily laden. The animal was lame, one foot being very much swollen and inflamed, and was evidently suffering much pain. By the inspector's orders the horse was taken to the stables. The defence was that defendant did not know of the state of the horse and that it was not lame when turned out in the morning. The Bench imposed a fine of 10s. and costs, total 275.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH OF A WIDNES OFFICIAL.
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH OF A WIDNES OFFICIAL.

We record with regret the sudden death of Mr. J. H. Wilson, chief clerk in the accountant's department of the Widnes Local Board and Assistant overseer of Penketh, near Warrington. Mr. Wilson went with the Sankey Parish Church excursion to Windermere, on Monday, and while there was taken very ill. On arriving home at night he was attended by Dr. Murray, but medical skill was of no avail, and he died on Tuesday. Pleurisy is believed to be the cause of death. The deceased was highly respected in Widnes and Penketh and his sudden death at the early age of 33 years has cast a gloom over a large circle of friends.

POPULATION OF RUNCORN. The preliminary report on the population and houses in England and Wales, according to the census taken on the 6th of April, is now issued by the Local Government Board, from which it appears that the increase of popu- lation in the last ten years has been 3,026,579, equal to 11.65, the smallest proportionate increase during the present century. The total population of England and Wales now is 29,001,018, being 14,050,620 males, and 14,950,398 females, occupying 5,460,976 houses. The population and inhabited houses in the Union is as follows :—lnhabited houses in 1881, 6,746 ; in 1891, 7.822. Population in 1881, 34,027; population in 1891. 42,517 ; increase, 8,490. FATALITY AT WESTON QUARRIES.

On Thursday morning a fatal accident occurred at the Weston Quarries of the Runcorn and Helsby Red . Sand- stone Company, Limited, the victim being William Law- Anson, aged 35 years, a native of Tarvin, who lodged with Thomas Darlington, of Weston. The deceased and two other men named Thomas Lloyd and Harry Weston were engaged in running a wagon of stone from one part of the quarry to the other. After the stone had been un- loaded at the crane, the men got upon the wagon to ride back. The line is laid on a slight gradient,and the wagon travelled with great speed down the wrong line, and, coming ix contact with some stationary wagons, the deceased was dreadfully crushed about the abdomen and had the thigh of one leg broken. He died a few hours later. The coroner has been notified of the occbrrence.
FRAUD ow ARIINCOTIN GROCIIR.

Yesterday at Runcorn Police Court, Thomas Large, who said he came from Woolwich, was charged with frequenting Percival's-lane with intent to commit a felony. Mr. George Hewitt, grocer and provision dealer, Percival's-lane, said the prisoner came to his shop on Tuesday last and produced a letter purporting to be from Wm. Gore, captain of a vessel lying at Weston Point. It was an order for one lb. of coffee, one lb. of tea, and two loaves, and asked for the loan of £2 to be placed to his account. The groceries were made up in a parcel and given to the prisoner, but Mr. Hewitt's suspicions being aroused, he told the prisoner he would see the captain about the money. He afterwards found out that the letter was a forgery. The prisoner pleaded guilty, and Sergeant Large said nothing was known about the prisoner, who had been picked up in Runcorn a week ago by the captain.—The prisoner was sentenced to 14 days' hard ,labour.
VVIDNBS COUNTY COURT.

His Honour Judge Shand held a sitting of this court, yesterday, when 113 plaints and 116 judgment sum- monses were disposed of. William Gibbon, contractor, Widnes,sued the Liverpool Sulphur and Copper Company for the sum of £l3 18s. for the non delivery of certain tanks purchased by the plaintiff from the defendants re- presentative Mr. Ince.—The company put in a counter claim of £l3 18s. for the delivery of the tanks, The plaintiff acknowledged receiving two tanks but stated that he ought to have four. Mr. Husband appeated for the plaintiff and Mr. Lewin for the dofendant.—His Honour gave judgement for the plaintiff on the claim and for the defendant for £9 18s. on the counterclaim. On the appliance of Mr. J. H. Lee. cab proprietor, the judge granted a commitment order against Alexandra Ramage a person stated to have an income of £4OO a year. Judg- ment had been given against him in February for £l6 17s. Bd. for the hire of cab &c.—There were no other cases of general interest.
A BATCH OF THIEVES AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, Edward Hop- kins (13), Lawrence Bowles (12), Andrew Fitz Harris (12), and Jas. Devereaux (13), all of Victoria-st.. pleaded guilty to stealing a quantity of timber value 21. from the L. &N.-'V. R. Co. As this was the boys' first offence they were discharged with a caution, and Mr. Gossage admonished the parents to take better care of their chil- dren.—James Edwardson, of Midwood-at., was charged with stealing a chicken worth 2.3., the property of Mr. Wm. Longton, farmer. Early on the morning of the 16th, James Ashburn, a farm servant, saw the defendant coming out of the fowl shed with something concealed under his coat. He pursued him and caught him 75 yards away with the chicken standing at his feet.—A fine of £1 or 14 days was imposed.—Mary Conway and Kate Carney, young women, were sentenced to 14 days' hard labour for stealing 17s. 6d., from the person of a shunter named Jas. Kenyon. It appeared that the man had been drinking with the women and afterwards missed the money. Conway was arrested the same night, and had 7s. concealed in her stocking. Carney was not arrested for several days afterwards. MAIN or BOWLS AT HALTON. On Thursday a main of bowls was played at the Nor- ton Arms Hotel, Halton, and was a great success. The main was for 64 players 11 up and the prizes amounted to £lO, being the subscriptions and £2 added by the proprietor Mr. George Twiley. Although the morning was very wet, the afternoon proved beautifully fine and there was a large assembly of bowlers from the neigh- bourhood of Runcorn and Warrington. The main had its full complement of competitors, and the green being in capital condition, some very close and exciting games were witnessed by the numerous spectators. Time would not allow the main to be brought to a conclusion, and Wm. Dugdale John Dugdale, and Jos. Holbrook (Warrington), were left in to decide the three first prizes. Tom Woods (Runcorn), secured the fourth, and the following were also prize winners :—F. Heywood, Jas. Woods. Jas. Welsby,Hy. Dugdale,Jos. Johnson, Jno. Sayles, Jas. Price junr., Thos. Wilkinson, John Newport, John Hampton, Robert Wright, and Samuel Dugdale. Mr. and Mrs. Turley provided a capital tea for the visi- tors. One outcome of the main was the arrangement of a match between Joseph Holbrook, of Warrington, and Thomas Woods, of Runcorn, for £25 a side. The game is to be played on Mr. Turley's green on Monday after- noon.
