div.head: ROSE GRONVING.
div.p: ROSE GRONVING.

Mr. Arthur J. Woolfull, late of Warrington, ob- tained second prize for twelve bloomi at Gresford Rose Show; and also won first at Christleton, Ches- ter, for the district and ten miles round Chestet. ILLNESS OF Mn. WRIGHT, M.P.

, . Mr. Caleb Wright, M.P„ for the Leigh division, is at present staying at his residence, Lower Oak, Tyldesloy, where he has been under medical treat- ment for about a fortnight. He was somewhat easier on Thursday, but will not be able to resume his Parliamentary duties during the present session. Mr. Wright is 80 years of age.
THE BRINE PUMPING (COMPENSATION FOR SUBSIDENCE) BILL.

Gratifying news of the above Bill was received in Northwich on Monday afternoon. It was contained in the following telegram :—" House of Commons, 3.20 p.m. ,To Cowley, Norzhwich,—Lords amend- ments agreed to, and Bill now only waits the Royal assent. A happy end to a long struggle. Hearty congratulations to you aII.—BRUNNICII." The fol- lowing reply was sent :—"To Brunner, M.P., House of Communs, London. Northwich congratulates you on success of your Bill, and will in due time thank you.—COWLEY." J. &W. DUTTON'S SUMMER SALE now on. Sankey Street, Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: ISLE OF MAN.-SPECIAL SEVEN DAYS TOURS.
div.p: ISLE OF MAN.-SPECIAL SEVEN DAYS TOURS.

The Isle of Man Steam Packet Co. are announcing an extra boat sailing from Liverpool to Douglas at 8.30 p.m. every Saturday, commencing on Saturday --zt, the 25th inst., and special Bank Holiday sail- ings on Saturday August Ist and 3rd. We would also draw special attention to the announcement of a seven days' tour from Liverpool to Douglas, Glas- gow, Dublin, and Belfast (900 miles sea trips), which th;s company are offering. To those of the public who are fond of sea voyaging, these tours will be found to be exceptionally attractive, and provision is made for visits to Glasgow, Dublin, and Belfast, trips round the Isle of Man, and a Sunday spent in the Isle of Man. PREMIER SAFETIES, Cash or Hire.—GARLAND. Warrington. —Adrt.

div.head: VYRNWY WATER SCHEME.
div.p: THE VYRNWY WATER SCHEME.

The Liverpool Water Committee on Tuesday dis- cussed at some length the question of Vyrnwy sup- ply and the quality of water. Mr. Parry,water en- gineer,reported that Vyrnwy water had been flow- ing into Prescot Reservoir No. 1 since last meeting at the rate of 3,430,000 gallons per day, except when it was shut off on the 17th inst. Mr. J. B. Smith mentioned that the committee saw their way to re- sume a constant service at the end of the present week,and in a few months the Vyrnwy waterwould be ready for use. Alderman Thomas Ilughes and Mr. Watts criticised very adversely the quality of the Vyrnwy water, and Alderman Garnett replied that it was a mere question of discolouration a little more or less.
J.& W. DUTTON'S SUMMER SALE now on. Sankey Street, Warrington. —.Advt. CHANGES IN THR CHESHIRE POLICE FORCE.

Arrangements have been made in the Cheshire Constabulary Force by which Superintendent Walker, of the Eddisbury Division, will be trans- ferred'to Altrincham. Inspector Meredith (Egre- mont) will be promoted to the rank of superinten- dent, and will take the place of Superintendent Walker; Sergeant Cooper (New Brighton) has been promoted to the rank of inspector at Runcorn; In- spector Bowyer (Runcorn) will be transferred to Egremont; Sergeant Skitt (Egremont) will have charge of the office at New Brighton; Acting-Ser- geant Hodkinson (Egremont) has been made a sergeant, taking the place of Sergeant Skitt ; and Constable Egerton (West Kirby) has been made acting-sergeant at Egremont. J. &. W. Durrow s SmintEE SALE now on. Sankey Street, Warrington.—Adrt. THE Ho zuz IRox TRADE.

There is no apparent change in the lethargic con- dition of the English iron market. Business con- tinues to be restricted to hand to mouth require- ments, and prices are Sin many instances barely maintained. N 0.3 Middlesbrough pig is quoted 9d. lower than last week, and mixed numbers of Besse- mer pig have declined 6d. • Scotch makers' iron is very quiet. and several brands have been reduced in price. Business in the Glasgow warrant market is still stagnant. There is no alteration observable in the manufactured iron trade, and the tinplate market is also dormant. The steel trade is still dull, and rails have gone down 2s. 6d. in the north- west. Shipbuilders and engineers continue fairly employed.—lron. J. & W.II9IITTON'a SUMMER SALE now on. Sankey Street. Warrington.-44det. CHRSIIMB COUNTY FINANCE.

At a quarterly meeting of the Finance Commit- tee of the Cheshire County Council, held at Crewe on Thursday, the county auditor (Mr. James Wil- liams) submitted his report on the finances of the county for the last quarter, from which it appeared that the magistrates' clerks returned to the county and police rates during the past year £6,443 18s. 2d. The county fund account now totals £286,000, and previous to the Local Government Act it averaged about £90,000 per annum. The county fund account for the current year, including the moneys for technical education, will exceed £300,000. The summary of accounts to 30th June, 1891, contains the following :—Expenditure under Main Roads Committee, £7,739; ditto Weights and Measures Committee, £O2; Cattle Diseases Committee, £465; Parliamentary Committee, £345; Standing Joint Committee, £3,945; expenditure to 30th June on County Fund, £16,379 88. 2d.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
ANNUAL INSPECTION.

The members of Widnes Local Board on Tuesday last made their annual inspection of the important public works which are under their control. After a heavy downpour of rain the weather cleared up, and the inspection was made under comfortable and enjoyable conditions. Meeting at the Town Hall, a visit was first made to the new fire engine station and firemen's cottages in Lacey-st., which are ap- proaching completion. The station will provide accomodation for one fire engine and one manual engine, and there is also a high tower for the pur- pose of drying the hose. It will also act as a belfry. On each side of the station are seven cottages in- tended for the accomodation of the firemen. At present the firemen are scattered in various parts of the town, and a considerable waste of time occurs before they ' can commence operations at any fire that may occur. This concentration in one centre will be of great advan- tage to all concerned. Messrs. Sayce and Randle are the contractors for the work. From here the members and officials were driven in a coach and four to the Accident Hospital on the Promenade, and the Matron, Miss War- burton, did the honours for the useful institution under her charge. Everything was bright and clean, and the nine patients that occupied the wards were evidently well-cared for and as comfortable as circumstances would allow. Returning through the town, the party were soon set down at the Gas Works in Newtown, an establishment for which the ratepayers have every reason to be thankful. Under the careful management of Mr. I. Carr, the engineer, gas is distributed at a much less price than any other town for many miles around, being at the same time a profit on the manufacture. This economical working is to some extent attributed to the adoption of the Dinsmore process which is now in more general use in the works than it was twelve months ago. During the year the new purifying house had been finished, and on Tues- day was in full operation. The gasholders overturned during the winter gales had been lighted, and altogether the works were in" apple-pie" order. It may be news to some of our readers to state that the total sum spent upon the gas works, including the purchase money of £8,669, is £67,466. Again entering the conveyance a pleasant drive was made to the Infectious Diseases Hos- pital, at Halton View, of which Miss Brew is the matron. It was a pleasing fact that although there is accommoda- tion for 26 patients, there was only one in the institution. The buildings and grounds were in beautiful order and condition, alike creditable to the Matron and the Hospi- tal Committee, of which Mr. D, Wright iF the chairman. The Hospital is an expensive necessity demanded alike by civilization and medical science, and the members ex- pressed themselves highly satisfied with the state of affairs. The Hospital cost £4,400. Pex Hill, the site of the covered reservoirs, was the next place of call. There was a good store of water in each reservoir, one of which has a capacity of eleven million gallons, and the other a million and a quarter gallons. Lunch having been par- taken of, Stock's Well pumping station was examined, but there is nothing new to record of this place. The drive was then continued to Netherley, where an in- teresting and important extension is being made. The present supply of water is little greater than the demand, and, acting on the advice of their en- gineer, the Local Board determined to sink another well at Netherley. The works now in progress will when completed consist of two boreholes, each 30 inches in diameter for a depth of 200 feet, and 18 inches for a further depth of 200 feet, making a total depth of 400 feet ; or 100 feet deeper than the existing well and bore-

hole. The engine will be of the direct-acting compound horizontal type with two deep borehole pumps and one double-acting piston force pump from the works of Messrs. Hathorn, Davey, and Co. Leeds. This engine will be capable of delivering into reservoirs at Pex Hill 2i million gallons per diem from a depth of 209 feet down the boreholes. The capacity of the existingH engine " James Cross" is 1f million gallons per diem lifting from a depth of 100 feet only. The boring contract has been entrusted to Mr. Chas. Chap- man, artesian well contractor, of Salford, who. is, by means of powerful machinery, making satisfactory progress with the works. The boring was commenced on July 9th, and by the 17th inst. a depth of 105 feet had been reached. On Tuesday the depth had been in- creased to 130 feet, and the members had an opportu- nity of seeing the boring machine at work. The nature of the strata through which the boring is being made is red sandstone rock, and the rate of sinking varies from 10 feet to 15 feet each day. At present capital water- bearing rock has been bored, and there is every prospect of a plentiful supply. An important matter in connec- tion with the boring is that the holes must be sunk as nearly perpendicular as possible on account of pumps of large diameter having to be placed therein to a depth of 200 feet. Mr. Carr's specification respecting this is very stringent, limit- ing the amount of deviation from the perpendicular to one inch per 100 feet- and on plumbing the hole at a depth of 105 feet, Mr. Carr found that the specified limit had not been exceeded. It may be stated that the contract for making the two bore holes is £1,400, while the cost of the adjoining borehole from which the "James Cross" pumps water, is no less than £B,OOO, a difference caused no doubt by improved and powerful machinery. The total cost of/the waterworks, as shown by figures prepared by the late Mr. Allen, has been £160,000. After a thorough and protracted inspection at Netherley, the journey was continued to Camp Hill, Woolton, the residence of Mr. F. H. Gossage. J.P., the chairman of the Board, who had invited the members and officials to dinner. Anticipating the desire of the guests, Mr. Gossage conducted them through his well-appcinted stables, his greenhouses and hothouses and gardens, from which much pleasure was derived. The dinner table was graced by the presence of Mrs. Gossage, and Mr. W. W. Gossage was also pre- sent. The guests were Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. S. Sadler,J. Midwood, J. Houghton, J. Taylor. B. Brown, R. Cook, G. I. Neil, D. Wright, H. S. Timmis, H. S. Oppenheim (law clerk), I Carr (engineer), S. Hoyle (accountant), J. S. Sinclair (surveyor), T. Craik (law clerk's assistant), and IV. Lowe (inspector). After dinner Mr. Gossage proposed the customary loyal toast, which was duly honoured and then Dr. O'Keeffe proposed in felicitous terms the health of Mr. Gossage, and the toast was en- thusiastically drunk. In responding Mr. Gossage favoured his guests with some interesting reminiscences of Widnes.
WIDNES CHILDREN IN A WELSH WORKHOUSE. ,SINGULAR ADVENTURES.

Two young chiliren from Widnes have just had a curious experience in North Wales. A woman from Widnes, apparently of the poorer class, stayed at Bangor last week, and towards the end of the week she forwarded 10s. to her children in order that they might join her. The children—a brother and sister, the one being seven and the other eleven years of age—booked by the Bonnie Princess on Friday. Upon the arrival of the steamer at Llandudno the girl, believing she was at her destination, disembarked, bat-, soon dis- covered that she had left her little brother behind. One of the crew of the Princess kindly took the boy to the Police Station at Bangor, and a few hours later the little fellow was gratified to find his sister directed to the same shelter. For some reason it would seem that the mother left the town on the day she expected her children to arrive, but they were well cared for by Inspector and Mrs. Roberts, who fed them from the family board for two days, and clothed the boy. From inquiries made from the Widnes police respecting the mother's whereabouts, it was ascertained that she was too poor to send for the children home. They were, therefore, taken to the Bangor Workhouse.

div.head: MARRIAGE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: MARRIAGE AT RUNCORN.

The marriage of Mr. John Peck to Miss Mary Ann Gittens, daughter of Mr. W. Gittens, boot and shoe maker, Lowlands-road, was solemnized at the Primi- tive Methodist Chapel, Greenway-road, Runcorn, on Wednesday. The Rev. C. Finch, resident minister, officiated. The bride, who was attire ll in a grey embroidered robe with hat to match, was given away by her father, Mr. William Gittens. The brides- maids wig) carried bouquets of flowers, the gift of the bridegroom, were Miss Peck, Miss Bean, Miss Hewitt, Miss Nellie Edwards, and Miss Julia Peck. A very large congregation assembled in the chapel to witness the cere- mony. Mr. William Gittens,jun., presided at the organ, and played the "Wedding March." The wedding lun- cheon was held at the home of the bride's father, after which the happy couple left for Blackpool. Messrs. Yarwood Rrothers supplied the coaches. Heaton saw the de- fendant acting in a strange manner, on Pex Hill. He was almost without clothing and could give no proper account of himself. div.head: PENKETII.
div.p: PENKETII.
TRIP TO WINDgRMP.RR.

On Monday the annual parochial trip of the parishioners of Penketh and Sankey took place to Windermere. 'Buses containing the party,number- ing about 100, left Sankey and Penketh at 6.39 a.m. to meet the train which left Warrington about 7.15. After a pleasant journey, Windermere was reached at 11.15. a.m. Here the party dispersed. During the day Ambleside, Bowness, Grassmere, Stock Ghyll Falls, and other places of interest were visited, and a large number had a pleasant sail on the lake. Dinner and tea were provided at the Queen's Hotel, at twelve o'clock and four o'clock respectively. After tea preparations were made for returning home. Ambleside was left at 5.10 p.m. for Bowness, and the train left Windermere at 6.40, Warrington being reached at 10.30 p.m., and Penketh about eleven o'clock.

SUDDEN DEXTII OF Mit. T. H. WILSON. The death of Mr. T. 11. Wilson, who for several years had filled the post of assistant overseer of Penketh, took place suddenly on Tuesday evening. Mr. Wilson was also Vicar's warden for the parish. He was highly respected in the village, and his death is greatly regretted by all who knew him. It appeared that the deceased, who was 33 years of age, and leaves a widow to mourn his loss, went with the parishioners' trip to 'W indermere on Mon- day. On arriving at Preston he was suddenly taken ill, and when Windermere was reached, medical aid was obtained. Mr. Wilson, however, remained with the party all day, but when he returned to Penketh at night, about eleven o'clock, he was attended by i Dr. Murray, who deemed it advisable to call n the services of Dr. Joseph, of Warrington. These gentle- men did all they could for Mr. Wilson, who, how- ever, grew weaker, and died on Tuesday evening, at i half-past seven. The deceased had not been n good health during the previous week. but he continued his duties, and it was his intention to take a holiday after his return from Windermere.
At Bishop's stortford, on Thursday, Charles Clarke was fined £1 and costs for drinking frTun a bottle of spirits in front of the altar zi,t Bischanger Church, while he was being married.

div.head: ON THE WAY TO AUSTRALIA.
div.p: ON THE WAY TO AUSTRALIA.
LETTER FROM MR. UNSWORTH.

fßelow we give a letter received from Mr. W. Unsworth, who is making the voyage to Melbourne. He sailed from Liverpool by the Liverpool Line on , the 23rd June, along with his wife and family (ten in all) with the object of settling in Australia. Mr. Unsworth was until lately a member of the firm of Messrs.Unsworth & Richmond,Ltd.,gas stove manu- facturers. He has a practical knowledge of every department of the business; and, as there is a wide field in the new land he is going to, he has every reason to hope that he will be able to establish a successful business. A large circle of kis friends in this district will read his letter with great interest. It is as follows:

S. S. Gulf of Guinea, June 20th, 1891 To the Editor of the" Warrington Examiner." Sir,—According to promise, I write you a few lines—as we proceed on our way to Australia, giv- ing you a description of what appears to me to be a pleasant journey. Well,on parting with our friends at Liverpool,with. the usual waving of handkerchiefs and not with- out some throbbing of hearts, we proceeded down the river, with nothing of importance, except the finding of an unlucky stowaway who had the mis- fortune to cough, and thus betray his hiding place. Ile was landed at Holyhead with the pilot, and I suppose sent adrift. We then took a last look at the land of our birth.wondering if we shall ever see it again, and you will quite understand our feelings at such a time when all our nerves had been un- strung with the parting farewell. iVe then turned our attention to our cabins, and having to provide for ten, it was no little matter ; this being done it was then time for bed and everybody ready.

div.head: WEDNESDAY.
div.p: WEDNESDAY.

Next day,when we were well out to sea two more stowaways turned up—these of course have to go on with us—but, poor beggars, they have a hard time of it. I saw one who! should think was about 18 or 19 try to cry out of it; but no ; down in the coal bunker be must go and shovel the coal to the firemen. By this time the sailors had got the ship in good form. Then came the very important work of giving out life belts to all the passengers which, although a very wise provision, was highly sugges- tive, and as I had mace up my mind if it became a question of swimming—l should go like a brick —this little arrangement was an agreeable surprise. The chief officer assured me they would keep 2001bs. afloat for 48 hours, but I trust the journey will be accomplished without their use. The re- mainder of the day was taken up with views at sea, and putting our cabins in what 1 thought first rate order.

div.head: THURSDAY
div.p: THURSDAY

was a splendid morning,the weather being fine from leaving home, and as we sat on deck we saw a shoal of whales spouting away ; they appeared to be very large ones. At 12 o'clock we entered the Bay of Biscay, the water being as calm as a mill-pond, and we congratulated ourselves on the fact that we were gotting over one of the most dangerous points of our journey so easily. But this was not so, for in 'ess than six hours the wind had changed from ;'4llth-east to west, and didn't we get a tossing! The waves came rushing over the sides of the boat, and )zie of my daughters more venturesome than the rest, and not sharp enough to get out of the way, was knocked right over and drenched. This lively state of things lasted 24 hours. The old proverb says "after a storm comes a calm ;"but not dO with us, for there was a swell in between,and if anything the swell is worse than the storm. I have often heard about sailors gaining their sea legs—which I can quite understand now, for the ship rolled from side to side, which to the sailors seems nothing; but to the passengers who had not got over their sea sick- ness it was too much of a good thing. While I was consoling my wife with the assurance that it would not last long, over the ship went, dipping her side almost up to the deck in water. Down we elided off our seats on to the deck, and before we could re- cover ourselves, we got a good drenching. Didn't I catch it! for I had persuaded her to go on deck to see if it would do her good, and being very poorly Ahe was in no very pleasant frame of wind. But, no matter, I must have a good laugh at the comical position. This settled my wife for the next 24 hours, for she came to the conclusion that bed was the best place. Now for my defective cabin arrangements, for, wishing to keep to ourselves, we take our meals in our own cabins using a box for a table in each one; and I can assure you the position was most comical, for, as the vessel heaved, the teapot would go sliding down the table, and in the attempt to save it you can just imagine the result. This, however, I think I have put right by suspending the table (which I made in the carpenter's shop), from the top of the cabin, with cords like the end of a scale, and hanging the teapot in the middle which answers very well so far.

div.head: SATUNDAY.
div.p: SATUNDAY.

We saw a couple of whales, some porpoises and a few grampus—a fish something like a whale. At 10 o'clock the whole of the ship's crew turned out for life-boat practice, and it was interesting to see the quickness with which they swung the boat over the side. These practices, I understand, take place every Saturday. During the day I made the ac- quaintance of the officers of the ship : they were first-rate men who know their business and do it; and if the Gulf Line of S.S., keep such men on all their boats they will soon have as good a line of steamers from Liverpool as any port in England. From that you will gather, Mr. Editor, that I am not sorry I called on you in preference to going by the Orient, and would strongly advise people com- ing out to Australia to give you a call ; and if you make as good arrangements for them as you did for me they will have little to complain of.

SUNDAY. was a very hot day. When I say hot I mean it. Al- though the awnings are up, the heat is very great, and as I write this, people are lying about on deck in all directions, with as little clothes on as pos- sible. Of course, being Sunday, the usual service had to be gone through, and as we had a Wesleyan minister on board, he was M.C. There was a fairly good muster; some being Roman Catholics who pre- fer their own service, others holding other views, there were, however, as many absent. The rest of the day was spent in convetsation and singing, my family joining in with them.

MONDAY. All are looking anxiously for Las Palmas,one of the Canary Isles, where we stop about 8 hours to take in coal, so that we shall have an opportunity of looking round the place, and posting this letter. Hoping we may arrive safely at Melbourne, whence I will write to you again, I am, yours &e., W. UNSWORTIL
A NARROW ESCAPE ON THE RAILWAY.

Last evening a platelayer named Talbot had a narrow escape from being killed at Ditton railway station. The 4.20 p.m. train from Liverpool to Stockport travels on the fast line until approach- ing Ditton, when it is changed on to the slow line. Talbot was standing in the fourfoot of the slow line a few yards beyond the points as the train approached, and the driver who was keeping a sharp look out, saw the man's danger and loudly whistled. Apparently Talbot thought the train would proceed on the fast line and took no notice lof the warning, and the driver immediately shut off steam and applied the break. Travelling at great speed, the train could not be brought i to a standstill before t was upon Talbot but tae train was on the point of stopping and after the engine had knocked Talbot down the tram did not more a yard over his body. Beyond a few skin wounds on the face and an injury to the arm Talbot was uninjured. The rail way officers, and a large number of passengers saw the occur- rence and Mr. Smith, the stationmaster sent his am- bulance men down to the spot with the stretcher expecting to pick up the dead and mangled form of the platelayer. The spectators were loud in their praises of the engine drivers' promptitude
The "Irish Times" states that confirmation has been received in Dublin of the drowning of four midshipmen of the Respite. at Vancouver. One was the son of the late Lord Mountmorris.

A CABMAN TOO FREE WITH HIS TONGUE

George Long, cab driver, was charged at the Warring- ton Police Court, on Monday, with using obscene lan- guage in the cab hut opposite the Central Station, on the 10th inst. Evidence was given that the defendant was called across the street into the hut obe present at a meeting of cabmen, which Mr. Alfred Woods, jeweller, had arranged, and that on entering the hut the defen- dant, probably amazed at the possibility of losing a chance of hire of his cab. used the objectionable espres- sic:G.—The defendant was discharged on payment of 55.. but was informed that if brought up again he would probably have his licence taken from Min.—The Chief Constable said it Would be his duty to bring the matter before.the Committee of the Corporation at the time for the renewal of cab-drivers' licenses.

div.head: STRANGE STREET SCENE.
div.p: A STRANGE STREET SCENE.

At the Magistrates Court on Monday. Joseph Caldwell, of 152, Winwick-road, was charged with using abusive language in that thoroughfare on the evening of the 15th ult. P.C.'s Turnei, Hollingsworth, and "Marsh gave evidence. It appeared that they went to look after a lot of young men bathing in a pond off Winwick-road, and who ran away on seeing them. Hollingsworth got the clothes of one boy agcd 10, and brought them into the street close to defendant's house, the lad following. The defendant came up with his wife and abused the con- stable for taking the boy's clothes, using the language complained of. He was like a madman and his wife was the same. Holline-sworth admitted that in reply to a joke by the defendant's wife he had told her that if she went to bathe in the pit she would make a big tide.— The defendant said Turner got bold of his arms and twisted them.—Thos. Gilmore said as he came out of Ball= Forge he saw the boy running about without his clothes, and heard Caldwell ask the constable to give the lad them, upon which he twisted Caldwell's arms, and Marsh said Turner merely pushed Caldwell ciway. The case was dismissed, the Mayor admonishing the defen- dant, but in an exeusatory manner referring to the fre- cwency withwhich he himself like most others had when a lad been chased by the police, especially for bathing. A TRUCULENT BEERHOUSE KEEPER AND HIS WIFE. •

At the Magistrates' Court, on Thursday, John Shaw, landlord of the Harp and Crown beerhouse, was charged with usinc, malicious threats to his wife Jane Shaw, on the night of the 21st inst. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the defence.—The wife did n6.t appear against her husband, and the Chief-Constable stated that the prose- cution was a police one, e, the wife wishing to leave the matter in their hands. She gave him the best of charac- ters.—lnspector Spinks said at 20 minutes to 12 on the night in question he was in the police station and heard screams proceeding from the Harp and Crown beerhouse opposite. As sood as he got across the otreet the door of the house was opened by theslefendant's wife who carried a baby in her arms and was screaming " murder " and "help." The defendant came out too, and said with an oath that he would cut her head off before two o'clock in the morning.' He went into the house and fetched an axe. Witness asked him to be quiet and he banged the door in his face. He got the woman into a neighbour's house, and in the morning, by the Chief-Constable's direction went to the defendant to try to make the peace between him and his wife, so that she might go back home. He said, " I may as well tell you. lam determined to finish her," and with :an oath repeated that he would cut her head off, adding, "I am sober now; I will do it."—By Mr. Browne: He said she had charged him with immorality with another woman and it was utterly untrue, and that was the reason he had used threats. He wept bitterly about the matter and seemed to feel the charge. He was a very decent man; and nothing wrong had been heard of him before. Mr. Browne said he did not deny the threats, but his client had had the provocation mentioned, and asked that the bench would deal with him by simply binding him over and ordering him to pay costs.—The Bench took the course suggested.—Mr. Hunt corrected an impression that existed that Mrs. Shaw had taken these proceedings, and said the police had taken them on their on account. She had nothing to do with them. ,
CHARGE OF STEALING A TOY.-GOING A FAIRING AFTER A
ROUGH FASHION.

At the Warrington Police Court on Monday James Ross, married man, aged 20, of 7, Briscoe-st., employed at the Runcorn copper and alkali works was charged with being drunk and disorderly in the fair ground on Saturday night, and assaulting P.C. Jones, Barlow' and Delahaye, also with stealing from the stall of Wm. Hewitt, in the fair ground, the same night, a child's musical toy, and Ann Gore, of Dakin's-court, was charged with receivingit knowing it to have been stolen. John Ross, father of James Ross, and who is employed by the Corporation and lives with Gore was charged with assaulting P.C. Delahaye on the same occasion. It appeared from the Chief Constable's statement and the evidence given that about 9 o'clock on the night in ques- tion James Ross who was drunk, John Ross who was sober, and Gore, who was also sober, went to the stall, of which Mrs. Hewitt had charge, in the temporary absence of her husband, and John Ross bought a toy there. James Ross 'picked up a musical toy similar to one now produced, and commenced to play upon it. Mrs. Hewitt asked him to pay her for it and let her go on with her business, but he said he had paid for it and also that he had not had it, and walked away without paying. She followed him and be put his hand on her chest, threatened her, and commenced using bad language to her. Police Constable Jones came up and remonstrated with him, upon which he struck the constable with his fist in the face. Jones then seized him and Jones and P.C.'s Barlow, and Delahaye, who came up, were indiscriminately assaulted by James Ross ; then Jain furiously assaulted Delahaye but probably did not know he was a constable as he was in plain clothes or, Mr. Hunt said, would not have done, having given the police assistance on various occasions. Delahave lost his bat in the struggle, and it could not be found.— Wm. Hunt,a toy dealer,whose stalls is opposite Hewitt's, said he never saw a man stand his ground better than Jones did with James Ross.—James Ross was sentenced to six months imprisonment with hard labour, on the charges of being drunk and disorderly and assaulting the police, the other charge being withdrawn, Gore was dis- missed, and John Ross was fined 10s. and costs, the Mayor remarking that the constables had behaved very bravely, and hoping that they would be recommended to the Watch Committee for some reward.
A FIERCE ATTACK ON A CONSTABLE.-THREATENING AN

INSPECTOR WITH A REVOLVER. At the Warrington Police Court yesterday Daniel Weston and Charles Naylor, Powey's-st., 'were charged with being drunk and disorderly the previous night; and assaulting P.C.Rylatt. Police-Inspector Spinks said about ten minutes past 11 that night Weston escaped from the custody of P.C. Rylatt on being apprehended for being drunk and disorderly, and witness with Sergeant Row- botham went to his house on the same night to appre- hend him. He asked Weston to open the door, but he refused, with an oath, and said they could burst the door open, and shouted with another oath, to. his wife to bring his revolver, saying he would see whether they would come in or not. They burst the door open, and arrested him and brought him to the station. He was mad drunk. He said when charged with assaulting Rylatt "I did give it to him; , there is no doubt." but said he struck in self-defence. Witness and Rowbotham also arrested Naylor at his own house, after being kept waiting a considerable time at the door, and he also admitted thumping Rylatt several times on being shoved by him. P.C. Rylatt deposed to

most savage assaults being committed upon him by the two prisoners earlier h 1 the night, and Sergeant Row- botham having corroborated the inspector's statement, Weston said he had used a certain expression to Naylor and another at his own door which he quoted, which is utterly unrenortable, and which was applied to Rylatt, who came and struck him on the mouth for us.- ing it; and he struck back as any Englishman would do. He was talking quietly at his door. He stated that Rylatt was under the influence of drink. Inspector Spinks and Sergeant Rowbotham were called, and both declared that he was sober, and was a most steady man. Naylor said Rylatt came up and 'shoved him and he struck him back. The constable must have been drunk or mad to interfere.as he did, for they were doing no- thing.—The Bench fined each of the defendants ss. and costs for the• first offence, and and costs for the as- sault.

div.head: QUARREL BETWEEI4 Two SHOWMEN,
div.p: QUARREL BETWEEI4 Two SHOWMEN,

At the Magistrates' Court, yesterday, Thomas White- ley, and Kate Whiteley his wife, a woman of very large build, proprietors of a tent show, in Warrington fair ground, were charged with assaulting,on Tuesday night, Wm. Hafercorn, a German by birth, and a sculptor, of Liverpool, who also travels about with an exhibition. Mr. Browne appeared for the complainant. He stated that his client was proceeding in Manchester County Court to recover from defendants certain articles of his which he alleged they had in their custody. He came on the day in question to Warrington fair to see Mr. Bur- nett, a show proprietor. He was talking to Mr. Burnett's man, Merritt when Mrs. Whiteley rushed out of the tent and got hold of the complainant by the throat and said, "You must come into my place," using a foul expression. He refused to go, and then Mr. Whiteley came and they dragged him into the tent. They pinned him in a corner, put their fists up to him, and used all kinds of threats to deter him from continuing his action against them. On Wednesday morning he came to Warrington for the pur- pose of taking out. summonses against them, when he met Mr. Whiteley, who used frightful threats to him.— The complainant in his evidence stated that he was liter- ally carried by the defendants into their tent. He con- firmed his solicitor's statement. On Wednesday morning Mr. Whiteley called him a scoundrel and said he had not hit him yet, but when he did he would know about it. The complainant admitted that Mr. Whiteley never hit him.—Alfred John Merritt John Hodgson, and a man named Allen supported the complainant's evidence, and Merritt said at his request he followed him into the tent; and he corroborated his description of his treatment there. Mrs. Whiteley said she took the complainant by the collar not the throat as stated for the prosecution, and said she did so after asking him quietly V) come into the tent, to give her a note that she did not owe for ground rent for his show at Wigan where he had used her name and not paid the rent.—Mr. Whiteley said he had brought the complainant and his family from a cellar in London where they were starving, and brought him up and made a man of him, besides allowing his father 15s. a week when ill and letting him have £l5 be- sides which was still owing. The complainant had been going about the country doing them (the defendants) all the harm he could. He had taken his young men from him; and came to Warrington to take another.—'the complainant denied the statement as to his procedure at Wigan.—The defendants called Mr. Pface,market inspec- tor, who gave them a good character, and their daugh- ter. who said her father only put his hand on Hafer- corn's shoulder, and her mother seized him by the collar. They were bound over to keep the peace for six months and ordered to pay costs.

The complainant said she had lost her purse containing five shillings, and had heard that the defendant's child had tound it and taken it to Mrs. Mason, who sent a message it she wanted it she must fetch it. She went to the defendant's for it when her mother met her at the yard door and gave her ss. saying. "there is your money make no bother about it." She demanded her purse. The defendant's mother said she would buy tier a purse. The defendant came and seized her by the hair and pulled her on to her back, and her head struck the wall. The defendant said her child never brought a purse or money to her, and her mother only gave the complainant ss. for quietness. She struck the complainant because she first struck her over her mother's shoulder. Her

"The County—Council - Year Book" for 1891 is a handsome, well-arranged, and comprehensive volume of over 600 pages. It has been prepared by Mr. T. B. Brown, the well-known advertising agent, who has spared no pains of 'cost to provide a thoroughly satisfactory work. It gives a survey of the working of the County Councils of England, Wales, and Scotland from their formation to the present time. As may be supposed there is a mass of detail, Mr. Brown having been assisted by offi- cials and local journalists in securing the requisite material and insuring accuracy as far as it may be possible. For frontispiece there is a highly-finished portrait of the Right Hon. C. T. Ritchie, M.P., Pre- sident of the Local Government Board, who piloted the County Councils Act through the House of Com- mons. There are, besides, portraits of the chairman of evety County Council, most of them being full- plate pictures, while all of them are executed in the most finished style. The volume opens with the ; Local Government-Act itself, and there is a series of special articles by specially qualified writers upon such subjects as "The housing of the working classes," "County Finance," "Sanitary functions of County Councils," 'Technical Instruction," " Medi- cal officers and sanitary inspectors," &c. This "Year Book" is invaluable to members of County Councils And all who are interested in the wailing of these important bodies. It is well bound and well printed, on superior paper, and published at 15s. "A handboolZ of the Rivers and Broads of Norfolk and Suffolk," by Mr. G. C. Davies author of " Nor- I folk broads and rivers," sets one a-longing to explore a region which is in great contrast to the ordinary holiday resorts. Mr. Davies seems to have explored every nook and corner of the broads; and he writes critically; and with a love of his subject. The handbook,which is one of 170 odd pages, is profusely illustrated with representations of the picturesque bits which are to be found on these rivers and broads. Anglers and yachtsmen will find all the information they require. There is a useful table of distances, and a lerge map which enables the reader readily to follow the author's 'descriptions in the various journeys which he takes. The book is published by Messrs. Jarrold and Sons,of London, and is well printed and handsomely bound. Mr. W. Bailey, ex-nresident of the Manchester AsSoci- tion of Engineers, has issued an address of 20 pages with the title of Outside the class-room—thoughts for young engineers." It touches on the discipline of the intellect; force of character ; the use of imagination ; and the reign of law. The address is as stimulating as it is thoughtful, and it is admirably calculated to encourage 'the love of accuracy and hard work.

"All About`the koyal Navy," is from the pen of W. Laird Cowes, who is well known as a writer upon this subject. The object which he has in view is benefitting the service and inducing ordinary readers to take an in- terest in it. The subjects treated include, battle ships as they are and as they used to be; heavy guns ; torpedoes; high explosives • submarine boats; battle ships; and the next naval battle. There is a useful chapter devoted to " llo,a to enter the royal navy." Another chapter gives a list of the ships up to May of the present year. There are six full page illustrations; and the handbook is published by Messrs. Cassell and Co., price is. The "Magazine of Art" for July has for frontispiece a powerful etching of William Thorne's painting known as "A romance without words." The leading paper is one on "Some portraits of Tkackeray " ; and it is capitally Illustrated with about a dozen reproductions of portraits and busts of the great novelist. Mr. W. S. Hunt has a paper on "Some Punch artists." There is a paper, illustrated, on" The Maddocks collection at Bradford " ; and an article, strikingly illustrated, on "The artistic aspects of figure photography." Other illustrated papers are "The metal ornament of bound books," and a sketch of the career of H. S. Leifchild.

The subjects of the "Cabinet Portrait Gallery" for July, published by Messrs. Cassell and Co., are Mr. Frederic Harrison, Mrs. Mary Davies, and Mr. Bancroft, There is, as usual,"a descriptive sketch of the subject of each photograph; and of the photographs themselves it is highest praise to say that there is no falling off in the artistic excellence which marked the first issue.

The extra summer number of "Cassell's Family Maga- zine" bears the title of 'The Crown of the Year." Its price is 7d., and it contains a capital story "A matter of skill," by Beatrice Whitby, "Three courses on an oil stove," by Lizzie Heritage, "In Flanders," by James Baker, F.R.G.S. ; "Little General Scott," and magazine gossip.

- The current serial stories in " Cassell's Magazine" are "A Quaker girl," and "The temptation of Dulce Car- ruthers." There are,besides, three complete stories, and a full supply of miscellaneous papers, including "My summer in a London garden"; "About London cabs"; "The garden in July"; and "The home of the con- queror," which is effectively illustrated by Mr. Herbert Railton.—The "Quiver " for July is up to its highest level both as to text and illustration. The serial stories are "For Erica's Sake," "On eagles' wings." Amongst the miscellaneous papers we have "A Sunday in Nor- way " ; "The sunshine of smiles"; "An afternoon at Barnes" ; "Building and blundering " ; &c.—" Little Folks" for this month has for frontispiece a charmingly finished chromo of" Granny's story. The illustrations are, throughout, varied and excellent,and the same may be said of the bright sketches, and odds and ends in prose and verse. The present issue is the first part of a new volume.

Messrs. Cassell and Co have just commenced the issue of their" Book of Sports:and pastimes." It is fully illustrated and will be completed :in twelve parts at 3d. each. Amongst the latest publications of their National Library (3d. each) should be mentioned "The life of Nelson," by Robert Southey. One may well ask what next and next for threepence.

We have also to hand the current numbers of Cassell's "Storehouse of General Information," a fine art edition of Robinson Crusoe," Familiar wild Flowers," "Figuier's Popular Scientific Works," " British Battles, on Land and Sea,"" Natural History," " Science for All," "The World of Adventure," and" The Dore Gallery." The leading paper in the" Newbery House Magazine" for July is from the pen of the Rev. G. S. Reaney, for- merly of Warrington. Its title is " Dessent at the May meetings," and its tone is quite in keeping with the pamphlet on his reasons for joining the Church of Eng- land. Mr. Reaney sees the smallest faults in Dissent- ing sects, but has no eye as yet for the glaring defects of the church he has joined. The contents also include The art of reading as applied to the clergy," " St. Gil- bert of Sempringham and his Order," " Historical sketches," "My friend Quiz," " The boy bishop,"" A dead city,"" Church notes and queries," &c. Portraits of celebrities at different times of their lives are continued in the "Strand Magazine" for July. Vogler & Co. It is from the pen of Mr. W. E. Geddes, the European manager for the Company, whose little work on " Do you know how to cook fish? "has been of great service in popularising a number of admir- able recipes. The souvenir has an eye to business all through, but, apart from that, it contains plenty of readable matter.

RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS AND THE SHIP CANAL. Along the whole line of the Manchester Ship Canal there is no district expecting to derive more advantage from the construction of the great water- way than that of Runcorn, and the governing body, the Board of Commissioners instead of harassing the promoters, in the Manner of many others, have on the contrary aided them all in their power. It is not strange therefore that the Company should invite the members to pay the works an official visit, and this took place an Wednesday. With the ex- ception of Mr. Dobson the whole of the Commis- sioners availed themselves of the invitation, there being present Mr.H.J. Grice the chairman,Messrs.P. Speakman C.C., J. W. Lightburn, Henry White, J. Pritchard, W. Hankinson, W. Timmins, E. Imison, R. Abel, W. Mellor, P. Smith, F. Wiswall, J. Meadow- croft, W. R. Wass, S. Taylor, E. Wynne-Humphreys, and W. Fisher. The following officials were also of the Company: Messrs. F. A. Lake (law clerk), E. Marshall, (secretary), W. Barker (surveyor), Dr. McDougall (medical officer), and J. B. Holland (treasurer). Leaving Runcorn by the 10 22 train they proceeded to Latchford, where they were met ny Mr. Hunter, chief assistant to Mr. Leader Williams who was unfortunately unable to be present. Mr. Hunter personally conducted the " tour" to Eas- tham. The magnificent locks and bridges at Latch- ford were first viewed and much admired, and then adjournment was made to the Saracen's Head,wh ere Mr. Speakman, by order of the Ship Canal Co., had provided a capital luncheon. The party then en- tered a saloon carriage attached to a loco, and werel driven off in the direction of Runcorn, catching glimpses of the. works as they proceeded. A stop I was made at Big field to see the arrangements for , the Vyrnwy water scheme. Then on through Run- corn to Weston, where they changed into another saloon. The weaver sluices were much admired. The great landslip near Ellesmere Port was noticed,and the scene of the recent sad accident was inspected. At Ellesmere Port the Commissioners detrained and embarked on board the steamer Fanny and had a pleasant sail down the canal to Eastham, where the docks and locks were viewed. The proceedings con- chided with a dinner at Eastham Hotel. The Com- missioners were well pleased with the courtesy and attention shown them, and greatly enjoyed their first visit to the works.

div.head: WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT.

CHARGES OF Tit Err. On Saturday morning, three boys, tramps, named Watkins, Kirkham, and Huxam, were charged before Mr. Z. Armitage, at thel Occasional Court, with stealing from a baker's cart in Liverpool-road, on the night of the 17th inst. The prisoners were walking together along the Liverpool- road, when, according to the evidence, one of them took a 41b. loaf from the cart, and ran away with it in the direction of Warrington. The driver of the cart was informed, and drove after and caught him. The other two prisoners were apprehended the same night. They were remanded till Tuesday morning, when they were again brought up, before Mr. Tinsley, and further re- manded till Wednesday next.—On Tuesday morning, William Bell was brought up charged with stealing a lock and a whitewash brush, value 83., the property of Josiah Furness, at Sankey, on the 14th inst. He was also charged with stealing two aprons, value 35., the property- of T. Jennings, at the same time and place. The pri- soner had absconded to another part of Lancashire, and there given himself up to the police for the thefts. He was also remanded till Wednesday next.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY. —Before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. Henry Reynolds.

CRUELTY TO A Hons.—John Gratton, a boatman, was summoned for cruelly ill-treating a horse by working it while in an unfit state, on the 7th July.—lnspector Dowty, R.S.P.C.A., said the aniinal was poor in condi- tion, aged, and suffering from ring bone. It was lame on the near fore leg, and there was an old suppurating woundmn the withers.—The defendant, who did not deny the offence, was fined 10s., and costs us. 6d. CADISHEAD AND IRLAM V. HARPURHISY 2m ELEVEN.— On Saturday Harpurhey met' Cadishead and Irlam, at Cadishead, for the first time this season. Going in to bat first, Harpurhey scored 17, to which Cadishead re- sponded by 43 runs, thus winning by 26 runs. In this match S. Taylor took seven wickets for 12 runs, and J. Daniels made 15 runs out of the 43. WARRINGTON v. BOWDON.—This return match was played at Arpley on Saturday. Although Warrington were victorious in the first match, the interest had not flagged in the least, and there was an average attend- ance present when Warrington commenced their innings on a good wicket.. Brelsford opened with a maiden, but Kennett was despatched for six in his first essay. The professional, however, reached J. J. Crosfield's wicket in his second over, and the board read 6-1-1. With Lee joining S. M. Crosfield runs came freely, the home cap- tain scoring rapidly, chiefly from the amateur. Boun- dary hits were frequent, so at 35 McKean relieved Ken- nett, but the change proved rather expensive, his first four overs yielding 19 runs. Brelsford continued to bowl a good length, and with the score at 59 S. M. Crosfield skied one to Gibbon. His 39 was the result of good cricket, and included seven fours. The next four wickets fell at 60, 66, 84, 85, but on Bell joining Lee, a complete mastery of the bowling was witnessed. Lee now opened his shoulders, and with the score at 113, completed his 50. Bell, too,put in some good strokes,his cutting being particularly fine. Stephens relieved Brelsford at 118, and in his second over Lee his first ball for 2, the second and third he lifted over the boundary by square leg hits, but by the fourth he was bowled for a fine 65, which included eleven fours. He had been at the wickets whilst 127 runs had been added, andhis performance coining so soon after his admirable display at Liverpool, should give his average a rare lift. W. H. Podmore became Bell's partner, and another protracted stand was made. Bell now hit out with vigour, and changes in the mode of attack were made, but all to no purpose. At 162 Brels- ford resumed at his old end, but Bell cut him finely to the boundary twice in one over ; but with a total at 189, Podmore was caught at the wicket, and the innings was declared closed. Bell's 50 was a good innings on the whole, and, judging from his play on Saturday, lie is sure to prove an acquisition to the Warringtonians. With a little over two hours to get the runs in, Bowdon commenced with T. Kennett and W. S. Gibbon to the deliveries of Smith and Bell. Runs came at a fair pace at the commencement, and after Gibbon had hit three balls to the boundary and a siggle, Bell reached his wicket with a beauty. Kennett retired eleven runs later., Bell also accounting for him. It was now Smith's turn, for at 44 Wainwright was dismissed by an extra fast one, whilst four runs had only been added when Stephens was run out owing to a brilliant piece of fielding on the part of George Clarke. McKean, ' however, batted finely, 'but Brelsford and Aubrey both fell victims to Smith, Clark bringing off a fine one- handed catch at the wicket,which accounted for Aubrey. Smith affected a fine catch which sent McKean to the right about at 68, but Ferneyhough knocked a dozen to- gether in quick time, when Podmore caught him from a lofty hit. The last pair offered a stubborn resistance, Livesey hitting freely. He soon put together 21, but with thetotaPat 106, Haworth was bowled, and War- rington were, left winners by 83 runs and two wickets. Score and bowling analysis :

NEWTON V. WIGAN.—A bowling contest between the Newton and Wigan clubs came off at Bedford Leigh on Tuesday. There was a fair attendance, but there was heavy rain during the play which together with the fact that the green was much larger than that to which the Newtonians have been accustomed at home, militated against them sorely. At any rate the Newton team, though the champion one of the county, had to submit to a reverse. The following were the scores : NEWTON. WIGAN. Mr. Liptrott. as captain of the Newton team, proposed the toast of the winning club, congratulating it on having reversed the result of the previous year so far as Newton is concerned. div.head: LIABILITY OF EMPLOYERS.
div.p: THE LIABILITY OF EMPLOYERS.
IMPORTANT DECISION.

The House of Lords gave a judgment on Tuesday which upsets all previous decisions under the Employers' Liability Act, as to the extent to which a man who ac- cepts dangeronS employment is precluded from an action for damages should he be injured. The effects of the decision is that if a man is so situate that he cannot use his eyes to see when danger is imminent, the employer is guilty of negligence if he does not take means to give him warning. In the case in question the man, a navvy, was employed in a cutting where he could not see the " jibbing " of some stones over his head by means of a crane. The Court of Appeal decided that as the man voluntarily undertook dangerous employment, he had no claim, but the House of Lords, Lord Bramwell dissenting have reversed this judgment.
MR DIGGLE ON THE INTERCEPTING DEPOTS AGAIN.

• At the Warrington Police Court, on Saturday mor- ning, Mr. William Diggle applied to the magistrates for a summons against the Corporation or the Sani- tary Committee of the Town Council. He said that on Friday the people living near the Howley inter- cepting depot were almost poisoned, and that mor- ning it was almost as bad. He had not been able to take breakfast in consequence of the smell, and was now quite ill. Alderman Burgess (the chair- man), said both he and his brother mdgistrate, Coun- cillor Voisey, were members of that committee, dud they consequently had no jurisdiction in the mat- ter.—Councillor Voisey : It means your application ii postponed.—The deputy magistrates' clerk said Mr. Diggle had been informed that he must apply to justices who were not members of the Corpora- tion.—Ald. Burgess (ironically) : And I would indict the Corporation if I were you, Mr. Diggle, and proye there is a nuisance. We don't refuse you anythina; we only tell you we have no jurisdiction.—The Deputy-Clerk: You will have to indict them as a common .nuisance.—Mr. Diggle: I quite understand you are the culprits, you know.—Alderman Burgess: We don't admit that; you are the culprit.—Mr. Diggle: You create a nuisance unnecessarily. You know it is a nuisance.—Alderman Burgess: We know very different; we have told you so often. As he was leaving the court, Mr. Diggle called out "I wish you'd go down and have a smell at it now."
SALES OF PUBLIC HOUSE PROPERTY
IN WARRINGTON.

On Wednesday, Mr. T. Tunstall offei6d for sale at the Blue Bell Inn, Warrington, the fully-licensed public-house known as the "Ram's head" and, also as the "Central Hotel," in Horsemarket-st. The auctioneer, in his renitarks, pointed out that it was very seldom now-a-days that a licensed house was put up for sale, owing to the monopoly of them which the brewers had obtained. The "Ham's Head," he considered, occupied one of the best posi- tions in Warrington, being close to the Central Station, opposite Scotland-road, near to Bewsey-st., and having frontages to Horsemarket-st. and Peter- st. and a back entrance from Golden Grove. There was a very considerable business done at the public- house, and this business, he considered, might be largely increased by the judicious expenditure of a little money on the modernising of the house and making it more suitable for business as it is now conducted. The bidding commenced at £2,000 and the offers came rapidly until £5,525 was reached, for which sum the property was knocked down to Messrs. Peter Walker and Sons, brewers, of Warrington. Until £4,000 was reached there were several bidders, but after the amount had been offered the competition for the property was prac- tically between Messrs. Walker and Sons, and Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Company. _ _ TEE LION HOTEL.

Messrs. P. Walker and Sons have also now be- come the, proprietors of the "Lion Hotel." The "Lion," it will be remembered,was put up.for sale by auction a few weeks ago, and £7,000 was offered for it, but it was withdrawn, the reserve price be- ing £7,500. Since then negotiations have been en- tered into with Messrs. Walker and Sons with the result that they have acquired the property at a price which is over £7,000 but less than £7,500.

div.head: WARRINGTON TEMPERANCE FEDERATION. ANNUAL REPORT.
div.p: WARRINGTON TEMPERANCE FEDERA- TION. ANNUAL REPORT.

In their annual report for 1890, which has just been issued, the Committee of the above Federation say that they " desire to place on record their supreme thankfulness for the measure of progress which the temperance movement has obtained throughout the country during the past year. The defeat of the Government compensation proposals, which if carried would have created a vested interest in licenses and re4dered any real reduction in the number of public-houses impossible; the judgment in the appeal of Sharpe v. Wakefield which has, it is be- lieved, given the death-blow to the idea of pecuniary compensation ; the second reading of the Welsh Direct Veto Bill • and last but one least, the passing of the Irish Sunaity Closing Act, are fruits of their labours, which ma i- well be hailed by all temperance reformers with gratitude and joy. Never was the question more keenly discussed by politicians of all shades of opinion. Licensing reform is fast becoming the problem of the day. Victory cannot be far distant. During the past year the Federation has not failed to bear its share of the battle. When the great conflict was raging around the compensation proposals already referred to, a public meeting was held, and resolutions were unanimously passed, protesting against the endow- ment of the traffic with public money. Copies of these resolutions were forwarded by the Secretary to the First Lord of the Treasury. the Home Secretary, and the President of the Local Government Board, and it was in response to such resolutions forwarded from all parts of the country, that the clauses were ultimately dropped. At the recent Brewster Sessions, acting on what was be- lieved to be sufficient grounds, the Federation opposed not only the applications for new licenses, but also a number of applications for renewal. No new licenses were granted and one application for renewal was refused. The recent decision in Sharpe v. Wakefield, setting forth the wide discretion of magistrates in cases of renewal, renders your Committee still more hopefnl as to the effect of any action they may take in the future. The main feature of the work of the year has been the formation, under the auspices of the Federation, of the Warrington Working-men's Open-air Temperance Mis- sion. Weekly meetings have been held in all weathers by the working-men themselves, whose self-denying labour cannot be too highly praised. No less a sum than £l3O has been raised by them for the work, which ap- pears to have been remarkably successful amongst the poorer classes of the town, and your committee have been glad to give them every help in their power, both in money and in providing speakers." The balance sheet shows that the expenditure for the past year has been £B2 6s. 5d., which leaves a balance in the bank of £2 16s. 3d. The ordinary subscriptions for the year amount to £36 7s. 6d., and the subscrip- tions received towards licensing expenses to £24 18s. 6d. Mr. H. H. Dutton has been appointed collector for the Federation.

div.head: 41 THE BISLEY RIFLE MEETING
div.p: 41 THE BISLEY RIFLE MEETING

At Bisley, on Saturday, the firing in the serond stage of the Queen's Prize competition, at 500 an 600 yards, resulted in Sergeant Milner, 2nd V.B. Der'oy, becoming the winner of the Silver Medal. Milner and Private Muirhead, 3rd Lanark, each made an aggregate of 209, and firing the tie shots late in the afternoon was a very exciting event. Sergeant Milner beat his opponent bY thirteen points as against 9. The Silver Medallist is a farmer and publican at Clay Cross. He first shot al Wimbledon in 1876,and won the Alexandra Prize in 1884- rile Belgian Cup has been won by the 3rd Lanark, the China Cup by the Lanark County team, the Prince of Wales's Prize by Captain M‘Mickling, 44th Battalion Canada, and the United Hospitals Challenge Cup by St. Thomas's. In the Mackinnon International Volley Firing competition the decision is reserved. Fine weathet prevailed in the camp at Ilisley on Mon- day, when there were several minor prizes competed fos. In the Mackinnon match the Canadians had withdrawn their protest against the English team being declared the winners, but the Jersey men persisted in their (Neer tion. The Council on Monday,,decided in favour of the English team. Sergeant A. Lawrence, Ist Dunbartonf , and Sergeant Parry, 2nd V.B. Cheshire, shot off their tle lin the Grand Aggregate, and Parry won by thirteen ,'points to eight. The London Scottish team beat the I Victorian Rifle team in a match for a shield value £lOO. I The Wimbledon Cup was won by Captain Mellish, 4th Notts. with a score of 65 points, and Corporal ROscamp. 2nd Northumberland Fusiliers, was the winner •of the Volunteers'. Aggregate. The All-Comers' Aggregate hog been won by Sergeant Keating, of Liverpool, with 179 points.

THE QUEEN'S PRIZE. The shooting in the final stage of the Queen's at the 800 yards range opened at 2.30 on Tuesday, and the fir ing points were lined with spectators. The weather was bright,but there was a wind blowingsteadily andstrongl9 from the left rear. After sighting shots a few bulls were scored, but a bad opening was made by many of the Queen's hundred. Earl Spencer was one of the most iO. terested of the spectators. Some of the best knovie men were unable to find the target. Corporal Caldwell, 2nd Renfrew, began his score with three inners, and totalled 19 only out of a possible 50. Sergeant Fenwickt who made the highest score at 600 yards, hopelessli broke down missing six times, and putting a bull on the wrong target. On the fifth round Sergeant Milner, the silver medallist led, Private Muirhead standing second. Milner and Sergeant Gibbons, 3rd Middlesex, at the finish of the 800 yards, stood equal firsts with an aggre- . gate of 225. At 900 yards Sergeant Milner very soon dropped out, and it soon became evident that the mall three possible men were Sergeant Gibbons, SergeanP Bugler Hill, and Private Dear. They all shot at the same butt, and here the pressure Of the crowd wee greatest.

- The Queen's prizeman proved to be Private Dear, of the Queen's Edinburgh, who took the goad medal in the- final stage, with a grand aggregate of 269 points* Sergeant-bugler Hill, of the 19th Middlesex, put on au aggregate of 268. When Hill had completed his shots. Dear stood at 263, and had two shots to go. Dear's ninth was a magpie (3), *filch brought his aggregateto 268. He had then to make a magpie to win, an outer (2) 03 tie, and a miss to lose. Everything depended, therefore, upon this one shot; and for the first time during his fir ing Dear betrayed some nervousness. Taking a long aini, he sent the bullet on its course. The magpie disc dull appeared, the target having been hit just within the mag- pie line, and the gold medal was won. A cheer went up, and there was an instant rush of the crowd over the ropes. Brigadier-General M`Donald (Lord Kingsburgh• Lord Justice Clerk of Scotland), the winner's command ing officer, shook hands and offered his warmest congra" tulations. The Queen's prizeman is a small, clean-shavea man, and, being so spare of stature, he was hidden frora I the view of all except a few who were pressing closel. upon him. There were some shouts of "Chair him; but, after a momentary delay, a start was made ori foot for the statistical offices, in the heart of the canal?' On the winner appearing with Brigadier-Gencral Mao' donald, the band of the Buffs struck up "See the coo- querino• hero comes." Private Dear was received hi Earl Waldegrave (President of the Council) and Coun- tess Waldegrave. He was at once conducted to tbo chair in whicn the Queen's prizeinen are annually carried shoulder high through the camp, and was photographed, undergoing the while a good deal of scrutiny from envi- ous eyes. This ordeal over, and the chair vacated* Countess Waldegrave advanced and, amidst cheers* pinned the Queen's badge upon the prizeman's arm, add' ing her congratulations upon his success. Private Dear then, in the capacious arm chair, was carried round the enclosure, accompanied by several members of the band, and thus started on his tour, receiving ovations ha his progress. In the camp of the London Scottish he waS received by Major Alexander, and the loving cup we; passed round. In the other camps, also, the hero of the day was received with befitting honours. The gold medallist is aged thirty-one, and is a solicitor's clerk in Edhaburgh. He joined No. 5 company of the Queen's Edinburgh in 1885. It is known as one of the best shooting companies of the brigade, and from the first Private Dear took a leading prition as a marksmah• He first came to Wimbledon in 1886, and the next year carried off prizes of the value of 50 guineas. At this year's meeting he has taken prizes in all the aggregate but he never until Tuesday won any first at the 'National Rifle Association meetings.

In Wednesday's competitions the Kolapore Challenge Cup was won by the mother country with a grand aggre- gate of 679 points. Canada being second with 672, Wen the Colonial money prize. Guernsey came third with 671 points, Jersey fourth with 641, and the Indian teaht last with 598. The Chancellor's Plate, competed for b 9 teams from Oxford and Cambridge Universities, scas won by Cambridge with an aggregate of 637 against 625. The United Service Cup has gone to the Volunteers. The winner of the Duke of Cambridges Cup is Capt. Gibbet 2nd Gloucester. On Thursday the Elcho Shield was won by England. The scores were :—England, 1,670; Ireland, 1,633 ; Scotland, 1,617. The Charterhouse team again took the Ashburton Challenge Shield, Banks,of Whitgift, wit:O3llLS the Spencer Cup in thesecond stage with 33 points. 11'w Public Schools Veterans Trophy was won by Cheltenhare with 214 points; Lance-Corporal Lichtenstein and Fri- vate Williams, of Charterhouse, secured the Cadet Challenge Trophy and Bronze Medal respectively ; afl in the Yeomanry Inter-Regimental Cup ccmpetition AY` was first, Warwick second, and Dorset third.

div.head: FOUR LIVES LOST IN THE CHANNEL.
div.p: FOUR LIVES LOST IN THE CHANNEL.

A Renter's telegram from Plymouth reports that the North German Lloyd's steamer Dresden from Bremen for Baltimore, with 800 emigrants on board, wehei . off the Start, at a quarter to one on Saturday morning, came into collision with the British brigantine Annie Harris, of Bristol. The latter sank immediately, and four of her crew were drowned, Captain Biscombe and the mate being saved. The Dresden put them on board a fishing smack, which landed them at Plymouth. She then proceeded on her voyage.

div.head: WAR IN CHILI. RUMOURED DEFEAT OF THE CONGRESSIONALISTS.
div.p: THE WAR IN CHILI. RUMOURED DEFEAT OF THE CONGRESSIONA- LISTS.

NEW Ironic, TUESDAY 111-0-11-NIN.G.—The Chilian Minister at Washington has received telegraphic advice agnounc- ing that a battle was fought recently at Huasco between a large force of the insurgents and the vanguard of the loyal troops. The former were routed, leaving 200 dead on the field, while a number of prisoners and a quantity of munition, of war were captured. . • WASHINGTON MONDAY.—A :telegram received from Chili confirms the news of the defeat of Congressionalists at Hua,sco, and states that the insurgent cavalry lost 200 killed, many prisoners, and all their arms.

INTERNATIONAL ,lONGREGATIONAL
COUNCIL.

The proceedings of the International Congregational Council on Saturday included a demonstration in favour of the temperance movement. Addresses were delivered by the President, the Rev. Newman Hall, and others. On Monday, the Council resumed its sitting, President Northrop in the chair. The subject was " How far does the desire for outwardly expressing unity prevail ?" The Rev. Dr. Allton, Rev. Dr. Taylor (New York), the Rev. James Stark (Aberdeen), the Rev. S. B. Handley, and several others took part in the discussion. A resolution was passed in favour of a fraternal confederation,without authority, of all Christian bodies. „ In the afternoon the subject for discussion was "The Lord's Day." The Rev. Arthur ;Attie (Dorchester Massachusetts the Rev. T. Roseby (Sydney), and the Rev. Dr. Bevan (Melbourne) took part in the discussion. On Tuesday, the last day, the claims of Congregational communities throughout the world on the sympathy and aid of the Congregational churches in England and America werg urged, whilst in the, afternoon and again in the evening the subject of missionary work was the chief topic. Amongst the resolutions the Council adopted was one asking that the forthcoming exhibition at Chicago should not be opened on Sunday. In the even- ing a public meeting was held in the City Temple, when the Rev. Dr. Parker delivered an aadress. On Tuesday night the Congregationalist members of the House of Comm:ma entertained at supper in the din- ing room of the House a number of delegates from the United States and Canada, who have been present at the meeting of the International Congregational Council.

div.head: CENSUS RETURNS.
div.p: CENSUS RETURNS.
THE PRESCOT UNION. _

-- - The complete return of the census for Prescot Union show a net increase for the decade of 22,947. The urban portions of the township of Eccleston and Windle, and the whole of the townships of Parr and Sutton, within the union, form the borough of St. Helens, and here we find an increase of 9,816. In eleven other townships there have been increases of population, but in Hale, Knowsley (Lord Derby's village), Rainford (a small mining centre), Speke, and Little Woolton there have been decreases in the numbers of the residents. NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
CRICKET.

•The match with Middlesex was the fourth Lancashire have lost this season, and, says the " Manchester Guar- dian," the demand for the infusion of" new blood" intN the team is again made. We- do not;of course, know why Hewitson and Heaton are not played. It is poss- ible that they may not be able to get away from their clubs; but that they would be valuable Members of the team we shall believe until experience convinces us to the contrary. Mr. Steel, we suppose; we cannot have; but in his absence we should like to see the following eleven representing Lancashire, and batting in the order given :—Barlow, Ward, Smith, Sugg, Briggs,'Heaton, Hewitson, Yates, Hamby, liemble, and Mold. Both the new men are, we believe, natives of the county, and their performances entitle them to a dial.

The cloud which settled over Yorkshire at the begin- ing of the season shows no signs of lifting. The Eleven were twice beaten last week, the victors being Notts and Surrey respectively. Messrs. Smith and JacksOn were not playing up to their reputation in the Notts match, and had it not been for the efforts of Ulyett and Hall the score would have been shockingly bad. Baggalev, the Notts colt, who is only just turned 18 years of age, quite roused the Sheffield crowd to enthusiasm. In the opinion of Arthur Shrewsbury, the youngster is one of the most promising players that the county has had for some years. After their defeat at Braman Lane; the Yorkshiremen journeyed to London, and again offered themselves as victims to Lolimann and Sharpe. The team could hardly have been improved, but in the first innings they could only score 67 runs. The second ven- ture showed a wonderful improvement, and Louis Hall, Cartman, and Mr. Jackson hit in excellent style • but the result, all the same, was a ten-wicket defeat'. Some of the Yorkshire papers are asking "where the county is to be" at the end of the season.

div.head: ROYAL COIIMISSIONS.
div.p: ROYAL COIIMISSIONS.

----- The Royal Commission resumed its proceedings on Wednesday, Section A, which deals with mining, iron, engineering, and cognate trades, sitting with Mr. Dale as chairman. Mr. Dennington, secretary of the Cleve- land Ironmasters' Association, gave evidence as to the constitution of the association and the miners employed. He stated that disputes were referred to a joint com- mittee of masters and miners, and the meth3d had worked well in practise. Mr. Hugh Bell, chairman of the Cleveland Ironmasters' Association, stated that the sliding scale had worked fairly well, but did not suffi- ciently respond to the changes in price -though it was one of the most useful means of preventing disputes. The Royal Commission upon Mining Royalties met again en Wednesday, Lord Northbrook presiding, when Mr. N. T. Williams, manager of the Morgan Gold-miuing Company, Dolgelley, spoke as to the gold-mining in his district. Mr. Williams expressed the opinion that the Welsh gold fields had an important future before them, if only sufficient capital was expended on the industry, and if the mines were economically worked. Ile favoured a reduction in the royalties charged.
