div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

The fourth match of the English football team, in South Africa, was played against a fifteen of Kimberley. The weather was fine and the contest proved more excit- ing than the previous one, in which the colonists were badly beaten almost without a struggle. On this occa- sion the Kimberley team fought hard, and, though they were worsted, they did much to redeem the reputation of the colonial players in the opinion of the large con- course of people who had assembled to witness the match. The game ended: England two goals one try, Kimberley nil. •

Referring to the Manhattan team who have now closed their visit to England, the "Manchester Guardian " says, three of their number have proved themselves to be superior tO any of our English athletes; but in an- other year, judging from the number of good men we have, one or two, it is hoped, will so improve their speed as to be able to successfully compete with Carey and Remington. The last public appearance of the visitors was made on Saturday at the Salford Harriers' summer meeting, when a magnificent programme of events was successfully concluded at Belle Vue, before a crowd of about 16,000 people. The Committee of the Salford Harriers deserve credit for the perfection. of their arrangements. No meeting could possibly have been better conducted, and the enormous entry received has certainly never been exceeded in this district.

That the successful team will have a hearty reception when they reach New York is beyond doubt. A few of the principal features of the great club they represent will prove interesting. The Manhattan Club is really the outgrowth of an earlier pioneer organization known as the Scottish American, and Mr. Lou Myers and Mr. Von Schaicke have from its inception been two of , the club's most ardent athletic supporters. Some 4,000 gentlemen now constitute the membership roll, and these are divi- ded under three heads—first, the life members, who are required either to pay a sum of 500 dollars, or to have won in open.. competition both an American and a foreign championship. Secondly, ordinary members who, after paying an entrance fee of 100 dollars, have to meet an annual subscription of 40 dollars; and thirdly, athletic men solely who require the privileges Qf the gymnasium and track, in exchange for which they pay 10 dollars per year, with an entrance fee of 25 dollars.

The premises of the club consist of a magnificent block of buildings in the heart of the city of New York, which were erected at a cost of one million dollars, and they are without equal in any part of the world. They are lighted throughout by eleetricity,whilst an elevator saves the members the trouble of mounting the staircase. In the sub-basement an extensive well provides an excellent supply of water, the engine-room being on the same level. In the basement proper, under the pavement of Madison Avenue, a rifle gallery has been made for the rifle corps, 65 yards long, whilst a smaller one, 30 yards long, is utilised for 'pistol practice. Then there is a swimming tank 100 feet long by 25 feat wide, varying in depth from 8 feet to 5 feet; also :Russian and Turkish baths; whilst there are seven skittle alleys and four tables for playing shuffleboard. On the ground floor are tho offices,reception-room, drawing-room, smoking-room, card-room, etc., and a billiard-room containing twelve full-size billiard tables. One of the prettiest theatres in New York occupies part of the building,being capable of holding 1,500 people. This can be entirely closed off ,and being provided with a separate entrance is largely used for private and amateur dramatic performances, thus yielding a considerable income to the club. In winter,the roof is flooded and the water frozen, if necessary, by artificial means; and last winter some of the best skating In New York was to be had on the top of the Manhattan club house. The "Manhattan Chronicle" is published every month, and is considered one of the leading club publications.

During their very short English tour the American team have won 51 prizes, including eleven championship events, the principal of which are the Amateur Athletic Association's 100 yards, 440 yards, and hammer throwing championships, and the 100 yards Northern Counties championship. Mr. Queckberner has also created a world's record with the hammer at 134 ft. 241 n., and an English record for slinging the 561 b. weight 30ft. sin. EXECUTION AT WANDSWORTH.

Franz Joseph Munch, aged 31, baker, was executed within the walls of Wandsworth Prison, at nine o'clock on Tuesday morning for the wilful murder of James Hickey, at Bermondsey, on April 22nd. For the first time in the history of this prison Pressmen were not ad- mitted. Efforts were made to secure the commutation of the death sentence upon Munch, but the Home Sec- retary declined to interfere with the law's course. Since his conviction, the culprit has paid devoted attention to the ministrations of the Rev. Father Galerau, Roman Catholic priest, who was with him from an early hour. The prison officials state' that the condemned man slept well. The Under-Sheriff (Mr. Metcalf), the doctor, officials, and the executioner (Berry) proceeded to the condemned cell shortly before nine, where Munch quiet- ly submitted to pinioning. Deathly pale, but with firm step, Munch walked to the scaffold, being understood to to say to the priest, " God forgive me." Berry pe r formed his duties expeditiously, and death was instan- taneous.

div.head: Zetters to the Vittor.
div.p: Zetters to the Vittor.
ANGLING IN WALTON RHSERVOIR.

Sir,--1 am glad to see from the local papers that the Corporation of the borough will soon be in possession of the Water Works. This will no doubt be to the advan- tage of the town generally. ,It wouldbe a great , privi- lege to the working-men if they could have an occa- sional day's angling inthe reservoir, a boon, which as a working-man myself,l am sure would give the liveliest satisfaction, and the liberty would not be in any way abused. A pure stream in this district is a matter of by-gone tradition. Thus a journey of .many miles has to be nsade before the "gentle art" can be practised. What peettier or more convenient spot could be found than Walton 2 -
I hope that the Water Works Committee will not fail to give the matter their consideration, and if facilities are granted ¶ am sure the committee-will receive the thanks .of every disciple of
OLD ISAAC WALTON.
A DANGEROUS NT.

Sir,---1 wish to point out to you what Will prove ulti- mately adeath trapin Orford-lane. Behind Forshaw-st. there isapatch of water from 2ft. to "3ft. deep which has been the scene of some score of children being nearly drowned. The other day a boy of three fell in, and would undoubtedly have been drowned but for the gallant behaviourof William Hunt, jun., who rescued him at his own personal risk, applied usual remediies, and after 30 minute:6' good work restored him to conciousness. I may say that this is the seventh or:eighth he has rescued. and I think he is a fit subject for the Humane Society's medal, and that it is high time to have the hole filled up. I believe I am right in asserting that the land belongs to the Land and Loan Co. Trusting you will insert this as a mark of bravery for William Hunt, jun., whom I publicly thank for his timely aid,-4 am, yours faithfully, ELLIS B. CLARE. 62, Leonard-st., Warrington.

rWilliam Plant is certainly entitled to the Humane Society's medal; and if or correspondent will for- ward a statement of .fects to the Society, there will be no difficulty about its being granted. Humane Society., London, will-ke a sufficient address.—En. Ex.]

div.head: NECESSITY Fti)R NEW POLICE
div.p: THE NECESSITY Fti)R NEW POLICE
PREMISES.

Sir,—The arguments advanced in favour of the erec- tion of new and more commodious premises in Warring- ton for the transaction of . our police and magisterial business, must, I am sure, have commended themselves to the public generally. But there is no class of the community more competent to speak from experience of the deplorable deficiencies of our Police Court than the reporters, and I feel certain, as being myself con- nected with the local Press that, though I have not their authority to say SQ, my brethren of the craft will with me thoroughly endorse all that has been said in condemnation of the present building. The reporters, as Mr. Browne, the solicitor, pointed out in, the Town Council, are .sub- jected to the utmostinconvenience in consequence off the want of accommodation at the Court. There is a place certainly, railed off and seated, provided expressly for their accommodation, but there is only room for five or six rep orters,and these are so cramped up that it is diffi- cult for them to perform their duties with ease and com- fort. Then, those who do not happen to come soon enough to obtain a seat within the privileged enclosure, are frequently obliged to literally sit at the feet of their more favoured brethren, that is, to squat in an uncom- fortable and undignified 'position upon the platform on which the reporters' desk is mounted. The worthy De- puty-Magistrates' perk minimise the difficulty as much as he can by allowing two reporters to sit at the solicitors' table, but this concession, courteous though it is, far from meets the exigencies of the ease. There is another argument that might be used from a reportorial point of view in favour of new police build- ings, and which has not yet been brought forward, per- haps because it does not concern the public generally. Inquests are frequently held in the parade room .of the -police station; and the accousticproperties of this room : are so bad that reporters have the greatest difficulty in I•eporting the proceedings ; indeed I have heard by no ,means deaf jurymen who have been seated close to. wit- nesses—much closer than the reporters—complain of nability to hear what is said. I submit these observa- • tons, claiming in all modesty that,though they are I:lade in the interest of one class, the reporters only, yet that class being an important and useful one, and, one w'oich woks hard in the public service, is entitled to considera- , tion in this /natter.
A PRESSMAN.

NEW THEATRE FOR WARRINGTON. Sir,—A letter over the signature of " A Working Man' dared in your issue of last week, but one, toa which thi.llike to have replied last week but Iwas prevented cour bting out of town. Your correspondent in the not nocN,hks remarks says he is of opinion that there is viz. 2 ite same necessity for a new theatre as then, patronage years ago, giving as his reason the lack oi To.ided to the companies performing at the t hali since hc He also me bad occasion to write. that theatres in other towns received large support the patrons of stalls and boxes, and informs his reacilathat box and stall patrons as a rule Are conspicuous h their absence. Quite true, but Abe people hopat tjze these parts of the house aro

educated to a Wigher standard of theatrical fare than the working-mcn. spoken of in his letter,who, as he says, cannot atfor'd to attend more than once or twice a week. It is this VC.:ry lack of patronage that we deplore so much, but we cannot expect persons who are accustomed to high class productions to waste both time and money in coming "to lend the light of their countenance" to the ordinary entertainment provided for them here. We are well aware of what "A Working-man " men- tions, viz. :—That some of the companies have been paying visits direct from the Court Theatre, but the performance as given in Warrington is net to be com- pared to the performance as given in Liverpool, as,even when the acting is the same, the production is spoilt by the small stage and poor scenery, to say nothing of the music. _ _ _

With regard to his first remark., I am still of opinion I that a large and well managed.house.erected,as he hopes, on a more suitable site than the one proposed, would pay well. Take for instance the performance of the last two nights. Ile house has been crowded by a highly respectable audience notwithstanding the many draw- backs inseparable front the Public IJall performances, which are hampered (I) by the biwarf proportions of the stage and building generally ; (II) by the poverty of the scenery; (III) by the entire absence of anything ap- proaching in orchestra. I know that only the popular parts of the house are full.but this would not be the case if the company were such as performed at Liverpool or Manchester. Look at Mr. Pearson's concert for ins- tance, when all the artistes are in the front rank of the profession. I would ask "A Working Man," are our local magnates absent on these occasions? No, certainly not. They are all "en evidence," at least as many of them as have been able to obtain seats, and not they alone, but _ aLso the gentry from the surrounding districts are pre- sent. _ _

can quite understand that it would not pay to bring .a big company down with all its attendant propertieg, as if even the Hall were completely filled it could not pay at anything like popular prices; and why? Because enough people would not be able to gain admission on account of the smallness of the building. Hence the necessity for a spacious theatre where a big company could perform at a profit to themselves, which would certainly be the case, as is happily proved to my mind by your correspondent, "R. Wilfer," in his remarks about the London theatres.

would like to apologize to Mr. Browne for not answering his business-like letter before, for the reason mentioned above, and I only regret not being in a posi- tion to invest money in any such concern, but I will be only too pleased at all times to do my best to further the interest of a good establishment by my individual sup- port. Thanking you in anticipation, and apologizing for trespassing at such length upon your valuable space, am, sir, yours, etc.,
"THESPIAN."
WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL AND "THE
SWEATING SYSTEM."

Sir,—Rising into the higher realm of humanity, and a calmer region of reason than mere political strife, as a working-man, I must give vent to the watm beatings of my grateful heart, and sincerely thank those noble thir- teen Liberals and two Conservative Town Councillors, who on the 7th inst., wisely entered their protests against the inhuman Sweating System, and against the stolid opposition of the eleven opponents, and triumphantly carried Councillor Flood's resolution, so saving the Coun- cil from further disgrace, and encouraging, as many did on the former and present occasion,to the danger of their seats, and lasting shame, the heartless, oppressive scc urge of our poor fellow British slaves. Let me also express my deep indebtedness to you, sir, for your report, and many wise and just observations made by you in your leading article in your issue of July 11th, 1891, a copy of which I shall long treasure, and keep for further reference, and which I trust other work- ing-men will rightly value and keep. I doubt whether any other resolution in the history of our Town Council was ever submitted for deliberation thereon which has so keenly cut the nation's heart and roused its con- science, as that under consideration. It is the sweating -system that underlies ruinous prices, unjust laws, unjust taxation, unjust apprentice terms, too many working hours, starvation wages, and hatred between employer and employed. These would all speedily disappear from our beloved Empire, were the principles involved in Councillor Flood's motion generally and properly carried out. As Goldsmith wisely puts it: 11l fares the land to hastening ills a prey, Where wealth accumulates and men decay; and the amassing together of immense wealth by a com- paratively small number by the impoverishing of the rest of mankind is something against which our whole being . rebels. I fully acquiesce in the irresistible logic of John Ruskin, that our boasted science of political economy has been little better than a science of selfishness ; and his declaration that, " No human actions ever were in- tended by the Maker of men to be guided by balance of expediency, but by balance of justice." What a con- trast here to Alderman Harrison, and all those who, like him, blindly contended against Councillor Flood's motion. They have been deluded on these fundamen- tal principles by false teachers of the Tennyson type who vainly glory in their superior birth, position, wis- dom;&c., "Cries to weakest as to strongest, 'ye are equals, equals born,' 'Equal born! o.yes,. if yonder hill be level with the fiat, . . .

Ciiarm us, Orat-or, till the lion look no large.. than the cat, Russia bursts our Indian barrier; emit we fight or shall we yield? Pause, before you sound the trumpet ;hear the voices from the field. Sir, you ask "when did it happen that the masses after due deliberation, made a demand which was not fair ?" When ? Only last Tuesday night, July 7th, 1891, when Alaerman Sutton said, as to "Councillor Flood's motion, he was of opinion that the resolution was a ridiculous one." Alderman Chandley opposed the resolution be- cause he contended it was "absolutely unnecessary and most dangerous." Alderman Harrison "Should vote against it. It was their duty and privilege to buy in the cheapest market and sell in the dearest.' We working- men, as you intimate, have a fine revelation of who are our true friends, and foes in our Town Council. Those eleven, whose hearts and heads, blinded by stolid politi- cal strife, failed them on this momentous and vital sub- ject, are utterly unworthy of our confidence; and I hope that all working-men will be true to themselves in future and to those of our friends whose minds can comprehend our just requirements, whose hearts can feel for us, whose tongues can successfully plead Our cause, regard- less of political party or social standing among us. We see what a working-man has accomplished for us in our Town Council, against cold contempt, political cant, and cunning reasoners. We must judge our friends and foes by their deeds, which are fruits, and not their words, which are only useless leaves; and render
Honour to whom honour is due! So vote for them who vote for you, Is what we working-men must do, Regardless of political hue. —.Yours truly,
_ . R. STOREY. 160, Orford-lane, Warrington, July 17th, 1891.

div.head: WISBECII ELECTION.
div.p: WISBECII ELECTION.
RETURN OF MR. BRAND.
GREAT LIBERAL VICTORY.

Polling was commenced on Thursday morning amidst a steady downpour of rain, which had an effect upon the voters, As few registered their votes within the first hour. Soon after nine o'clock the weather cleared, and the polling became more brisk. Mr. Brand, the Liberal candidate, accompanied by his wife, made a tour of the constituency in a carriage and pair. Mr. Duncan made a similar tour in a four-horse drag, with postillions in pink. It was supposed that half the con- stituency had polled at two o'clock. Captain Selwyn, the late member,had been ill for two daysibut rose from his bed to record his vote. There are 25 stations, and carriages are being used by both sides. The result was declared yesterday, as fcllows : HON. A. BRAND (GL)- *- - 3,979 MR. S. W. DUNCAN (C)- - - 3,719
Majority- - - - MR. .BRAND ON HIS .VICTORY.

• Immediately after the declaration of the poll Mr. Brand was escorted to his committee rooms, where he addressed a large crowd. He said : This is essentially a working- man's victory, and I hope it will be a source of comfort to our great leader. (Cheers.) ,It is also a Radical victory and a triumph of popular principles, and it will be ac- cepted as a pledge of the faith reposed in our cause by the labouring population. I intend to keep the majority by which I have won this election. (Cheers.) Mr. Duncan, in addmks.sing his followers, thanked them for the support they had given him,and he added: " Keep your courage up and we shall live to fight another day.,, So confident were the Conservatives of victory that Mr. Duncan, *speaking to a crowd outside the Rose and Crown, at Wisbech, on Thursday night,assured the elec- tors three times that he was their member. The agricultural labourers carried the day against the Conservatism a the towns.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JULY 25, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JULY 25, 1891.
PARR'S BANKING coarAiy.

An extraordinary general meeting of the share- holders of this Bank was held yesterday, at the Bank Premises, Winwick-st., Warrington. Mr. J. C. Parr, the chairman of the directors, presided, and the other directors present were Sir G. T. Frost, Colonel Gamble, C. 8., Colonel, McCorquodale, Messrs. P. Stubbs, E. Greenall, N. Eckersley, A. Hewlett, A. Turner, H. Warren Meade-King, C. F. Parr, J. Dun, and E. W. Nix. There was a large attendance of shareholders.
THE DIRECTORS' RETORT.

The Directors submitted the following report :—" The Directors have had before them the audited Balance Sheet of the Bank at 30th June, 1891, and they beg to re- port that the profits of the half-year, after providing amply for all bad and doubtful debts, have been satis- factory. The Directors recommend that there be now declared for the half-year ending 30th June, an interim dividend at the rate of 19 per cent. per annum, free of income tax, add payable on and after 28th July. After providing for this dividend, there remains a consider- able balance, which is carried forward to the next ac- count. The position and prospects of the business con- tinue to be in every way satisfactory. The General Manager, Mr. John Dun, having since last meeting been elected by the Beard to be a Director of the Company and a member of the Select Committee, without, howevei , vacating the office of General Manager, which he has held for upwards of 25 years, the Shareholders will be asked to confirm his election as a Director. As announced by circular on the 13th June, the directors have concluded an arrangement to amalgamate the old- established banking business of Messrs. Fuller, Banbury, I Nix and Co., of 77, Lombard-st., London, with that of this Bank. This arrangement, which has been effected on advantageous terms, has secured the admission of the Bank to the London Clearing House, which will involve the transference of the registered office and the head office of the Bank to London but care will be taken that the business in the country ;hall continue to receive the same attention from the directors and the general mana- ger as heretofore. Mr. E. W. Nix and Mr. Edward Ban- Miry, two of the active partners of the firm of Fuller, Banbury, Nix and Co. ,have joined the Board of the Bank, and will give for some timeto come all requisite services in the management of the London business. The share- holders will be requested to confirm their election as directors. In order to carry out this amalgamation, the shareholders will be asked to create 2,500 additional shares in the Company, of which 1,400 shares, with £2O per share paid thereon, shall be issued to the partners in the firm of Fuller, Banbury, Nix and Co., or in such names as they may direct • 1,006 shares shall be allotted to the shareholders of the Company,l whose names shall appear on the register on the 24th July, 1891, at the price of £5O per share, and in the pro- I portion of one new share to each 30 then held; and 100 I shares shall be placed at the disposal of the Directors, to be sold at their discretion at the market price of the ds.s• —the premiums to be received on such 1,000 and 160 shares to be applied to the extent of £28.,000 to make good the sum of £2O per share to bepaid up on the 1,400 shares to be issued to Messrs. Fuller, Banbury, Nix & Co., and the balance to be carried to the reserve fund of the Company. The result will be to raise the nominal capital of the Company to £3,250,000, and the paid up capital to £650,000, and to add probably about £B,OOO to the reserve fund, besides giving to theexisting share- holders a substantial bonus by the allotment of the 1,000 shares at a price so much below the market value." The CHAIRMAN, in moving the adoption of the report, referred to the amalgamation of the business with that of Messrs. Fuller, Banbury, Nix and Co., and said this was a progressive step in advance, and had not been taken by the directors without much thought and careful consi- deration. They, however, recommended it to their ap- proval, fully believing that the shareholders would welcome it with as much satisfaction as the directors had pleasure in submitting it. The business of their bank had increased very considerably in the last few years, and he might also point out with some little pride that the business had not only increased in volume but also in strength and earning pewer,as evidenced by its reserves, investments, and dividenda paid. 'The total turn-over of the bank had now reached a very large figure, of which rather more than one-half passed through London. They had for some time past considered it desirable to seek an opportunity of uniting with some good bank in the city of London whereby all the various objects they had in view might be secured, and, therefsre, he had plea- sure in announcing the amalgamation to which the re- port referred. He wished to re-assure their country friends—their old-fashioned friends, who were their best friends—that they had no intention of neglecting them or their interests, or, in other words, of forsaking their old love for the new. (Hear, hear.) Their Committee would give then' usual attendances at War- rington and Liverpool, their general manager would be there to meet customers very much as he had been, and their Chairman would continue to live near Warrington and superintend the business of the bank from the home of his earliest associations, which were so closely con- nected with the time-honoured business of Parr and Company and the old bank in Warringtoni (Applause.) In conclusion the Chairman. remarked that there had been a considerable increase in the number of accounts during the past six months, this increase being very evenly distributed over the whole area, there not being one branch or sub-branch which did not show an , increase in the number of its accounts. ,(flear, hear.) Mr. N. ECHER&LEY seconded the adoption of the report, which was agreed to.
A vote of thanks to the CL airman brought the proceed- I ings to a close.
SHOCKING DOUBLE MURDER. BY A MOTHER.

Mary Jane Heathcote, residing with her husband at Stoke Newington, has surrendered herself to the police, confessing that she on Wednesday night drowned her daughters, Morrie and Cissie, aged 3 and 5, in Epping Forest. The bodies have been recovered. Mrs. Heath- cote was sound near Chingford Hotel on Thursday morn- ing in a wet and distressing condition, and it was through the statement made by her to a man named Higgs that she was arrested. She confessed to the police, who discovered the bodies in a ditch, but the woman gave no reason for the commission of the crime. Mrs. Heathcote was taken before a magistrate on Thursday, and remanded.

THE BURIALS QUESTION AT ASHTON- IN-MAKERFIELD. In the House of Commons, on Monday, Mr. Sum- mers. on behalf of Ur. Jacob Bright, asked the Home Secretary whether he had received three memorials from the officers and members of three Nonconformist congregations in the parish of Holy Trinity,Ash ton-in-Makerlield, Lancashire, represent- ing that, notwithstanding an intimation to the in- cumbent from the Home Office that such a notice was not consistent with the object and provisions of the Burials Act of 1880, the accounts of burial payments for the churchyard of that parish continue to state that a " breadth " or grave "is appropriated only on condition that no other than the Church of England service is ever used"; that new graves had been refused by the rector when the Church of England service had not been required; and that, as a result, parishioners who would otherwise have availed themselves of the Act of 1880 had, in order to obtain new graves, submitted to have a Church of England service; whether he would grant an official inquiry into the facts with a view to the withdrawal of such intimation, and the impartial exercise of the incumbent's discretion in respect to bur- ials, without regard to the burial services which might be performed; and whether any and what answer had been given to the memorialists. Mr. Matthews: I have received three such memorials.

I have more than once made Inquiry into this matter, and the results were given in answer to questions on the 13th August last year and the 10th March this year. I stated on both those occasions that the question at issue between the vicar and the complainants was one of law, which I have no jurisdiction to determine, and I have answered the petitions in that sense.

div.head: DI'VIDENTI.
div.p: THE DI'VIDENTI.
On the motion of Mr. A. TURNER, seconded by Mr. J. WRITE, a dividend in accordance with the recommenda- tion in the report was declared.
APPOINTMENT OF 3IR. DUN TO RE A DIRECTOR.

The CHAIRMAN moved that the election by the directors of. Mr. J. Dun to be a director and a member of the Election Committee, without having vacated his office as general manager, be confirmed. He referred in com- plimentary terms to the eminent services Mr. Dun had rendered to the bank,and remarked that the attention he had given to the interests of the Company had mainly contributed to the great success that had been met with. (Hear, hear.)— Dq. C. WHITE seconded the proposal, and said that anything which would express the confidence of the shareholders in Mr. Dun was sure to be well received. (Hear, bear.)—Tbe proposal was then agreed to unani- mously.—Mr. Dux thanked the meeting for that marked testimony of their good feeling towards him. He had laboured, not without success, in the service of that bank for nearly six and twenty years, which was a very considerable span out of one's life, and if the directors in suggesting that he should become a director had also suggested at the same time that he should vacate his office of general manager be should have felt compelled to decline the honour because he hoped to be able to serve them in the capacity of general manager for many years to come. (Applause.)

div.head: SPECIAL RESOLUTIONS.
div.p: SPECIAL RESOLUTIONS.

The following special resolutions were adopted on tile motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. Eckersley, viz. :—" That the agreement dated sth dune, 1891, for the acquisition of the Banking business carried on at 77, Lombard-St., London, by Messrs. Fuller, Banbury, Nix and Co. as from the 13th day of June, 1891, be hereby approved and that the Board of Directors be authorised to take all the steps which they may deem necessary for the purpose of carrying out the said Agreement, subject to such additions or variations as may be found neces- sary or expedient." That the capital of the company be increased from three million pounds, its present amount,to three million two hundred and fifty thousand pounds by the creation of 2,500 shares of one hundred pounds each. That of such issue of 2,500 shares 1,400 shares on which £2O per share shall bo considered as paid up shall be issued to the partners of Fuller, Banbury, Nix, and Co., in such names as they may in writing direct; 1,000 shares shall be issued at the price of £5O per share, of which £2O per share shall be paid as capital, and £3O per share shall be paid as premium, and such shares shall be allotted at that price to the holders of shares of the company whose names shall appear on the register of the company, on the 24th day of July, 1891, in the proportion of one share for every 30 shares standing at that date in their names respectively : the price payable for such 1,000 shares to be due and payable to the companyon the first day of October, 1891 ; and 100 shares shall be placed at the disposal of the directors to be &sued by them from time to time at the market price of the day in such manner as they may deem desirable for the benefit of the Company: the premium of £3O per share to be paid on the 1,000 shares to be allotted to the shareholders to be applied to the extent of £28,000 to make good the sum of £2O per share to be paid up on the 1,400 shares to be issued to the partners of Fuller, Ban- bury, Nix, and nd to the extent of £2,000 to in- crease the reserve Co.,eund of the Company and the excess of price realized for the beforementioned 100 shares beyond the £2O per share to be paid thereon to be likewise carried to the reserve fund of the Company. The whole of the said 2,500 shares shall participate in profits from 30th June, 1891. Any of the 1,000 shares herein provided to be issued at the price of £5O per share in respect of which the sum payable shall not be paid on or before the day on which the same shall be due shall be absolutely for- feited and the directors shall be at liberty to sell or dis- pose of such forfeited shares in any manner they shall think proper for the benefit of the Company. "That Article 6 of the Articles of Association shall ibe altered so as to read as follows :—" The head or chief office and the Registered Office of the Company shall be removed from Warrington to London and the business of the Company shall be carried on there and at such other place or places, part or parts, as the Board may deem advisable." "That the alteration made in the Articles of Associa- tion by the special resolution passed on the 28th Janu- ary 188 IS and confirmed on the 12th February, 1883,with regard to the number of the Select Committee of the directors shall bo amended so as to ,read as follows : "The number of the Select Committee of directors shall for the time being be increased to eleven and shall not in future be more than eleven or fewer than Eve."

XLECTION OF NEW DIRECTOR, IS_M. On the motiou of the Chairman the eledion of Mr. Edward Nix and Ur. Edward Banbury as directors was confirmed. It was also resolved that the remuneration of the directou.stipv4 jnereased from f;S,OPL-9,.-C6,000 per aptku,m.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT RUNCORN, &c.
BV •AN OCCASMNAL CORRESPONDENT.

Policernen on wheels is to be the next sensation in Runcarn. Our constables have got weary of the continual tramp, tramp, tramp, and intend to go in for a little pedal exercise. Five are to be mounted on bicycles, and three of the heavy brigade will seek a safer seat on tricycles. Two of the officers went out for practice the other night, and one, thinking his iron horse was made to steeplechase, precipitated himself and his machine over a hedge at Old Quay, and had other exciting adventures. The other ran full tilt at the Fountain, but the ancient structure nobly withstood his assault, and he re- tired defeated. When the other six get to work, we may anticipate lively doings. Of course, by reason of his extra ponderosity the guardian of Old Quay will be made captain of the Cycle Corps, as he will be able to have a good view of his men as they career along the leafy lanes. The steeplechaser is already talking of a tour to London, and after another week has passed, he will perhaps be essay- ing to break the record—in a ride to John O'Groats.

Recently the quarterly meeting of the Runcorn Wesleyan Circuit decided to present a petition to the magistrates drawing their attention to the great evils of the liquor traffic and asking them to do all in their power to restrict the trade. This week a meeting of ministers of religion was held in Bethesda Lecture Hall with a view of acting in concert at the forthcoming Brewster Sessions, and, after a discussion, it was resolved to memorialise the Bench not to grant any new licenses in the future. Two of the gentlemen present were deputed to present a memorial to their worships.

It may be mentioned that the ministers present, at the meeting were Rev. Canon Wood (vicar), Rev. Dr. Preston (vicar, Holy Trinity), Revs'. Holden, Kingston, Seeley, and Jameson (curates), Dr. Gas- taldi (Catholic), E. Finch (Primitive Methodist), and J. Simpson (Congregational). The Wesleyan ministers and the Rev. J. Pulford Williams (Presby- terian) were conspicuous by their absence, and this fact has caused some comment. I should have thought these gentlemen would have been anxious and willing to co-operate with their brethren on such an important subject, and it would be reassur- ing to those interested in temperance work to know whether their absense was due to accident and not design.

The memorial to the Lord Chancellor praying for better County Court arrangements at Widnes as been presented by Mr. T. C. Edwards Moss, M.P., to the proper quarter,and the memorial has been officially acknowledged. In a letter sent to Mr. Job Stott, Mr. Moss says he has had an interview with the Lord Chancellor's secretary, who assured him that the matter would have careful and immediate at- tention. This will be highly satisfactory to suitors.

For the first half year's working the directors of the United Alkali Company, have declared a divi- dend at the rate of 5 per cent, per annum. It is said that the Widnes works have generally done very well, one having made a profit of £30,000 and some smaller works a profit of £5,000 during that time. It is certain that the Union will endeavour to conduct their trade with fewer works than exist at present, and the weakest will go to the wall. Let us hope that Widnes and Runcorn will prove well able to hold their own.

The annual inspection of Widnes Local Board took place on Tuesday and the members found the extensive and valuable property of the ratepayers in a highly satisfactory condition, a state of things highly satisfactory to the various officials in charge. The Infectious Diseases Hospital, lately described as a white elephant, was found looking like anything but that rare animal. The interier and the .exterior were a model of order, care, and cleanliness, and should the town be visited by an epidemic, from which the fates preserve us, the In- stitution will be found well adapted for the pun- poses for which it was constructed. The most im- portant work is now in progress at Netherley, where two wells are being sunk to supply the in- creasing demands of the township for water. There is every prospect that the borings will reveal vast subterranean stores of water to supply future generations.

By the time the next inspection arrives Widnes will have attained the dignity of a Corpora- tion, and this cccasion may be described as the tarewell visit of the Local Board. Mr. Gossage, the respected Chairman, signalised the event by invit- ing the members and officials to dinner at his resi- dence, and he placed a repast before his guests that would have satisfied the delicate appetite and fine taste of an epicure. To Dr. O'Keeffe was allotted the honour of leading Mrs. Gossage to the table, and his face was wreathed with smiles as be escorted the future Mayoress through the hall. The hospitality of the host and hostess was suitably acknowledged, and Mr. Gossage personally took leave of each of his guests when they departed, shortly after ten o'clock.

In my "par "respecting the charities of Sutton last week, I omitted to mention that Mr. Robinson, the schoolmaster, took a prominent and useful : part in unravelling the mystery surrou,nding the money in the hands of the overseers. As I like to give honour where honour is due, I mention the circum- stance now.

According to the census returns just issued, the population of Widnes Parliamentary Division is 64,507 as compared with 53,951 in 1881. The present population of the township of Widnes is 29,971 against 24,723 in 1881, 14,359 in 1871, 6,893 in 1861, and 3,217 in 1851.

The extensive police changes in Cheshire affect Runcorn by the removal of Inspector Bowyer, who is promoted to the inspectorship of .Egremont. Mr. Bowyer came to Runcorn two years ago, at a bime when the force was undergoing a severe trial, and great tact and discretion was required.and he proved fully equal to the situation. He is of a calm and judicial mind, and while performing his duties with conscientious strictness, has not made enemies of the general public. Superintendent Large will be -sorry to lose such an able assistant. His successor will be Sergeant Cooper, of Egremont, who is ad- vanced to Inspector, and who is credited with be- ing a smart and intelligent officer.
THE CATHCA RT LUNACY INQUIRY.
MRS. CATHCART DECLARED SANE.

On Thursday, on the resumption of the inquiry into the mental condition of Mr. Cathcart. it was stated by Sir Charles Russell that the lady objected to any examin- ation whatever except in open court. The master said it was customary in these cases to examine in private, and he would not depart from the ordinary practise. Subsequently Mrs. Cathcart was examined in the pri- vate room,the leading counsel on each side being allowed to be present. The jury found that Mrs. Cathcart was of sound mind. ROYAL AGRICULTURAL SHOW AT BURY.

The Royal Manchester. Liverpool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society holds its annual show at Bury this week for the first time. The local committee are expected to raise £l,OOO to- wards the expenses and prize list of the show; at Bury more than £1,500 has already been paid into the bank for this purpose. A lasvish dis- play of bunting in the streets expressed the goodwill of the general public towards the show on the occasion of kg opening on Thursday. A night of incessant rain had left the showyard in a sodden condition, but bright warm weather was enjoyed during the day, and the ground, which is about a mile out of Bury, within sight of the green hills, was visited by nearly 3,000 people. About £350 was taken at the gates, as compared with .£lB3 at Crewe on the opening day of last year. With a total entry of 2,839, this year's meeting maintains the numerical avemaga. Although, how- ever, the restrictions which exist with regard to the transit of cattle were relaxed in favour of the show, there was not such a large collection of live stock as has been seen in some years, which might be ac- counted for by a certain extent by the tact that two other great exhibitions were being held at the same time.

Fine weather again favoured the Show yesterday, and there was a large attendance. The total receipts on Thursday at the gates and on the ground were £535, against £229 at Crewe last year. At a special general meeting of the Society yesterday morning, it was un- animously decided to hold next year's show at Liverpool.
A Lloyd's telegram states that the schooner Ma Florence, of Yarmouth, has stranded at the entrance to Dunbar imbour, and will probably become a tots]. wreck.

div.head: -4.--_ FRODSHAII.
div.p: -4.--_ FRODSHAII.

SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY.—On Sunday two ser- mons were preached in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Frodsham, morning and evening, by Mr. W. Windsor of Manchester. In the afternoon a children's service was conducted by Mr. B. Parker, of Helsby, during which several scholars gave recitations. Mr. Windsor gave an address. Special hymns were rendered by the choir, assisted by a string band. The collections amounted to £l6 12s.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

CHURCH BELLS.—On Monday, the new peal of bells, which had been expected for a considerable time,arrived at Lymm from the manufactory at Loughborough. MUSIC AT THE CROSS.—On Saturday evening the Man- chester City Mission Band playei a capital selection of music at the Cross. Mr. J. Bradbury acted as conduc- tor.

ANNIVERSARY SERVICES.—On Sunday, at the Cherry- lane Baptist Chapel, the anniversary services were held. The sermons were preached morning and evening by Mr. Eddison, of Rochdale. There were good congregations throughout the day, the collections morning and even- ieg realising the satisfactory slim of £2O. SLEEPING OUT.—At the Lymm Police Court, on Monday morning, before Dr. Brabazon, Edward Davies, Broom Edge, was charged with sleeping in a out-building be- longinc, to Mr. James Gold, of Foxley Hill, Farm, on Saturday night.—P.C. Ennion gave evidence in support of the charge and defendant was sentenced to 14 days' imprisonment, with hard labour.

CRICKET MATCH—ST. MARY'S V. CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH.—St. Mary's again came off victorious on Mon- day evening, defeating the Congregational by six runs. St. Mary's lost the toss, and went in first, making a total of 22 runs. They then easily dispensed with their op- ponents for the meagre total of 16. Hinde, for St. Mary's took six wickets at a very small cost. EXCURSIONISTS.—A great number of excursionists paid Lvmm a visit on Wednesday, amongst whom were the shop assistants of Altrincham, who had tea at the Masonic Hall. The Pendleton industrial Co-operative Society (Limited), to the number of 227, came by seven Manchester Carriage Company's 'buses, and were ac- commodated by the landlord of the Spread Eagle. TERMINATION OF THE CUTTERS' STRIKE.—On Wednes- morning a Committee meeting in conneetion with the Lynam branch of the Cutters' Federation was held to decide what steps should be taken with regard to the dispute. Mr. H. Percival presided, and after a short discussion, the Committee agreed to accept the terms of the masters. The strike is, therefore, at an end. GOOD TEMPLARY.—The weekly session of the Tower of Refuge Lodge was held at the Cocoa rooms, Post Office Place, on Tuesday evening. In the absence of the C.T. Bro. L. Ellison, of Latchford,presided. There was a fair attendance of members, and there were visitors from the Latchford Lodge. For the good of the order short addresses were given by the following :—Bros. Newman,- Thomas Homey, Holliday, Ellison, Richardson, and F. Jenkins. A very pleasant evening was spent. .

SUPERINTENDENT LEIGUTON.—Ii is announced that Superintendent Leighton, of the Altrincham division, is ' about to retire from his police duties. Much regret will be felt by all those with whom,in the course of his duties, the Superintendent came into contact. Mr. T. P. Norris, chairman of the Lymm Petty Sessions, stated that, during the whole time the Superintendent had been at Lymm, there had never been the slightest hitch between himself and the Bench. Superintendent Leighton has been for upwards of thirty years in the Manchester and Cheshire constabulary. "AFTER MANY DAYS:"-At the Lymm Police Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. C. Lister and Dr. Brabazon, James Smith, alias West, alias "Gipsy Jo," Ship Canal miner, who was apprehended on Tuesday, at Runcorn, on a warrant, was charged with assaulting Police-con- stable Buchanan in the execution'ef his duty on the sth October, 1889, and also with having been on land in search 3f game at the same time and place. Police- constable Buchanan said at ten o'clock on the day in question he was in company with Sergeant Wynne and Sergeant Griffiths in Statham-road, when he met three or four men. Be stopped them, and he and the prisoner had a struggle, during which he noticed the prisoner had"pegs" in his pocket. The prisoner kicked the wit- ness in the stomach and on the legs, and also set his dog upon him.—Police-sergeant Wynne corroborated.—For the first offence he was fined ss. and costs, or 14 days; and a like sum for the second, or seven days. As no money was forthcoming, the prisoner was taken to gaol.

div.head: ST. HELENS VOLUNTEERS AT BISLEY.
div.p: ST. HELENS VOLUNTEERS AT BISLEY.

The St. Helens men at Bisley had to battle with conditions the reverse of pleasant when they went to the targets on Friday morning to fire in the com- petition for the St. George's Vase. There was a dazzling light and a rapid variation in the wind. The cup wasultimately won by Corporal Ritchie, of the '2nd Renfrew, with a score of 34. Sergeant Dwerryhouse was the too scorer of the local men, scoring 31, thus winning a prize of £7, while Private Preston, who was next with 29, won a prize of £3. The following are the scores :—Sergeant Dwerryhouse, 31 ; Private Preston,29 ; Lieutenant White. 27 : Corporal Taylor, 27 • Corporal Norbury, 27; Corp:mat Foster, 26 ; Sergeant Wilspn, 25 ; Private Lockie, 24 ; Private McGill, 24 ; Sergeant Arm- strong, 23 ; Corporal Milligan, 23 : Private Roberts. 23 ; Armourer-Sergeant West, .21 : and Private Forsyth, 19. _ _

In the Graphic Competition Lieutenant White won a prize of £5 with his score of 64 points. In the Martin's Competition, the first prize in which was won with a score of 34, Corporal Foster and Ser- geant Dwerryhouse won prizes of £2 each, with scores of 30. _ _ _

- The English Twenty Club prizes were awarded to the best aggregate scorers, with two shoots in the country at 200,500, and 600 yards, added to the scores made at Bisley for the Queen's, Alexandra, and St. George's prizes. The following are the local prize winners :—£2, Lieutenant White, 341; £1 Corporal Norbury, 323; £1 Private Preston, 321; £1 Armourer Sergeant West, 319. Among the prize winners in the tyro aggregate in con- nection with the Queen's competition are Corporal Mil- ligan, who scored 81, and Private Lockie, who scored 79. Each wins £l. . - . .
The China Cup was won by Lanark with a score of 395, Lancashire only scoring 370. Corporal Norbury and Corporal Foster were in the Lancashire team, and they scored 39 and 36 respectively.

DROWNING FATALITY.—On Friday afternoon, James Lord, 11 years of age, son of James Lord, collier, Cam- ber-lane, Whiston, went in company with a number of other boys to a pit in Greenhouse-lane,Rainhill,to bathe. After he had been in the water a short time the deceased went out of his depth and sank. He could not swim and was drowned. The body was recovered an hour and a half afterwards. CONGREGATIONAL BAND OF HOPE.--011 Saturday, the Band of Hope in connection with the Prescot Congrega- tional Sunday Schools held their second annual trip to Bidston Hill. The party with visitors numbering about 70, leftthe Prescot Station by the 1.31 train and arrived at Bidston Hill about 3.30. The weather was extremely fine, and z most pleasant afternoon was spent. Among those present were Mrs. Truesdaie, Mr. P. Chorley, Mr. Thomas Orchard, and Mr. Charles Dickinson, secretary. The whole of the arrangements were carried out by Mr, Thomas Orchard,

VACANCIES ON THE PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The nominations for the three vacancies on the Prescot Board of Guardians were received on Friday. The Rev. H. Mitchell, vicar of Prescot, and Mr. W. Tyrer, solicitor who resigned his position on the board to apply for the clerkship, were nominated for Prescot; Mr. G. H. Hal- las, mining engineer, and Mr. Ottiwell Ward, farmer, for Whiston, in the place of Mr. John Leatherbarrow (who also resigned to apply for the clerkship) ; and Mr. J. Whalley, for Bold, owing to the death of the late guardian (Mr. Chadwick).

LATEST NEWS.
CRICKET.
Lancashire beat Gloucester by four wickets. MR. SPURGEON'S CONDITION.
Mr. Spurgeon has had a quiet night with a fair amount of sleep, and has taken nourishment. RAILWAY DIVIDEND.
The Midland Railway O-r-dirTS-ri-s-t-O;Ii- dividend for the past half-year will be 51 per cent. per annum. ANOTHER RUMOURED ROYAL MARRIAGE. _ _
It is now rumoured at Bucharest that the Roumanian Crown Prince will marry a daughter of the Prince of Wales.
WASHED ASHORE AT DOVER.
Two bodies were washed ashore near Dover on Thurs- day, it is supposed from the sunken steamer Dun- holme.
LORD DARTMOUTH NO WORSE.
Yesterday's bulletin states that Lord Dartmouth passed a fairly good night, and that there is no increase in the gravity of his symptoms.
FATAL EXPLOSION IN MANCHESTER.
At the Barton Arcade, Manchester, where a sewer is being made, and dynamite used for blasting purposes, it exploded yesterday and one man was killed.

THE PRINCE OF NAPLES. The Prince of Naples was early astir yesterday morn- ing, and at ten o'clock visited the Tower of London, after which he returned to the city, and lunched at the Italian Embassy. THE WESLEYAN CONFERENCE.

The Wesleyan Conference was mainly engaged yester- day morning in considering the relationship of mission- aries and native ministers. Twenty-six candidates for ordination were accepted. THE INDIAN FAMINE.

A telegram received at the India Office yesterday from the Viceroy and Governor of Madras states that there is no improvement in the condition of affairs in the famine threatened districts of Madres presidency. DEATH OF THE EARL OF WICKLOW. _
____ . • . The Earl of Wicklow died yesterday morning after a short illness.
Cecil Ralph Howard, sixth Earl of Wicklow, was born April 26th,1842. The new earl isßalph Francis Howard, formerly Lord Clonmore. THE BRISTOL WILL CASE.

The hearing of a will suit, White v. Woodhead and others, was resumed in London yesterday. Evidence was given as to the testator purchasing chloral, and Miss Winslow, recalled, said the deceased once stated that he was tempted to commit suicide.

div.head: BISLEY MEETING.
div.p: THE BISLEY MEETING.

The ties in the Association CJIT A.R. were fired off yesterday morning between Captain Fremantle, Ist Bucks, Lieut. Lander, Seaforth Highlanders, and Private Waterson, Ist Aberdeen. Lieut. Lander won by two points. Captain Fremantle, Ist Bucks, is the winner of the Dudley A.R. prize with 74 points. The Royal Cam- bridge Shield, 500 and 600 yards aggregate, has been won by a team of 14th Hussars with 88 points. The sth Dragoons came second with 83. The 2nd V.B. West Kent has won the Cyclists' Prize, 10 shots at 250 yards. Mr. H. Andrews (Woolwich) has been placed first in the Extra Prizes, A.R. Competition.
THE SHIP CANAL DISASTER. PRATT AGAIN REMANDED.

Yesterday morning, the boy George Pratt, aged six- teen, whose home is at Hollins Green, near Warrington, was brought up in custody on remand at Mr. W. H. Churton's (Clerk of the Peace) offices, Chester, charged with causing the death of ten men on the Ship Canal works at Lone, last Saturday morning. The magistrates present were Sir T, G. Frost and Mr. B. C. Roberts. _

Mr. Churton asked Superintendent Walker whether, after the result of the inquest on Thursday, the police intended continuing the prosecution of the boy. Superintendent Walker replied in the affirmative, and remarked that the police were ready with their witness- es to proceed with the case, and conclude it to-day, in order that prisoner might be dealt with at the Chester Assizes, which will be held on Monday next. Mr. Churton said if that was the intention of the police, it was fair to the prisoner that the case should not be rushed through that morning. There were several wit- nesses to be called, and their evidence would have to be taken fully. Superintendent Walker said sdveral of the witnesses were waitirN. at Ince. -
The magistrates then forinally remanded the prisoner until next day.
YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter past four. STRAITS SETTLEMENT.—Lord BRASSEY called attention to the increased military contribution demanded by the Imperial Government from :the colony of the Straits Settlements for the maintenance of that garrison. Con- sidering importance of Straits Settlements coaling sta- tian, he thought the increased contribution unpolitic.— Lord KNIITSFORD replied that he could not give a de- finite answer to questions raised until time had been given for its consideration. Demobs BlLLs.—The Post Office Accounts Amend- ment Bill was read a second time. The Factories and Workshops Bill, the Elementary Education Bill, the Trustees Amendment (Scotland) Bill, the Tramways Ire- land Act, 1890, Amendment Bill, the County Councils Elections Bill, and the Markets and Fairs (Weighing of Cattle) Bill were read a third time. The House adjourned at 7.15. HOUSE OF COMMONS.

The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past three o'clock. RAILWAY RATES AND CHARGES, A SCENE.—On the consideration of the London and North-Western Railway Company (rates and charges) Provincial Order Bill, as amended, Mr. Philip Stanhope moved that this house,in view of the dissatisfaction expressed by the trading community throughout the country, while unwilling to decline to adopt the report of the Select Committee, is of opinion that its conclusions do not afford a final or equitable settlement of railway rates and charges, and that further amendments in relief of trade are urgently required. Sir Charles FORSTER seconded the motion. Mr. Atkinson supported the motion, and announced his intention of preventing by every means in his power the passage of these bills, on the ground that they would ruin the timber trade. In the course of the hon. mem- ber's observations he referred to the petition which he presented on the previous day, but was not allowed to read. This gave rise to cries of " Order" from different parts of the House. Mr Atkinson (addressing an hon. member on the Opposition benches :—You are not the Speaker). When Mr. Speaker calls me to order I shall sit down to hear what he has to say, and then when he has finished I shall get up again and say all I intended to say (loud cries of" 014," and" Order").—The Speaker took no notice of this remark.—On a division the motion was rejected by 130 votes to 64.—The House then pro- ceeded to consider the vote as amended by the Govern- ment Committee. Various amendments were moved and rejected after discussion, notwithstanding that Mr. At- kinson repeatedly attempted to divide the House, but was unable to do so for lack of a teller. GREAT WESTERN RAILWAY BlLL.—This bill was read a third time after discussion on an amendment by Sir M. H. Beach, which was agreed to. _ _
• SALARIES OF OFFlciAis.—Reductions were moved on certain of these salaries but rejected, and another was withdrawn.

LOCAL NEWS.

A SHOCKING SIGHT. A Rochester publican named Charles Hatnbers Clank rnitted suicide on Wednesday morning at Hawkhursts Kent, by cutting his throat. When discovered his wife was found lying insensible across her husband's be* bathed in his blood, apparently having swooned when she saw what he had done. . A NEW LONDON INSTITUTION. The Prince and Piincess of Wales drove from Marlborough House to New Cross, on Wednesday afternoon, and opened the Goldsmiths Company's Technical and Recreation Institution, founded at a cost to the Geld' smiths Company of £280,000. An address was presented to the Prince, who replied, and declared the buildinB open. • LANCASHIRE AND CRESFIIRE CON- FERENCE ON RAILWAY RATES. • A special meeting of the Lancashire and Cheshire Co_vn- ference on Railway Rates and Charges (representing 60 corporations and a population of nearly 2,000.000) was held at the Town Hall, Manchester, on Tuesday after noon, Alderman Sir John Harwood presiding. The following resolutions were adopted :- 1. That this Conference deeply regret, owing to the manner in which the arguments of counsel and state- ments of witnesses tendered on behalf of this Conference have been received and dealt with, that they have been placed under the necessity of withdrawing from the plc- ceedings before the Joint Committee in Parliament. ' 2. That, under the circumstances, the Conference ' must appeal to their representatives in Parliament with a view to securing the due consideration of the intereste , of the traders in this most important matter. 3. That an appeal bemade to all the members of Par liament and county members of Lancashire and Cheshire, asking them to support the case of the Con" ference in Parliament when the several ragway BillS come under the consideration of the House of Conr mono. 4. That the Chairman of the Conference be requested ti send to the mayors of all the boroughs of the united Kingdom a like request, giving them notice of the thne when the several railway Bills come under the considera- tion of the House of Commons. 5. That a meeting of the Conference and Exeeutfve Committee be held by adjournment in London at the Westminster Palace Hotel on Thursday text, at noon, when the attendance of members of .Parliament is hr vited. It was pointed out that as the proposed new rates were' not intended to come into operation until 1893, Parlia- ment might very well be asked not to deal with the Bine until next year rather than run the risk of legislating tat hastily.

SHOCKING ACCIDENT TO A WORKMEN'S TRAIN. TEN MEN KILLED. PRESBURG, THIIRSDAT.—A deplorable accident to a workmen's train occurred near here yesterday. in con- sequence Of a landslip the train was precipitated down an embankment and was smashed to pieces. Ten men were killed and a large number injured, some of them seriously.

MANCHESTER TRADE, -FRIDAY. - Cotton is steadier ap- parently in Liverpool, and the estimate has been raised from 8.000 to 7,000 bales, but what can permanently help cotton - so long as the weather keeps good? Yarns are no better. Spinners are eager to sell, but manufacturers buy only as they need, and at the moment their needs are rather small. There is said to be a small bundle trade doing at low prices. The workable cloth demand is not perceptibly better. Printers are dull and somewhat irregular.
